not_worth_it.title: LowDelayVBR with MaxBitRate = 1.5x mean (airhand mf.rs:522-535)
not_worth_it.reason: Rejected by L on its merits. It replaces the per-frame CBR budget that the measured `nominal` rate model and the one-way latch rest on (qos.rs). VBR banks bits on still content and spends them in bursts, which risks false latches and longer transmit time near link capacity. airhand itself falls back to CBR wherever the mode is refused. No gain has been shown.

not_worth_it.title: Long-term reference recovery (airhand mf.rs:395-418, 541-553, 804-817)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper sends video on one reliable, ordered stream. A frame is lost only where pb-mapper drops one itself, which is rare by design, and every recorded run shows 0 resync drops. Without B's per-frame streams, which were withdrawn after measurement, LTR replaces a rare IDR. Its costs are per-vendor trust, a viewer gap-decode check and a helper bump. The effect stays negligible (C critique).

not_worth_it.title: Raise thread C or the capture thread to ABOVE_NORMAL (airhand capture/mod.rs:729-739, pipeline.rs:176)
not_worth_it.reason: This is F, withdrawn after measurement: no gain under an all-core load. No design here removes that result, so it stays withdrawn. GPU scheduling priority (R3-gpu-priority) is a different mechanism and is proposed separately.

not_worth_it.title: Dirty and move rects from GetFrameDirtyRects / GetFrameMoveRects
not_worth_it.reason: airhand does not use them either. Hardware encoders already code unchanged macroblocks almost for free. Converting only the dirty region would need a persistent NV12 target, which conflicts with the rotating MF sample pool. ROI QP has no portable MF property across NVIDIA, Intel and AMD.

not_worth_it.title: AccumulatedFrames and other frame-info metadata
not_worth_it.reason: These only count presents coalesced between acquires. Beyond a diagnostic they would change no frame, latency or bit.

not_worth_it.title: Keyed-mutex texture sharing for cross-adapter encoding on hybrid laptops
not_worth_it.reason: Capture, conversion and encoding share one device, and MFTEnum2 already filters by the capture adapter's LUID (codec.rs:84-104). Sending frames to another GPU's encoder would add a PCIe copy and cross-adapter synchronisation to every frame, for an encoder that is not clearly better.

not_worth_it.title: CPU conversion and software-encoder fallbacks (airhand mf.rs:764-795, encoder/software.rs)
not_worth_it.reason: These are slower paths for machines without a D3D11 video processor or a hardware MFT. pb-mapper requires both, and JPEG remains its compatibility path. They would add no performance where hardware exists.

not_worth_it.title: Pool the per-frame output samples (codec.rs:326-337)
not_worth_it.reason: The allocation happens only for MFTs that do not provide their own samples. It is a VirtualAlloc of a few tens of microseconds plus page faults on the bytes actually written, which is negligible next to a 1.6-3 ms encode.

not_worth_it.title: Synchronous encode with a GetEvent spin of 250 us (airhand mf.rs:710-735, 825-840)
not_worth_it.reason: airhand blocks its encoder thread until each unit is out. pb-mapper's pipelined async MFT with ENCODER_DEPTH already overlaps encodes. Only the prompt wake is worth taking, and R3-mf-output-events does that event-driven rather than spinning.

not_worth_it.title: A smoke-test encode at open (airhand mf.rs:637-651)
not_worth_it.reason: It catches an encoder that never asks for input in milliseconds rather than at FIRST_SUBMIT_WAIT (3 s). Such failures are rare, and the H.265 process latch already turns the codec off after the first one. Encoding a frame in every probe would add start-up time to every session.

not_worth_it.title: Shrink the VBV (CODECAPI_AVEncCommonBufferSize) to about one frame
not_worth_it.reason: airhand does not do it. It would bound each unit's transmit time, but cost the quality of IDRs and of the first frame after a large change, and no MF property guarantees vendors honour it. Send credit already bounds queueing. The trade-off is not clearly positive.

not_worth_it.title: Intra refresh or slice output instead of whole-frame IDRs and units
not_worth_it.reason: There is no portable MF property for gradual intra refresh, and IDRs are rare and coalesced on a reliable stream. Hardware MFTs return whole access units, so sub-frame output saves at most a fraction of a 1-3 ms encode.

not_worth_it.title: Hand the worker's private pipe straight to the host, skipping the service relay
not_worth_it.reason: After R3-helper-pipe-transfer and R3-helper-push, the relay costs one extra hop of tens of microseconds per message. Removing it would take away the service's mediation of revocation and session watch at the privilege boundary.

not_worth_it.title: Virtual display driver for monitor-off sharing and privacy mode (airhand e25862e)
not_worth_it.reason: It is a new capability that installs a third-party IddCx driver, not a performance change to an existing capture path.

not_worth_it.title: Pre-warm Media Foundation when sharing starts
not_worth_it.reason: It would save only the cold part of the first connection's encoder build (measured 280 ms cold against 200 ms warm, docs/remote-desktop.md:1415-1420), once per process. Meanwhile an idle host with no viewer would hold the runtime, which goes against #62's no-idle-work goal.

critique.area: R3: Windows host capture and encoding after #62 (DXGI capture, video processor, Media Foundation encoder, helper pipe, thread C capture)

reviews.factual_errors:
- Line drift: HELPER_PROTOCOL is at platform/windows/helper/mod.rs:129 and the helper pipe name at :137, not 127 and 135. background.rs:8 is correct.
- The platforms list includes macos-host, but the design dates only DXGI pictures. The Mac gains nothing until the macOS host area stamps ScreenCaptureKit arrivals (an `arrived` field in platform/macos/capture.rs Latest) and MacVideo implements presented_at. Only the neutral pacer and thread C part is shared.
- The figures (3.23→1.00 ms at 60.00 Hz, 7.54→1.01 ms at 60.05 Hz) come from the E critique's model with the armed tick. They are not measurements, and the proposal hedges them correctly. One addition: a nominal 60.00 Hz panel and Instant differ by tens of ppm (crystal tolerance), so over minutes a panel at pace = refresh passes through both modelled cases. The gain therefore applies to most panels running at pace = refresh, not only to an exact 60.00 Hz.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real and moderate, for pace = refresh: Balanced or Smooth at 60 on a 60 Hz panel, Smooth at 120 on a 120 Hz panel.
- In those cases it removes about 2-6.5 ms of mean present-to-capture wait.
- It also removes the present the grid drops once per drift cycle, a visible hitch.
- No effect when the pace is below the refresh, on much faster panels, or on typing echo; the shipped armed tick already covers echo.
- Through the helper it works only once the protocol-11 field exists.
- It complements R3-dxgi-present-waiter rather than duplicating it: a push source whose present lands just before the grid tick still waits for pacer.next(). The Mac has the same sawtooth.
reviews.corrected_design:
Keep the researcher's pacer, seam and thread C design: `anchored`, earliest(), consume(now, presented) with clamping, and submitted_picture_at forwarded in all five deny(missing_trait_methods) impls (backend.rs:228, native.rs:114 and 422, oop/client.rs:237, examples/input_acceptance/guarded.rs:35). Add:

1. Windows stamp
   - Convert LastPresentTime by its age, as airhand clock.rs:44-76 does: QueryPerformanceCounter now minus the stamp, with QueryPerformanceFrequency cached in a OnceLock.
   - A negative age (the read-order race) counts as 0; an age over 1 s gives None.
   - Add the Win32_System_Performance feature.
   - std's Instant is QPC-based on Windows, so the conversion is exact up to read skew.

2. latest_at
   - Keep latest_at beside latest_pending.
   - A picture left pending by Full or an empty allocator keeps its old stamp. consume drops it once it is older than a period, which falls back to the grid. That is correct.

3. Sample times
   - Use the present Instant, kept strictly increasing, for pts_us and the sample duration of fresh pictures; repeats use now.
   - Durations then follow the display's cadence instead of poll jitter, which matters to any timestamp-budget MFT.

4. Measurement counter
   - Add `coalesced_presents`, the sum of AccumulatedFrames - 1 over fresh acquires, to Statistics and video_bench.
   - It counts directly the presents the pacing skipped, the dropped present this change removes. This is the one real use of AccumulatedFrames.

5. Helper
   - Add presented_ago_us to the Video reply, and to the Fresh push of R3-helper-push.
   - Make it one HELPER_PROTOCOL 11 bump, shared with R3-helper-push and R3-av1-encode.
   - The host converts the age against its receive Instant and ignores ages over 1 s.

6. Diagnostics
   - A once-a-second debug event `desktop_capture_pacing`: present-to-submit p50/p95, coalesced presents/s and empty polls/s, using reused buffers.

7. Docs
   - Reword rule 2 (docs/remote-desktop.md:1218-1220) and the host paragraph. Keep its sub-rules: skips only for backpressure, the long-run rate, the 3/4-period floor and the ≤1/64 creep.

The macOS arrival stamp is left to the macOS host area.
reviews.invariant_risks:
- No desktop wire or ALPN change.
- The Response field needs HELPER_PROTOCOL 11 with both `.v11` pipe names, shared with the other protocol-11 items. Both ends bound the age at 1 s.
- Backend gains a provided method, which every forwarder must forward.
- Thread C keeps calling its Backend statically.
- A dated source may run up to 1/64 above the QoS pace; document it.
- checked_sub only, no unwrap.
- The Windows code compiles only on the CI runner.

reviews.factual_errors:
- "0.5-1.3 ms sooner per frame" overstates the gain. The first drain comes 2 ms after the submit, but from then on the worker's long-poll collects with 1 ms sleeps (oop/server.rs:276-293). Today's pickup therefore lags completion by about 0.35 ms for NVIDIA's 1.65 ms 1080p encodes and about 0.9 ms for 3.1 ms 4K encodes. Push saves roughly 0.3-1 ms.
- The long-poll is bounded by min(4 ms, time to the next tick) and returns as soon as a unit is out (worker/capture.rs:362-381). The input lane typically waits under 1-2 ms; 4 ms is the worst case, with slow encoders.
- Five desktop verifications is right for a submitting Video request: context 1, capture_video 2, cursor 2. A drain request costs three.
- The interim Fresh source ("AcquireNextFrame(0) on the worker every 2 ms") needs a new acquire-only VideoSource method, because capture_video drains and submits in one call. Stream.hot_ms exists only for that interim.
- The worker's timer guard follows Video-request recency (helper/worker.rs:16 and 111-125). With pushes it should follow Stream{on}.
reviews.corrected_design:

- If neither usage gives acceptable text, a shader area-filter downscale into an intermediate BGRA texture, followed by a 1:1 video-processor conversion, is the follow-up. It is not part of this item.
reviews.invariant_risks: None beyond possibly slower processing on some iGPUs, which the gate catches. The code compiles only on CI.

reviews.factual_errors: None. codec.rs:227 sets 0 and ignores the result; airhand sets 60 at encoder/mf.rs:539-540.
reviews.effect_assessment: Likely real quality per bit on vendors whose higher-complexity presets stay fast: NVIDIA's 1.65 ms at 1080p leaves headroom. The cost is added dwell, which goes straight into latency. Both are unknown until measured, so adopt it per vendor.
reviews.corrected_design:
- Take QualityVsSpeed from EncoderSettings and set it where it is set today, before the media types. Read it back and log it.
- Add `--qvs` to video_bench.
- Choose a per-vendor default by MFT friendly name, only where the device run shows lower mean QP or higher PSNR at equal bitrate, with dwell p95 at most a quarter of the frame period at the session's largest size and pace (4.2 ms at 4K60). Otherwise keep 0.
reviews.invariant_risks: Added dwell may lower fps on iGPUs; the per-vendor gate covers it. The code compiles only on CI.

missed.title: Keep the capture tick armed while an MFT holds a unit and has not yet asked for input, instead of spending it as backpressure
missed.design:
Today: Encoder::submit returns Full whenever `need_input == 0` (video/mod.rs:506-508), and Full spends the tick (mod.rs:108-116). The picture stays in DXGI until the next grid tick, a full period later.

The code itself says some MFTs send METransformNeedInput only once ProcessOutput releases their previous output (mod.rs:481-484). For those, a unit that takes longer than about a period halves the frame rate:
- the tick finds no NeedInput and is spent;
- the next submit comes a whole period later, instead of when the encoder frees up.

Change:
- Add `Submit::Waiting`, whose spends_tick() is false, for `need_input == 0 && pending.len() < MAX_IN_FLIGHT`. It returns before any acquire.
- Full remains for MAX_IN_FLIGHT and for an empty allocator.
- Thread C then retries at its 2 ms armed poll today, or at once when R3-mf-output-events wakes it on NeedInput.
- The helper needs no change: v10's submitted:false already means "keep the tick armed".
- An MFT that never asks is still failed by FIRST_SUBMIT_WAIT (unsubmitted, mod.rs:630-636).
- Add a Statistics counter of Waiting results.
missed.expected_effect:
Only on serializing MFTs whose encode time e lies between about one and two periods, such as 4K60 or 1440p120 on an iGPU, or 1080p120 on older iGPUs:
- unique fps goes from 1/(2p) to about 1/e, up to about 2×;
- the picture no longer waits a full period.

No effect on pipelined encoders such as NVIDIA's at 1080p60. Whether any vendor serializes this way is shown by the new counter.
missed.verifiable_here: ci-build-only

missed.title: Crop the odd column or row instead of resampling the whole picture when the only size change is rounding to even (airhand crop_only)
missed.design:
Today:
- scaled_size (qos.rs:161-182) rounds the encoded size down to even.
- For a desktop with an odd dimension that needs no downscale, such as 1365×767 under 1080p limits, the encoded size is 1364×766.
- The video processor scales the full source rect (converter.rs:68-89) by a factor of about 0.999. That resamples every pixel at a drifting phase, so text towards the middle of the screen is half-pixel blended.

airhand crops instead (encoder/mod.rs:149-151, encoder/mf.rs:221-235).

Change:
- Add a neutral `crop_only(input, output)` beside scaled_size: true when each input dimension is at most 1 above the output's.
- When it holds, Converter::new sets the source rect to (0, 0, width, height), using rotated dimensions under R3-rotated-display, so the video processor copies 1:1 and drops the last column or row.
- Input mapping is unchanged: the Display keeps its geometry, and the missing edge pixel is off-video.
missed.expected_effect: An odd-sized desktop is encoded pixel-exact instead of blurred all over. Odd sizes are rare on physical displays, but common for VM guests with dynamic resizing and for custom resolutions. Only those users see a difference.
missed.measurement_plan:
On this Mac: a unit test of crop_only next to scaled_size's tests.

Windows device or VM with an odd custom resolution (e.g. 1365×767):
- `video_bench --output` with the GDI-text pattern, before and after;
- PSNR against the captured source cropped to the encoded size.
missed.verifiable_here: ci-build-only

missed.title: Skip the helper worker's cold H.265 probe on later sessions by caching its answer in the host process per adapter and driver
missed.design:
Today:
- Every privileged session runs in a fresh worker process.
- When the viewer offers h265, that worker probes H.265 cold before Accepted (Request::H265, oop/server.rs:162-169): 320-350 ms in a fresh process.
- Then it builds the session's encoder (about 200 ms warm).
- The in-app backend caches per adapter (probe.rs PROBED), but no worker lives long enough to benefit.

The host process (the app, or the background host) does outlive sessions.

Change:
1. The worker's Start answer reports the capture adapter's LUID and driver version in StartCaps (protocol 11, shared bump; cheap DXGI queries).
2. RemoteBackend keeps a process-wide cache (LUID, driver version) → h265. describe(true) answers from it without sending Request::H265.
3. A miss probes as today and fills the cache.
4. H265_FAILED, which thread C already sets when the worker reports EncoderFailed{H265}, also clears that cache entry.
5. A wrong cached answer costs what a failed H.265 build costs today: one capture_failed and a reconnect to H.264.
missed.expected_effect:
Every privileged session start or reconnect after the first in a host process, with an H.265-capable viewer, reaches its first picture about 0.2-0.3 s sooner.
- Today: probe about 320 ms plus build about 200 ms.
- After: one cold build of about 280 ms.

That is an estimate from the documented times. Reconnects after a network blip benefit the most.
missed.measurement_plan:
On this Mac: oop client tests in which a second RemoteBackend with the same LUID and driver sends no H265 request; a different driver probes again; H265_FAILED clears the entry.

Windows device, privileged sharing: time from connect to first unit, for a first and a second session in the same app run, before and after.
missed.verifiable_here: build-and-test-on-this-mac

areas.name: input and cursor path, hosts and viewers

research.area: R4 input and cursor latency end to end (Windows/macOS hosts and viewers, Linux viewer)

candidates.title: Desktop viewers: show host pointer shapes as native OS cursors and switch shapes without waiting for a Flutter frame
candidates.airhand_evidence: client/src/lib/session.ts:788-822 turns every host shape into a CSS `url(png) hx hy` cursor. It is scaled to the picture, clamped to 0.35-2x and at most 128 px, and cached per scale at :815-821. session.ts:832-836 sets it on the picture element, so the WebView shows it as the OS hardware cursor. session.ts:751-777 swaps shapes by slot as they arrive. The painted cursor is never used for the controller.
candidates.pb_current: ui/lib/src/pages/remote/viewer/remote_cursor_layer.dart:46-73 decides what a controlling desktop viewer shows. Only for the named kinds (systemCursorOf, :90-105) does it use this OS's own pointer. `upArrow` and `custom` get SystemMouseCursors.none plus a bitmap that Flutter paints at the local pointer position (_paint :203-221, CustomPaint layer :234-251). That bitmap is repainted on each hover (remote_input.dart:542-547), so it carries Flutter's whole input-to-present latency. Custom shapes are common. The Mac host names only 7 standard cursors (crates/pb-mapper-desktop/src/platform/macos/cursor.rs:134-142), so open or closed hand, context menu, drag and diagonal or column resize are `custom`, as is every app cursor. The Windows host names 14 shared handles (platform/windows/cursor.rs:20-35), so every HCURSOR an app loads itself is `custom`. A shape change reaches the pointer only through several steps: the view poll (desktop_store.dart:411 per frame, :509-517 every 16 ms), then _publishShape (:1930-1960), then a RemotePointerRegion rebuild (remote_cursor_layer.dart:158-182), and finally MouseTracker applies the cursor after the next frame.
candidates.change:
1) Dart: add `RemoteShapeCursor extends MouseCursor` in remote_cursor_layer.dart. Its session (createSession) listens to DesktopCursor.shape and the viewport scale. On activate and on every change it calls the platform directly, with no widget rebuild:
- a named kind calls SystemChannels.mouseCursor 'activateSystemCursor' {device, kind} with the strings SystemMouseCursors uses;
- upArrow or custom calls the native custom cursor below.
RemotePointerLook.of returns this cursor for mouse && controlling && atLocalPointer. Painting stays for viewers that do not control, for touch, and as the fallback when a platform call fails.

2) Bitmap: start from DesktopPointerShape.definition (straight RGBA, desktop_store.dart:1974-1998). Scale it by the picture's scale times devicePixelRatio, clamp the side as airhand does (at most 128 logical px), and cache per (content, scale within 2%), at most 16 like _shapeCache.

3) Windows: no runner code. The Flutter Windows engine already handles 'createCustomCursor/windows' {name, buffer BGRA, width, height, hotX, hotY}, 'setCustomCursor/windows' and 'deleteCustomCursor/windows' on the mousecursor channel (engine shell/platform/windows/cursor_handler.cc:19-42, 78-142). Dart swaps RGBA to BGRA.

4) macOS: add 'cursor_create' {id, rgba, width, height, hot_x, hot_y, scale} and 'cursor_set' {id} to DesktopVideo.swift's pb_mapper/desktop_video channel (:29, :1098). It creates NSCursor(image:hotSpot:) with the image sized in points, caches it by id and calls set(). FlutterView.cursorUpdate: re-sets the engine's last cursor (engine FlutterView.mm:125-139), so while a custom cursor is active the runner re-asserts it from an NSEvent local monitor for cursorUpdate.

5) Linux: add the same methods in desktop_video.cc (kChannel :34, OnCall :381). They call gdk_cursor_new_from_pixbuf and then gdk_window_set_cursor on the FlView's GdkWindow, the same window the engine sets (engine fl_view.cc:160-166).

6) Delete native cursors when evicted and at session end.

Tests: a Dart widget test with a mock SystemChannels.mouseCursor handler (Windows target override) asserting the create and set calls on a shape change with no rebuild; mocked runner channels for macOS and Linux; updated RemotePointerLook tests.
candidates.protocol: none (Dart to runner method channels only; no Rust, FFI or wire change)
candidates.expected_effect:
Estimates:
- While the host shows a non-standard shape, the controller's pointer becomes the OS hardware cursor. That removes Flutter's event-to-present pipeline from pointer motion, about 2 frames (about 30 ms at 60 Hz, about 15 ms at 120 Hz).
- Every shape change, standard ones too, skips the rebuild and the post-frame MouseTracker pass, about 1 frame sooner.
- The effect is frequent with Mac hosts, which name only 7 cursors.
candidates.measure: Before: SchedulerBinding.addTimingsCallback together with PointerEvent.timeStamp gives the event-to-rasterFinish time of the painted cursor; the native cursor has none. Device: film a viewer at 240 fps with a phone while sweeping the mouse over a Mac host showing a custom cursor (open hand, window corner), and count frames between the physical move and the drawn pointer's move, before and after. For shape changes, log the time of _publishShape and of the platform call against the next frame.
candidates.risk:
- macOS: FlutterView's cursorUpdate: can briefly override the runner's cursor, which may flicker.
- Linux: Wayland compositors may limit cursor size.
- Windows: the engine's deleteCustomCursor uses DeleteObject on an HCURSOR (cursor_handler.cc), so a few handles leak.
- The native cursor must be dropped when the pointer leaves the picture, and re-created on zoom.

candidates.title: Windows viewer: hold 1 ms process timer resolution while a viewer session is connected and visible
candidates.airhand_evidence: none as a separate idea. airhand's viewer runs in WebView2/Chromium, whose timers are not tied to the 15.6 ms tick. Its leading-edge move throttle (client/src/lib/input.ts:63, 267-298) is the same mechanism as pb-mapper's gate, and it is precise there.
candidates.pb_current: Dart's move gate is a Timer: `_moveInterval = 4 ms` (ui/lib/src/state/desktop_store.dart:64), armed after each delivered move (:2586-2600) and flushing the newest pending move when it fires (:2641-2647). The view leaf carries cursor shapes, peer cursors and status when no video frame is drawn, and is polled by Timer.periodic(_viewTick = 16 ms) (:63, :509-517). Only host thread C raises Windows' timer resolution, while capturing (crates/pb-mapper-desktop/src/worker.rs:877; timer.rs:1-22; platform/windows/timer.rs:46-80). The viewer process never does, and the Flutter Windows engine has no timeBeginPeriod call (none in engine shell/platform/windows). Dart wakes its timers from the VM event handler's completion-port wait, so on Windows they expire on the process's 15.6 ms tick (estimate). This is the same mechanism timer.rs:1-7 documents for tokio and quinn timers.
candidates.change:
1) In crates/pb-mapper-desktop/src/viewer/mod.rs, give Viewer a `parking_lot::Mutex<Option<TimerResolution>>`. It is taken after Accepted in connect (~:443), dropped in pause (:853), taken again in resume (:868) and dropped on disconnect or Drop.
2) The macOS `timers::acquire` is a host NSActivity that disables display sleep (platform/macos/timer.rs), so add `TimerResolution::hold_for_viewer()` mapping to a new `platform::timers::acquire_viewer`/`release_viewer` (platform/mod.rs:59-69):
- Windows: the existing counted acquire (timeBeginPeriod(1) plus the EcoQoS and timer-throttling opt-out);
- macOS and Linux: no-op.
3) Test on Windows CI by extending platform/windows/timer.rs's sleep_2ms median test: a viewer guard makes a 2 ms tokio sleep finish under 5 ms.
candidates.protocol: none
candidates.expected_effect:
Estimates:
- Dart's 4 ms trailing gate fires 4-5 ms after arming instead of 4-19.6 ms (mean about 11.8 ms on a 15.6 ms tick). A 500-1000 Hz mouse then drives the host at a steady 220-250 moves/s instead of about 85/s spaced irregularly 4-20 ms apart. That spacing jitter shows as uneven drags and beats against a 60 or 120 fps capture.
- Coalesced moves leave about 7 ms sooner on average.
- The 16 ms view poll ticks every 16 ms instead of 16-31 ms.
- The viewer's tokio and quinn timers (writer deadlines, QUIC ACK and pacing) get 1 ms granularity.
- Cost: some power, only while a session is visible.
candidates.risk:
- Power: limited to connected and not paused. Windows 11 ignores the request for an occluded or minimized window anyway.
- The Dart timer granularity on Windows is inferred, not measured. If the Dart VM already raises it, nothing changes, so measure first (cheap).

candidates.title: High-resolution (pixel) scrolling: 1/120-notch wheel input negotiated by capability, injected smoothly on Windows and macOS hosts
candidates.airhand_evidence:
- crates/airhand-proto/src/session.rs:905-911: `Wheel { dx: i16, dy: i16 }`, 120 = one notch.
- Viewer client/src/lib/input.ts:518-530: every wheel or trackpad delta becomes 1/120 units (deltaMode-aware) with a fractional carry.
- macOS host client/src-tauri/src/host/input/macos.rs:322-349: posts CGScrollEventUnit::Pixel with a carry, on a source whose pixels_per_line is set (:171-174, :24).
- Windows host input/windows.rs:152-162: SendInput MOUSEEVENTF_WHEEL/HWHEEL with the raw delta.
candidates.pb_current:
- Wire: `Input::Wheel { horizontal, vertical }` carries whole notches (crates/pb-mapper-desktop/src/input/mod.rs:43-46), clamped to ±100 (ui/lib/src/state/desktop_input.dart:151-170).
- Viewer: accumulates 30 px per notch and sends only whole notches (remote_surface.dart:19, :230-238), for wheel signals (:199-211) and trackpad pan/zoom (:215-226).
- Windows host: injects notches through enigo, 120 per notch (platform/windows/input.rs:64-76).
- macOS host: posts CGScrollEventUnit::Line, one line per notch (platform/macos/input.rs:313-329).
candidates.protocol:
- Capability `wheel_hires` in Accepted.capabilities.
- New `Input::Scroll {horizontal, vertical, continuous}` (1/120 notch), sent only to a host that listed it.
- StartCaps.hires_wheel.
- HELPER_PROTOCOL 11 with .v11 helper and background pipes.
- No FFI export change: the existing `input` op carries Input JSON.
candidates.expected_effect: Estimate. Trackpad, precision-touchpad and free-spinning-wheel scrolling moves remote content on every viewer event (60-120 Hz) by the distance the fingers moved. Today it moves by one whole notch (about 3 lines on a Windows host) per 30 px of finger travel, so inertial scrolls arrive as jumps. Mac viewers mostly use trackpads; Windows precision touchpads arrive in Flutter as pan/zoom; GTK smooth scroll on Linux benefits the same way.
candidates.measure:
Device:
- On a Windows host, a test window logs WM_MOUSEWHEEL deltas and times (the owned Tk fixture style of docs/validation/desktop-input-backpressure.md) while 300 px are scrolled on a Mac viewer's trackpad. Compare the message count and delta distribution before and after.
- On a macOS host, an NSView logs scrollWheel: deltaY and hasPreciseScrollingDeltas.
Here: cargo test -p pb-mapper-desktop --all-features and flutter test for the Rust and Dart parts.
candidates.risk:
- Legacy Windows apps that integer-divide by 120 ignore sub-notch scrolls until 120 accumulate, as they already do with precision touchpads.
- Mouse wheels must keep their discrete feel (continuous = false).
- The helper protocol bump means the service and app update together, as with every bump.

candidates.title: Windows host: keep the display and system awake while a viewer session runs, as the Mac host already does
candidates.airhand_evidence: client/src-tauri/src/host/power.rs:1-20 explains that once a Windows display turns off, desktop duplication delivers no new pictures and a viewer that only watches freezes, and that Modern Standby sleeps the session. power.rs:70-104 holds PowerCreateRequest + PowerSetRequest(PowerRequestDisplayRequired, PowerRequestSystemRequired) for the life of a session, and power.rs:131 wakes the display once at session start.
candidates.pb_current:
- The macOS host keeps the display awake while capturing (platform/macos/timer.rs acquire: NSActivityOptions::IdleDisplaySleepDisabled), held by thread C (worker.rs:874-878).
- The Windows guard only sets timer resolution and opts out of power throttling (platform/windows/timer.rs:46-80). Nothing in crates/ or ui/ calls PowerSetRequest or SetThreadExecutionState.
- Remote moves use SetCursorPos (platform/windows/input.rs:53-58), which is not an input event. A controller who only moves the pointer neither resets the idle timer nor wakes a display that is off; only buttons, wheel and keys (enigo SendInput) do.
candidates.change:
1) Add a counted guard in platform/windows (a new power.rs):
- the first holder calls PowerCreateRequest (simple reason string) and PowerSetRequest for DisplayRequired and SystemRequired;
- the last holder calls PowerClearRequest and closes the handle.
2) Hold it where the backend runs, so the request comes from the interactive session on both paths:
- in process: inside the Windows timers guard held by thread C while capturing (worker.rs:877, platform/windows/timer.rs:46), mirroring macOS;
- background service: in the helper worker from Start until Close (oop/server.rs), since thread C runs in session 0 there.
3) On acquisition, wake an already dark display once with a zero-distance relative SendInput. The opt-in injection regression already sends such a move (docs/validation/desktop-input-backpressure.md).
candidates.protocol: none (the helper worker acts on its existing Start and Close; no new request)
candidates.expected_effect:
- For a watcher, the picture no longer freezes at the host's display-off timeout (often 5-15 min).
- A Modern Standby laptop no longer sleeps mid-session.
- A controller who only moves the pointer keeps the host awake.
- The effect is large when the timeout would hit, and costs one request handle per session otherwise.
candidates.measure: Windows device: set the display-off timeout to 1 min, connect a view-only viewer to a changing screen and watch for 3 min. Before, the picture freezes and received_fps falls to 0. After, it keeps updating. `powercfg /requests` lists DISPLAY and SYSTEM entries while connected and none after.
candidates.risk:
- Battery: keeps a laptop awake while someone views, as the Mac host does.
- A lid close or a Sleep chosen by the user still wins.
- Every session end path must clear the request, which the guard's Drop covers, panic unwind included.

candidates.title: Host: read the pointer's shape 2 ms after an injected move instead of waiting for the 16 ms cursor clock
candidates.airhand_evidence: client/src-tauri/src/host/capture/dxgi.rs:601-630: the capture call that sees a pointer update also reports visibility and a new shape (DXGI PointerShapeBufferSize/LastMouseUpdateTime). pipeline.rs:254-282 sends that cursor change as soon as the capture slot reports it; no separate cursor clock delays it.
candidates.pb_current: worker/cursor.rs:11 sets CURSOR_INTERVAL to 16 ms, and sample_cursor (:21-37) reads position and, when negotiated, the shape only when that clock is due. An injected move (worker/control.rs:369, :390-405) makes capture hot (worker/capture.rs:157-164) but leaves cursor_due alone. So a shape an app sets in answer to the controller's move (a hand over a link, an I-beam over text) waits 0-16 ms, about 8 ms on average, before thread C reads it. Through the helper, the worker observes the shape on every Video or Capture answer (oop/server.rs:225-240), which hot polling sends every 2 ms. Thread C still fetches it only on its 16 ms clock (oop/client.rs:272-292).
candidates.change:
1) Engine (worker.rs) gains `shape_due: Option<Instant>`. After a Move from a slot that negotiated cursor_shapes is injected (control.rs:390-405), set shape_due to min(shape_due, now + 2 ms), with one more look at +8 ms for slower apps and at most one pending.
2) worker/cursor.rs gains `sample_shape(now)`. When shape_due has passed it reads backend.cursor() and cursor_shape() and sends a report only if CursorEcho::reshape says the shape changed. CursorEcho::sample already reports a new shape even at the echo position (:196-214). Positions keep the 16 ms clock, so watchers get no more traffic.
3) deadline() (worker.rs:954-993) includes shape_due.
4) Through the helper, cursor_shape() crosses the pipe only when shape_serial moved (oop/client.rs:283-285).

Tests: worker/tests.rs with the synthetic backend and a stepped clock: a shape change 1 ms after a move is reported within about 2 ms (16 ms today); an unchanged shape adds no report; a slot that does not control adds no backend calls.
candidates.protocol: none
candidates.expected_effect: Estimate: hover feedback caused by the controller's own move leaves the host about 6 ms sooner on average (wait from about 8 ms to about 2 ms), in-process and through the helper, on Windows and macOS. Together with R4-native-custom-cursor, the viewer also skips the extra frame. Cost: at most about 250 GetCursorInfo or CGSCurrentCursorSeed reads per second while the pointer moves; no extra wire messages unless the shape changed.
candidates.measure: Here: the stepped-clock worker test for the move-to-shape-report delay, and RUST_LOG=off cargo run --release -p pb-mapper-desktop --example host_send_bench on the moving-pointer case; allocations per frame must stay at about 59.1 (docs/benchmarks/2026-11-24-desktop-pipeline/README.md). Device: log the viewer's cursor-shape number change time against the injected move's send time while hovering links.
candidates.risk: Reads the pointer more often in helper sessions; those reads are cached, with no pipe round trip unless the serial moved. Positions must not be reported more often.

candidates.title: Windows host: inject pointer moves with absolute SendInput instead of SetCursorPos
candidates.airhand_evidence: client/src-tauri/src/host/input/windows.rs:125-131 injects absolute moves as SendInput MOUSEEVENTF_MOVE|ABSOLUTE|VIRTUALDESK, normalized to the virtual desktop by to_absolute (:104-117). :206-226 sends each message's events as one SendInput array.
candidates.protocol: none (Input::Move unchanged; the helper's request and response shapes are unchanged)
candidates.risk:
- Normalization can land 1 px off. The ceil formula and the settle window cover it, and the viewer tolerates 1 px.
- UIPI: an in-process (medium-integrity) host's SendInput is dropped over elevated windows, where SetCursorPos still moved the pointer. A 0 return falls back, but a silent drop may need a GetCursorPos check after the settle window.

candidates.title: Relative pointer mode with pointer lock for apps that hide and recenter the host pointer (games, 3D viewports)
candidates.airhand_evidence:
- crates/airhand-proto/src/session.rs:30-55: absolute vs relative moves, and the auto, desktop and game mouse modes. `InputEvent::MouseDelta` at :891-896; deltas are summed by coalesce at :953-976.
- Viewer client/src/lib/input.ts:1-40: modes and auto-lock rules, with AUTO_LOCK_AFTER_MS = 300 (:58) and ESC_HOLD_MS = 1000 (:65). Pointer lock with unadjustedMovement at :361-380; moveBy at :400-411.
- Hosts: input/windows.rs:136-139 sends relative SendInput MOUSEEVENTF_MOVE; input/macos.rs:236-243 posts MouseMoved at the current point plus the delta, with the delta fields set.
candidates.pb_current:
Only absolute `Input::Move` exists (crates/pb-mapper-desktop/src/input/mod.rs:31-34).
- A Windows host applies it with SetCursorPos, which produces no raw input, so raw-input games and viewports get no motion at all.
- A macOS host posts an absolute MouseMoved whose delta comes from the last injected point (platform/macos/input.rs:275-295).
- When a host app hides and recenters the pointer (FPS games, Blender or CAD orbit with continuous grab), absolute moves fight the recentering: the view jumps, or stops at the picture's edge.
candidates.change:
1) Protocol and host:
- A host capability `relative_pointer` from BackendCaps (Windows and macOS injectors).
- `Input::MoveBy { dx: i32, dy: i32 }` with |d| ≤ 4096, sent only to a host that listed it. Outbound::submit sums a MoveBy onto a tail MoveBy (outbound.rs:249-261).
- Injector::pointer_by: Windows uses relative SendInput MOUSEEVENTF_MOVE; macOS posts MouseMoved at the CGEvent location plus the delta, with MouseEventDeltaX/Y set.
- native.rs maps MoveBy. Thread C records no injected echo for it (worker/control.rs:390-405), so the sampler reports where the OS actually put the pointer.
- The helper protocol bumps, shared with R4-hires-scroll.

2) Viewer runners lock the pointer and read raw deltas, which reach Dart over their channels on the platform thread and leave through the existing `input` op:
- Windows (desktop_key_capture.cpp pattern): ClipCursor to the picture, hide the cursor, RegisterRawInputDevices for WM_INPUT deltas.
- macOS (DesktopVideo.swift): CGAssociateMouseAndMouseCursorPosition(false), NSCursor.hide, and an NSEvent local monitor for deltaX/deltaY. Flutter's positional deltas are zero once the pointer is dissociated.
- Linux (desktop_video.cc): a GTK pointer grab with XInput2 raw motion on X11; zwp_relative_pointer_v1 and zwp_locked_pointer_v1 on Wayland.

3) Dart modes, as airhand's:
- auto: lock when the host's cursor report is hidden while a button is held, or hidden through 300 ms of movement; unlock when it shows and all buttons are up;
- desktop: never lock;
- game: always lock, and the viewer paints the host's reported pointer through the existing RemoteCursorLayer, so the host does not composite it.
A 1 s Esc hold releases the lock.
candidates.protocol:
- Capability `relative_pointer`.
- `Input::MoveBy {dx, dy}`.
- HELPER_PROTOCOL bump with .v<n> on both pipes (one bump if shipped with R4-hires-scroll).
- New runner method-channel methods.
- No FFI export change.
candidates.expected_effect: Apps that hide and recenter the pointer become controllable: raw-input games and 3D viewports on Windows hosts, which get no motion today, and jump-prone ones on macOS. Ordinary desktop use is unchanged, because auto mode stays absolute while the host pointer shows.
candidates.measure: Device: a raw-input test window and a 3D viewport (Blender orbit with continuous grab) on a Windows host, driven from Mac, Windows and Linux viewers; WM_INPUT deltas must arrive and the view rotate smoothly. Also check that Windows' hide-while-typing (the pointer hides, then shows on a move) never triggers auto-lock.
candidates.risk:
- Three runner pointer-lock implementations; on Wayland, the protocols are not wrapped by GTK3.
- Auto-lock can misfire.
- The host's pointer speed and acceleration apply to relative moves.
- An escape out of the lock must always work.

not_worth_it.title: Input as QUIC datagrams
not_worth_it.reason: airhand itself sends input on its reliable, ordered control stream (crates/airhand-proto/src/session.rs:13, 600-606) and uses datagrams only for acks, pings and probes. In pb-mapper the viewer-to-host direction of the one stream carries only small messages, so the only head-of-line case is retransmission of a lost packet. Datagrams would need app-level redundancy and replay rules, and they do not exist over relay TCP or LAN TCP.

not_worth_it.title: A separate bulk lane for cursor images and a control lane ahead of video (airhand session.rs:14-20)
not_worth_it.reason: The session is one tunnel stream (research B). B-send already writes cursor reports and shapes ahead of queued video (session/sender.rs ordering), and the controller's own pointer never waits for the host. What remains is bytes already handed to the transport, which send credit bounds. A second tunnel per session for an occasional shape bitmap is not worth it.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's 8 ms leading-edge move throttle and urgent flush (input.ts:63, 267-298)
not_worth_it.reason: Already achieved: pb-mapper's gate is 4 ms (desktop_store.dart:64), buttons and keys go at once with the pending move first (:2586-2600), and Rust replaces a queued tail move (outbound.rs:249-261). Only the Windows timer granularity under that gate is missing, covered by R4-win-viewer-timer-resolution.

not_worth_it.title: Input age stamp INPUT_MAX_AGE (airhand session.rs:57-61, 783)
not_worth_it.reason: Already covered differently. The host injects only for a presentation produced within 2 s (auth.rs:11, 74-80). An overflowing queue revokes control (outbound.rs:267-275), a full lane ends control (lane.rs:44-59), and barriers drop stale queued input. A second age rule adds nothing measurable.

not_worth_it.title: A dedicated Windows injection thread (airhand input/windows.rs:206-226)
not_worth_it.reason: Input is drained before and after each single capture call (worker.rs:833-856). The installed helper measured 3.1-3.4 ms mean, p95 about 5 ms and max 6.9 ms from viewer send to observed move on one PC (docs/validation/desktop-925-installed-input.json). input_wait p50/p99 is traced against a documented gate that triggers this design. Nothing shows the gate failing, and the gain is bounded by one capture call of about 1-2 ms (estimate).

not_worth_it.title: Coalescing queued moves on the host lane, or batching a drain into one SendInput or one helper request
not_worth_it.reason: The viewer already coalesces to 4 ms and replaces a queued tail move. Dropping intermediate host-side points would cost drawing apps their stroke points. Batching saves microseconds in process and about 0.1-0.2 ms per extra event over the helper pipe, and click or modifier sequences are at most about 8 events.

not_worth_it.title: macOS event source with CombinedSessionState and a zero local-events suppression interval (airhand input/macos.rs:171-174)
not_worth_it.reason: No remote-latency effect. The suppression mostly matters for CGWarpMouseCursorPosition, which pb-mapper never uses; whether posted events suppress local input by default is uncertain. Revisit only if a host owner reports their own mouse freezing while being controlled.

not_worth_it.title: CGWarpMouseCursorPosition instead of CGEventPost for Mac host moves
not_worth_it.reason: Warping generates no mouse-moved events, so hover, tracking areas and drags break. CGEventPost to the HID tap is not a measurable cost at 250 moves/s.

not_worth_it.title: Host composites the pointer into the video (airhand QualitySettings.draw_cursor, session.rs:805-809)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper paints the reported pointer for watchers and would do the same in relative mode (R4-relative-pointer). Compositing costs a GPU pass per frame on DXGI and is only needed for a visible pointer in game mode.

not_worth_it.title: Running the viewer's writer in its own task, or bypassing the loopback TCP pair
not_worth_it.reason: The writer waits behind at most one reader poll, which tokio's coop budget bounds (microseconds normally, about a millisecond after a buffered burst). The loopback hop costs tens of microseconds per message. Neither is visible next to the network leg; both belong to the transport area.

not_worth_it.title: Binary instead of JSON for the Dart-to-Rust input FFI
not_worth_it.reason: About 20-50 µs on the UI thread per call at most 250 calls/s (estimate); no latency effect.

not_worth_it.title: Back and forward mouse buttons (airhand MouseButton::Back/Forward)
not_worth_it.reason: A feature gap (pb-mapper's Button is Left, Right, Middle at input/mod.rs:68-73), not a performance item. It is a small, separate capability change.

not_worth_it.title: Bypassing GTK motion compression on the Linux viewer
not_worth_it.reason: The Linux viewer's local pointer is the hardware cursor anyway. GTK delivers motion once per frame-clock cycle, and bypassing that would need XInput2 or Wayland raw events in the runner for at most a frame on one viewer. The effect on remote moves is speculative.

critique.area: R4 input and cursor latency end to end (Windows/macOS hosts and viewers, Linux viewer)

reviews.factual_errors:
1) The Windows engine path is not a good base. Its createCustomCursor/windows builds the AND mask with a GetPixel/SetPixel loop over every pixel (engine shell/platform/windows/cursor_handler.cc:230-262, GetPixel at :249). A 128 px shape costs about 32k GDI calls on the platform thread, which also runs Dart under the default merged-thread policy. Its deleteCustomCursor calls DeleteObject on an HCURSOR (:177), so every eviction leaks the handle.
2) The macOS viewer is worse off today than the proposal says. The macOS engine maps only 21 kinds (FlutterMouseCursorPlugin.mm:33-56) and falls back to the arrow for any other (:58-61). So systemCursorOf's wait, progress, help, move, resizeUpLeftDownRight and resizeUpRightDownLeft (remote_cursor_layer.dart:90-105) all show as a plain arrow on a Mac viewer. A Windows host's busy, move and diagonal-resize cursors are never seen there. The fix must therefore map kinds per viewer OS, not only for upArrow/custom.
3) macOS: FlutterView.cursorUpdate: re-sets _lastCursor immediately and again on the next run-loop turn (FlutterView.mm:125-139). An NSEvent cursorUpdate monitor would race that deferred re-set. Updating _lastCursor through the view's didUpdateMouseCursor: (:115-117) avoids the race.
4) The proposal misses that the painted layer schedules a Flutter frame on every hover event. DesktopCursor.moveTo notifies (desktop_store.dart:178-184), and RemoteCursorLayer repaints from input.cursorChanges (remote_cursor_layer.dart:239-244) even when it paints nothing. That is covered as missed item R4-no-frame-per-hover.
5) Engine citations come from the local Flutter 3.50 engine; re-check them against CI's 3.44.9.
reviews.effect_assessment:
The effect is real, and large while it applies.
- Today a controlling desktop viewer over a custom or upArrow shape hides the OS pointer and has Flutter paint the bitmap at the last hover position. That pointer trails the hand by Flutter's event-to-present pipeline, about 1.5-3 refreshes (25-50 ms at 60 Hz, about half that at 120 Hz). It feels floaty next to the hardware cursor the user sees over named shapes.
- It happens often. Mac hosts name only 7 standard cursors (platform/macos/cursor.rs:134-142), so open or closed hand, context menu, drag-copy and the window-corner resize cursors are custom. Windows hosts name 14 shared handles (platform/windows/cursor.rs:20-35); every cursor an app loads itself (browser grab, Office, Adobe, CAD) is custom.
- On a Mac viewer the platform-aware mapping also fixes missing busy, move and diagonal-resize feedback from Windows hosts.
- A shape change skips the MouseRegion rebuild and the post-frame MouseTracker pass, about 1 frame sooner.
reviews.corrected_design:
1) Runner methods. On all three runners, add three methods to the existing pb_mapper/desktop_video channel (DesktopVideo.swift:1098, desktop_video.cpp:1153-1200, desktop_video.cc:367-446). Do not use the engine's Windows methods.
- `cursor_create {id, rgba (straight), width, height, hot_x, hot_y}` (sizes in physical pixels after Dart's scaling)
- `cursor_set {id}`
- `cursor_delete {id}`

2) Windows runner.
- Create the cursor with CreateIconIndirect from a 32-bpp top-down DIB section (BGRA) and a 1-bpp mask derived from alpha.
- Delete it with DestroyIcon.
- Show it with ::SetCursor on the platform thread. The engine's WM_SETCURSOR returns TRUE for HTCLIENT without setting a cursor (flutter_window.cc:725-731), so the runner's cursor stays until Dart activates a system cursor, which MouseTracker does on enter and exit.

3) macOS runner.
- Build NSCursor(image:hotSpot:) from an NSImage. The image holds an NSBitmapImageRep at pixel size, and its size and hotspot are in points (pixels / backingScaleFactor).
- Call set().
- If the FlutterView responds to `didUpdateMouseCursor:`, call it with the cursor so the engine's cursorUpdate: restores ours. Otherwise fall back to re-setting from a cursorUpdate local monitor.

4) Linux runner. Use gdk_cursor_new_from_surface (a cairo image surface with the device scale) and gdk_window_set_cursor on the FlView's window, the one the engine uses (fl_view.cc:158-166).

5) Dart.
- Add `RemoteShapeCursor extends MouseCursor`. RemotePointerRegion passes one constant instance while mouse && controlling.
- Its session listens to RemotePointer, DesktopCursor.shape and the viewport scale. On activate and on every change it calls the platform directly, with no rebuild.
- Kinds the viewer OS has: SystemChannels.mouseCursor activateSystemCursor. This mapping is per viewer platform; on macOS, wait, progress, help, move and both diagonal resizes take the bitmap path.
- Kinds it lacks, plus upArrow and custom: the bitmap path. Scale by picture scale × devicePixelRatio, clamped to 0.35-2 and at most 128 logical px (airhand session.ts:802-821). Cache per (content, scale within 2%), at most 16 like _shapeCache. Send cursor_delete on eviction, at session end and on dispose.
- Not atLocalPointer: as today, the local pointer shows the system shape or basic, and the layer paints.

6) Painting stays for viewers that do not control, for touch, and as the fallback when a channel call throws.

7) The Dart desktop_video client and its test fake gain the three methods.

Tests:
- A widget test with mocked mouseCursor and desktop_video channels (target platform overridden per OS): a shape change issues create+set with no widget rebuild; a macOS target sends 'wait' to the bitmap path; eviction deletes.
- Updated RemotePointerLook tests.
reviews.measurement_plan:
On this Mac:
- Build the macOS app; Flutter 3.50 is local, so also note CI's 3.44.9.
- Run `cargo run -p pb-mapper --features desktop --example desktop_ui_host -- --clip clip.h264 --dir target/desktop-ui`. Its pointer bands include resize-nwse and a custom checkered disc, so this needs no Screen Recording permission.
- Connect the app, take control, and sweep the custom and resize bands.

Measure, before and after:
(a) Shape-change latency: the host_shape log line against an os_signpost or log emitted by the runner (after) or by the engine's activateSystemCursor/MouseTracker path (before), on the same clock. Expect at least one frame less.
(b) Painted-pointer latency before: SchedulerBinding.addTimingsCallback paired with PointerEvent.timeStamp, giving event to rasterFinish plus one refresh. After, by construction, no Flutter frame sits in the pointer path. Confirm by eye or with a 240 fps phone video over the custom band.
(c) That a Mac viewer over a 'wait'-shaped band (add one to desktop_ui_host) shows the host bitmap rather than an arrow.

Windows and Linux viewers: CI builds (windows-latest, linux-app). On a device:
- 240 fps video of a sweep over a Mac host's open-hand cursor, before and after;
- on Windows, GetGuiResources(GR_USEROBJECTS) stays flat across 200 shape changes.

reviews.factual_errors:
The premise is wrong. The Flutter Windows engine does raise the timer resolution, outside shell/platform/windows:
- fml/platform/win/message_loop_win.cc:17-31 calls timeBeginPeriod(1) on Windows 10 and later in every fml MessageLoopWin constructor.
- The Windows embedder runs its IO and raster threads on fml threads (shell/platform/embedder/embedder_thread_host.cc:153, :179).
- timeBeginPeriod is per process since Windows 10 2004, so the whole viewer process, Dart VM event handler included, already runs with 1 ms resolution for its lifetime.
- The FFI's tokio and quinn timers live in the same process.
- Windows 11 withdraws the guarantee only when every window of the process is minimized or occluded, and then the viewer pauses anyway.
reviews.effect_assessment: Already achieved by the engine. Dart's 4 ms move gate and the 16 ms view tick already fire at about 1 ms granularity on Windows viewers. A second guard would change nothing.
reviews.measurement_plan: None needed. To confirm on a Windows device, `powercfg /energy` lists the Flutter app's 1 ms timer request with no session open, and a debug Stopwatch histogram of Timer(4 ms) clusters at 4-5 ms.
reviews.invariant_risks: None (not implemented).

reviews.factual_errors:
1) The proposed conversion round(px × 120 / kWheelPxPerNotch) with kWheelPxPerNotch = 30 (remote_surface.dart:19, :229-238) carries over today's per-platform scaling error. A Flutter viewer's wheel notch is:
- Windows: lines×100/3 physical px (flutter_window.cc:468-478, :798-808; flutter_windows_view.cc:660-661), so 100/DPR logical at 3 lines;
- macOS: 40 × scrollingDeltaY logical (FlutterViewController.mm:735-757);
- Linux: 53 logical (fl_scrolling_manager.cc:108).
At 30 px per notch, one Windows-viewer notch at 100% becomes 3.33 host notches in an uneven 3,3,4 pattern, and the proposal would send 400 units. See missed item R4-wheel-notch-fidelity.
2) The wire unit needs a precise meaning. airhand's is 120 = one notch = 100 px of continuous travel (UNITS_PER_PIXEL 1.2 and PIXELS_PER_LINE 100/3, airhand host/input/macos.rs:22-25; viewer input.ts:519).
3) The risk note is inaccurate. Legacy Windows apps that compute zDelta/WHEEL_DELTA do not accumulate sub-notch deltas across messages: they drop them, so they may not scroll at all on continuous input. Precision touchpads expose the same behavior, but the risk is real and must be measured, not assumed away.
4) Flutter drops OS momentum on macOS (FlutterViewController.mm:614-625) and DirectManipulation inertia on Windows (direct_manipulation.cc:73, :152). Smooth deltas alone still stop dead when the fingers lift; see missed item R4-trackpad-momentum.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real for trackpad, precision-touchpad and free-spinning-wheel users, who are most Mac viewers and many laptop viewers.
- Today a 30 px trackpad move becomes one whole notch: 3 lines (about 100 px) on a Windows host, or 1 line on a Mac host. Remote content therefore jumps in steps and scrolls about 3x too fast on Windows hosts.
- With 1/120 units, the host content moves on every viewer event (60-120 Hz) by the distance the fingers moved.
- Mac hosts also get IsContinuous, so apps scroll precisely rather than by lines.
reviews.measurement_plan:
Here:
- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`, `cargo test -p pb-mapper-desktop --all-features`; `flutter test` and `flutter analyze` in ui/.
- On this Mac, the macOS viewer against desktop_ui_host:
  - its host_input log must show one Scroll per trackpad event, continuous=true, about 1.2 units per logical px (a 300 px swipe sums to about 360);
  - a mouse-wheel notch must sum to exactly ±120 (before: 1-2 notches per notch).

Device:
- Windows host: an owned Tk or Win32 fixture logs WM_MOUSEWHEEL count and delta while a Mac viewer scrolls 300 px on its trackpad, before (about 10 notches of 120 in bursts) and after (many small deltas).
- Legacy check on a Windows host: a classic Win32 listbox and a Java Swing list must still scroll under continuous input. If either does not, add a viewer setting to turn smooth scroll off.
- macOS host (needs Accessibility): an NSView logs scrollWheel deltaY, hasPreciseScrollingDeltas and isContinuous.

No data-path benchmark is needed: only the viewer-to-host input lane changes.
reviews.invariant_risks:
- The new Input variant reaches only hosts that listed wheel_hires, so deny_unknown_fields stays intact and ALPN is unchanged.
- HELPER_PROTOCOL changes with both .v<n> pipe names, so the service and app update together.
- The viewer-to-host input lane carries no video, so the relay path is untouched.
- Both ends of the helper pipe validate the new variant (Input::validate).

reviews.factual_errors:
1) Waking with "a zero-distance relative SendInput" is unreliable: a zero move may generate no input at all. airhand wakes with a one-shot SetThreadExecutionState(ES_DISPLAY_REQUIRED) without ES_CONTINUOUS (host/power.rs:131-134).
2) In the background path, thread C runs in the service in session 0. The request and the wake belong in the helper worker, which runs in the interactive session; airhand's host runs as SYSTEM in the console session (power.rs:15-17).
3) Holding the request from Start to Close would also keep the display on while the viewer is paused. The Mac host's guard is held only while capturing (worker.rs:874-878).
4) The rest checks out. Nothing in crates/ or ui/ calls PowerSetRequest or SetThreadExecutionState, and the Windows guard (platform/windows/timer.rs:46-80) covers only timers and power throttling.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real.
- A view-only viewer's picture freezes when the host's display-off timeout fires, often after 5-15 minutes; DXGI gets no new pictures.
- A Modern Standby laptop sleeps mid-session, which kills it.
- A controller who only moves the pointer neither resets the idle timer nor wakes the display, because SetCursorPos is not input.
- If the display is already off when a session starts or resumes, waking it gives the first picture without anyone touching the host.
- Cost: one power request per capturing session, like the Mac host's NSActivity.
reviews.corrected_design:
1) platform/windows/power.rs holds a counted guard.
- The first holder calls PowerCreateRequest (simple reason string) and PowerSetRequest for PowerRequestDisplayRequired and PowerRequestSystemRequired.
- The last holder calls PowerClearRequest for both and CloseHandle.
- On every acquisition (session start and resume after pause), it wakes the display once with SetThreadExecutionState(ES_DISPLAY_REQUIRED).

2) In process: take the guard inside the Windows timers::acquire/release (platform/windows/timer.rs), which thread C holds only while capturing (worker.rs:874-878). This mirrors the macOS activity's IdleDisplaySleepDisabled.

3) Background service: the helper worker (oop/server.rs serve, run by platform/windows/helper/worker.rs) takes the guard on the first Capture or Video request. A 1 s watchdog task in the worker drops it 2 s after the last such request, and at Close or pipe loss. No new request is needed, so the helper protocol is unchanged.

4) Drop covers panic unwind.
reviews.invariant_risks:
- OS APIs stay under platform/windows.
- No change to the helper protocol or the wire.
- Battery: the laptop stays awake only while a viewer watches, as on macOS. A lid close or a user-chosen sleep still ends requests.
- Every end path must clear the request (Drop plus the watchdog).

reviews.factual_errors:
1) The citations check out:
- CURSOR_INTERVAL is 16 ms (worker/cursor.rs:11), and sample_cursor reads the shape only when that is due (:21-37).
- An injected move makes capture hot (worker/capture.rs:160-165) but does not move cursor_due.
- Through the helper, Video and Capture answers observe the shape (oop/server.rs:225-240), and thread C fetches it only when shape_serial moved (oop/client.rs:272-292).
2) One correction: every CursorReport carries a position, and the echo and watermark rules live in CursorEcho::sample (:183-212). A "shape-only" report therefore cannot bypass them. On a detected new shape, run the normal per-slot sampling at once, rather than building a separate report path.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real but modest.
- Hover feedback caused by the controller's own move (hand over a link, I-beam over text, resize at a border) leaves the host about 6 ms sooner on average (0-16 ms wait down to about 2 ms), in process and through the helper.
- On a LAN the whole shape path today is roughly 8 ms (host) + network + up to one viewer frame + the MouseTracker frame. This and R4-native-custom-cursor together cut most of it.
- Positions keep their 16 ms clock.
reviews.corrected_design:
1) Engine (worker.rs) gains `shape_due: Option<Instant>`.
- Set it to now + 2 ms after a Move is injected for a slot that negotiated cursor_shapes (worker/control.rs:390-405), only while self.cursor_shapes.
- After that look, allow one more at +8 ms for slow apps.
- At most one is pending; a new move restarts the 2 ms look.

2) worker/cursor.rs gains sample_shape(now). When shape_due passes and the session is not paused or unavailable:
- read backend.cursor() and, if visible, backend.cursor_shape();
- if the shape changed for any cursor_shapes slot (CursorEcho::reshape returns true), run the same per-slot sampling sample_cursor does, then reset cursor_due;
- otherwise do nothing.
Watchers therefore get an extra position report only together with a new shape.

3) deadline() (worker.rs:968-993) includes shape_due.

4) Through the helper, cursor_shape() still crosses the pipe only when shape_serial moved. On Windows the 2 ms hot polling after input refreshes that serial.

Tests (worker/tests.rs, synthetic backend, stepped clock):
- a shape changed 1 ms after a move is reported by about 2 ms (16 ms today);
- an unchanged shape adds no report;
- a slot that does not control, or a session without cursor_shapes, adds no backend calls.
reviews.invariant_risks:
- Thread C still calls its Backend statically, with no new dispatch.
- No wire or helper change.
- At most about 250 extra GetCursorInfo or CGSCurrentCursorSeed reads per second while the pointer moves.
- Positions must not be reported more often than the 16 ms clock except with a new shape.

reviews.factual_errors:
1) "Raw-input consumers see them: 3D viewports, game menus" overstates the gain. An absolute SendInput reaches WM_INPUT as RAWMOUSE with MOUSE_MOVE_ABSOLUTE|MOUSE_VIRTUAL_DESKTOP and 0..65535 coordinates in lLastX/lLastY. Games that read raw deltas as relative misread them; that case needs R4-relative-pointer.
2) UIPI fallback: SendInput blocked by UIPI is not reliably reported ("neither GetLastError nor the return value will indicate the failure was caused by UIPI blocking"), so "fall back when SendInput returns 0" does not catch it. The arrival check must come from the settle logic.
3) Missed benefit: today's SetCursorPos moves always collapse into one WM_MOUSEMOVE at the app's next GetMessage. With MOUSEEVENTF_MOVE_NOCOALESCE on moves made while a button is held, a drawing app gets every 4 ms stroke point.
4) airhand normalizes with round((px − vx) × 65535 / (vw − 1)) (host/input/windows.rs:104-117), not ceil(× 65536 / vw). Either is fine if a unit test proves exact landing on every pixel.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real, as robustness and fidelity; latency is unchanged at one syscall.
- Remote moves become real input: WH_MOUSE_LL hooks see them; GetLastInputInfo idle resets, so presence and inactivity-lock policy, which power requests do not stop, behave as if someone were there; and a dark display wakes on a move.
- Remote drawing gets the full 250 Hz point stream instead of one point per app pump.
reviews.measurement_plan:
Windows device, CI build only:
- Re-run the installed input acceptance of docs/validation/desktop-925-installed-input.json. move_roundtrip and the 30 and 60 Hz movement means must stay at about 3.1-3.4 ms (p95 ≤ 5.1 ms), since SendInput applies asynchronously.
- A RegisterRawInputDevices fixture counts WM_INPUT during remote moves: 0 before, more than 0 after.
- GetLastInputInfo advances on a move-only remote session after the change, not before.
- The Tk fixture counts WM_MOUSEMOVE during a 1 s remote drag at 250 Hz while it sleeps 15 ms per message: about 60 before, about 250 after.
- With a monitor left of the primary, an absolute move lands on its exact pixel.
- With an elevated window in the foreground, an in-process host's moves still arrive (fallback).

reviews.factual_errors:
1) Auto mode cannot rely on host visibility on Mac hosts: the macOS cursor source reports the pointer as shown whenever it is on the shared display (platform/macos/cursor.rs:1-4; airhand has no Mac hidden detection either). There, only the explicit game mode applies.
2) On Windows, WinCursor::read treats a cursor as showing from the flags alone (platform/windows/cursor.rs:58-60). A game that calls SetCursor(NULL) keeps CURSOR_SHOWING with a null hCursor and would never trigger auto mode. airhand counts a null handle as hidden (capture/dxgi.rs:968-975).
3) The Dart move gate keeps only the newest pending DesktopMove (desktop_store.dart:2586-2600, 2631-2647), and a NOT_FRESH refusal keeps the last move for replay (:2653-2663). Applied to MoveBy, both would lose or replay motion; the design must sum deltas and drop stale ones.
4) In relative mode the viewer paints the host-reported pointer. Those reports come from a 16 ms sampler (worker/cursor.rs:11), so the painted pointer would trail by up to 16 ms plus the network.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real for a whole class of apps.
- Raw-input games and 3D viewports on a Windows host get no motion at all today, because SetCursorPos is not input. Apps that hide and recenter the pointer (FPS cameras, Blender or CAD orbit with continuous grab) fight absolute moves on both hosts: the view jumps or stops at the picture's edge.
- Relative moves make these apps usable, as in airhand (proto session.rs:30-55).
- Ordinary desktop use is unchanged, because auto mode stays absolute while the host pointer shows.
reviews.corrected_design:
1) Protocol and host.
- Add capability `relative_pointer` from BackendCaps (Windows and macOS injectors; synthetic too, for desktop_ui_host).
- Add `Input::MoveBy { dx: i32, dy: i32 }` with |d| ≤ 4096, sent only to a host that listed the capability (Viewer::input NotOffered).
- Outbound::submit sums a single MoveBy onto a tail MoveBy (outbound.rs:249-261).
- Injector::pointer_by:
  - Windows: relative SendInput MOUSEEVENTF_MOVE (the OS pointer follows speed and precision settings; raw-input readers get exact deltas);
  - macOS: MouseMoved (or Dragged while a button is held) at the current location plus the delta, with MouseEventDeltaX/Y set and the injector's cached position cleared, as airhand does (input/macos.rs:236-243).
- native.rs maps MoveBy. Thread C records no injected echo for it, and starts the 2 ms hot cursor sample (R4-hot-shape-sample extended to positions after MoveBy) so the painted pointer follows within about 2 ms.
- WinCursor::read reports a null hCursor as hidden.
- HELPER_PROTOCOL bump with .v<n> on both pipes, one bump shared with R4-hires-scroll if they ship together.

2) Dart.
- DesktopStore.send sums MoveBy into the pending slot within the 4 ms gate. NOT_FRESH drops MoveBy rather than keeping it.
- In relative mode the viewer takes every cursor report: no cursor_sequence set-aside, since no absolute move of its own exists. RemoteCursorLayer paints the host pointer, and the OS pointer is hidden and locked.

3) Modes, as airhand's (input.ts:1-40):
- auto: lock when the host reports the pointer hidden while a button is held, or hidden through 300 ms of movement; unlock when it shows and every button is up;
- desktop: never lock;
- game: always lock;
- a 1 s Esc hold releases the lock, and so does focus loss.

4) Runners. Each accumulates raw deltas and posts them at most once per loop turn over its existing channel.
- Windows: ClipCursor to the picture, ShowCursor(FALSE), RegisterRawInputDevices on the top-level window for relative WM_INPUT.
- macOS: CGAssociateMouseAndMouseCursorPosition(false), NSCursor.hide, an NSEvent local monitor reading deltaX/deltaY.
- Linux, X11: gdk_seat_grab with XInput2 XI_RawMotion (adds libxi-dev). Linux, Wayland: zwp_locked_pointer_v1 with zwp_relative_pointer_v1, code generated by wayland-scanner in CMake (adds wayland-protocols to the linux-app CI job).
- Every lock path restores association and visibility on unlock, dispose and focus loss.
reviews.measurement_plan:
Here:
- Rust tests: serde, validation, Outbound summing, a viewer refusing MoveBy to an older host, a protocol bump round trip, the null-hCursor rule as a pure function.
- Dart tests: auto-lock rules, including Windows' hide-while-typing (a pointer that reappears within 300 ms never locks), MoveBy summing in the gate, the NOT_FRESH drop, Esc hold.
- The macOS viewer against desktop_ui_host on this Mac, with relative_pointer listed by the synthetic backend: in game mode, host_input logs MoveBy deltas while the local pointer stays locked and hidden, and an Esc hold restores it.

missed.title: Viewers: one wheel notch on the viewer is exactly one notch on the host (today 3.3x on Windows viewers, about 1.3-1.8x on macOS and Linux, unevenly)
missed.design:
Problem. remote_surface.dart turns every PointerScrollEvent into notches at kWheelPxPerNotch = 30 logical px (:19, :229-238). But each Flutter embedder reports one mouse-wheel notch as a different pixel distance:
- Windows: lines×100/3 physical px (flutter_window.cc:468-478, :798-808; flutter_windows_view.cc:660-661), so 100/DPR logical at the default 3 lines;
- macOS: 40 logical per line (FlutterViewController.mm:735-757);
- Linux: 53 logical (fl_scrolling_manager.cc:108).
At 100%, one Windows notch therefore sends 3,3,4,3... notches (9-12 lines on a Windows host), and macOS and Linux send 1,1,2 and 2,2,1 patterns.

Fix (Dart only, every host, no protocol).
- For a mouse-kind PointerScrollEvent, notches = delta / pxPerNotch, where pxPerNotch is per viewer platform: Windows 100 × lines/3 / devicePixelRatio, macOS 40, Linux 53. The carry stays.
- `lines` comes from a new `wheel_lines` method on the Windows runner's pb_mapper/desktop_video channel, which returns SPI_GETWHEELSCROLLLINES; use 3 if the call fails.
- Trackpad PanZoom and trackpad-kind scroll keep their own distance per notch (30 px today; 100 px = 120 units with R4-hires-scroll).
- Update docs/remote-desktop.md:237-238 and add a CHANGELOG bullet.
missed.expected_effect:
- A mouse-wheel notch scrolls the remote content as far as a local notch would. From a Windows viewer at 100% that is 3 lines on a Windows host instead of 9-12.
- The irregular 3,3,4 and 1,1,2 step patterns disappear, giving even, predictable wheel scrolling on every host, old ones included.
missed.measurement_plan:
Here:
- `flutter test` cases with debugDefaultTargetPlatformOverride for Windows (DPR 1, 1.5, 2), macOS and Linux: one notch event yields exactly one host notch, and N notches yield N.
- With a mouse on this Mac, the macOS viewer against desktop_ui_host: host_input logs one Wheel notch per physical notch (before: 1,1,2 pattern).

Device: a Windows viewer at 100% and 150% against a Windows host's Tk wheel logger, counting WM_MOUSEWHEEL per physical notch, before (3-4 × 120) and after (1 × 120).

missed.title: Viewers: carry a trackpad fling's momentum to the host (Flutter drops OS inertia on every desktop platform)
missed.design:
Problem. Flutter does not forward OS scroll momentum:
- macOS skips momentum-phase events, expecting "the framework" to generate momentum (FlutterViewController.mm:614-625);
- Windows suppresses DirectManipulation inertia updates (direct_manipulation.cc:73, :152);
- GTK and libinput produce none.
pb-mapper reads raw PanZoom events in a Listener (remote_surface.dart:213-226), so no framework momentum exists there either. A fling therefore stops dead on the remote computer when the fingers lift. airhand's Chromium viewer forwards OS momentum as wheel events (input.ts:518-530).

Fix (Dart, in RemoteSurface).
- Track PanZoomUpdate pan deltas with a VelocityTracker (trackpad kind, event timestamps).
- On PointerPanZoomEnd with speed above kMinFlingVelocity, run a Ticker-driven decay with the viewer platform's physics: macOS's 0.998/ms deceleration (as BouncingScrollSimulation's friction), and a ClampingScrollSimulation-like curve on Windows and Linux.
- Each tick sends the integrated delta through _wheelBy: continuous Scroll units with R4-hires-scroll, else notches with the carry.
- Cancel on PointerScrollInertiaCancelEvent (sent when fingers touch again on macOS and Windows), a new PanZoomStart, a pointer down, a discrete wheel event, focus or control loss, or a generation change.
- Outbound summing (R4-hires-scroll) bounds the queue.
missed.expected_effect:
- A trackpad fling keeps scrolling the remote page and decays as it would locally, about 0.5-1.5 s, instead of stopping when the fingers lift.
- Long documents take one or two swipes instead of many.
- It applies to every host, old ones included (as notches); with wheel_hires it is smooth.
missed.measurement_plan:
Here:
- `flutter test` covers the simulation: decay, a total distance within platform bounds, and cancellation on ScrollInertiaCancel, PanZoomStart, down and control loss.
- On this Mac, the macOS viewer against desktop_ui_host: after a fast two-finger swipe, host_input shows a decaying series of Wheel or Scroll events for about 1 s after PanZoomEnd (before: none). A second touch stops it within one event.

Device: a Windows viewer with a precision touchpad, and a Linux viewer with a touchpad, against any host.

missed.title: Viewers: stop scheduling a full Flutter frame on every pointer move when the cursor layer draws nothing
missed.design:
Problem. Every hover or move calls DesktopCursor.moveTo, which notifies (desktop_store.dart:178-184). RemoteCursorLayer's CustomPaint repaints from input.cursorChanges (remote_cursor_layer.dart:239-244) and is always mounted (viewer_stage.dart:228). Each mouse event therefore marks paint and schedules a frame, even when the painter returns null. That happens with RemotePointerPaint.none, the normal case for a controller over a named shape, and for every controller once R4-native-custom-cursor lands. Moving the mouse thus forces a full-window Flutter build and raster, composing the video Texture and overlays, at the display rate (60-120 Hz) even while the host picture is still.

Fix.
- Give RemoteCursorLayer a derived ValueNotifier<RemoteCursorPaint?>, recomputed from viewport, cursorChanges and pointer. It notifies only when the paint result changes (null to null never does), and the painter repaints from it.
- The per-frame view-leaf read (_onFrame, desktop_store.dart:411-415) then loses its hover-driven frames. To keep shape latency, read the leaf from the move gate as well (at most once per 4 ms while the pointer moves; it is a cheap synchronous FFI read) and from the 16 ms timer as today.
missed.expected_effect:
- While the controller moves the mouse over a still picture, the viewer renders frames only when the picture or a painted overlay changes, instead of 60-120 full-window frames per second. That is less GPU work and battery on laptops, with no latency change.
- Shape-change pickup stays at least as fast, through the move-gate leaf read.
