missed.title: macOS host: wake a sleeping display when a session starts or resumes, so the first picture (and therefore input) can arrive
missed.design:
Problem. The Mac host keeps the display awake only while it captures (platform/macos/timer.rs:28-40, NSActivity IdleDisplaySleepDisabled). That prevents idle sleep but never wakes a display that is already asleep. Nothing in crates/ calls IOPMAssertionDeclareUserActivity or checks CGDisplayIsAsleep.

airhand reports that ScreenCaptureKit delivers no picture from a sleeping display, and that on macOS the first frame then never arrives (host/power.rs:1-6, :21-28). In pb-mapper that is worse than a black picture. Input is admitted only for a presented frame produced within 2 s (auth.rs:11, :74-80), so a viewer cannot even wake the Mac by moving the mouse.

Fix, in platform/macos.
- When capture starts or resumes (the timers guard's acquire on thread C), if CGDisplayIsAsleep(bound display), call IOPMAssertionDeclareUserActivity(kIOPMUserActiveLocal) once, as `caffeinate -u` does.
- Also call it when the capture has delivered no frame for 1 s while CGDisplayIsAsleep is true, at most once per 10 s.
- Skip it when the lid is closed and the built-in panel is the only display, as airhand does, to avoid a 10 s wake/sleep loop.
missed.expected_effect: An unattended Mac whose display had slept shows its picture, often the lock screen, within about a second of a viewer connecting or resuming. It no longer stays blank until someone at the Mac touches it, which also unblocks input.
missed.verifiable_here: device-only (clippy and unit tests of the gating logic here)

areas.name: viewer core shared by all platforms

research.area: R5: the shared viewer pipeline (network to native decoder input, and receipts back to the host)
research.summary:
The copy and hop path is already lean; the two real gaps are in what receipts tell the host and in how the viewer's fps cap probes past a slow decoder.

**Path of one video unit (direct QUIC)**
- Copies:
  1. kernel to quinn
  2. quinn to the forwarder's buffer (pb-mapper-protocol buffer.rs:8-16, forward.rs:401-470)
  3. forwarder to loopback TCP (client.rs:580-594)
  4. loopback into rustls, in reads of at most 4 KiB (rustls buffers.rs:220)
  5. rustls plaintext into one Vec per 16 KiB record (common_state.rs:557)
  6. into one BytesMut per unit (wire.rs:195)
  7. one memcpy into the native decoder's buffer at the FFI (desktop_video.rs:225)
  8. Windows only: a second memcpy into an MF buffer (desktop_video.cpp:878-881). Darwin converts to AVCC in place (DesktopVideo.swift:299-335); Linux pulls straight into a pooled GstBuffer (desktop_video_gst.cc:887).
- Thread hops: quinn driver, then the forwarder task, then the viewer session task (reader and writer in one task, viewer/session.rs:211-215), then the sink Condvar (sink.rs:410-412, 666-689), then the native decoder thread, then the platform thread (frame available), then the raster thread, whose acquire is the presentation receipt (DesktopVideo.swift:702-731, desktop_video.cpp:587-626).
- Per-unit locks and allocations (registry, sink, stats and outbound mutexes; a header-sized serde buffer; the payload buffer) add up to well under 0.3 ms of CPU per unit. This is an estimate, and there is nothing there worth changing.

**Receipts today**
- They are sent on arrival: after the whole payload is read and before the sink sees it (viewer/session.rs:317-321).
- They are cumulative and go out ahead of input (outbound.rs:195-197, 315-321).
- The host uses them for send credit (credit.rs:149-273), the ack-queue clamp, the probe-cut witness (session.rs:343-357) and the shadow receipt-rate estimator.
- Every one of those, and the QoS probe controller (qos.rs:466-514, 613-668), works on host-timed round trips.

**Against airhand**
- airhand also acks on arrival. Each ack carries the frame's first-byte arrival time on the viewer's clock (wire.rs:112-125, merge.rs:289-292, airhand-proto session.rs:704-712).
- Its host therefore controls on the one-way queue in the host-to-viewer direction (flow.rs:6-17, 270-331). That queue leaves out the ack's way back and each frame's own transfer time.
- In pb-mapper, a queue on the viewer's upload reads as video congestion. It cuts frame rate and bitrate, and it shrinks the credit window.

**The fps cap problem**
- The viewer fps cap rises by 5 every second after a 3 s hold (fps_cap.rs:13-24, 118-134).
- With a slow decoder this repeatedly overshoots into the sink's 250 ms backlog drop.
- Recorded on this Mac: 3 backlog drops and 3 keyframe requests in 20 s, with a mean pace of 12.4 for a consumer that can decode about 14.9 frames a second (docs/benchmarks/2026-11-24-desktop-pipeline/slow_link.txt:12).
- airhand's flow.rs fixes this pattern for bitrate by remembering the capacity at which it had to cut (flow.rs:580-607).

candidates.title: Stamp receipts and probe echoes with the viewer's arrival time, so the host judges congestion on the queue toward the viewer, not on the round trip
candidates.airhand_evidence:
Each ack carries `arrived`: ControllerDatagram::Ack{seq, arrived} (crates/airhand-proto/src/session.rs:704-712).

How `arrived` is taken: the time after the frame's length prefix is read, which is its first byte, or the end of the previous frame if it was already queued (crates/airhand-link/src/wire.rs:112-125). Merge hands it over as max(arrived, previous handed) (merge.rs:289-292). The controller attaches it to the cumulative ack (controller/mod.rs:727-746).

How the host uses it:
- One-way delay = arrived minus send time.
- Queue = that delay minus a windowed minimum (flow.rs:270-276; WindowMin flow.rs:101-126; MIN_RTT_WINDOW 10 s, flow.rs:71).
- The module doc says this queue excludes the UI hop, the ack's way back and the frame's own transfer (flow.rs:6-17).
- The busy delivery rate comes from the spacing of arrival times (flow.rs:319-331).
candidates.pb_current:
Viewer:
- The reader reads the header (viewer/session.rs:278-288).
- For video it reads the whole payload, then queues `receipt(seq)` (session.rs:317-321).
- For probes it queues `probe(nonce)` (session.rs:363).
- Neither slot holds a time (outbound.rs:111-112, 191-197). The writer sends Received{seq} and ProbeEcho{nonce} (outbound.rs:315-321; protocol.rs:168-178).
- The host writes the video header and payload as one vectored write (wire.rs:103-108), so rustls puts the header in a first record of up to 16 KiB.

Host:
- `book` stamps sent_at (credit.rs:201-216).
- `on_receipt` takes the delay as now minus sent_at (credit.rs:220-273). That delay includes the way back, the viewer's writer and the unit's own transfer.
- `ack_queue` is the median receipt delay minus the probe base RTT (credit.rs:306-331).
- The window uses t = base RTT + 100 ms. Above 100 ms of ack queue it clamps bytes to 1.25 x the delivery rate x t, with a 32 KiB floor (credit.rs:149-184).
- `fits` refuses once more than pace x t frames are unreceipted (credit.rs:189-196).
- The QoS delay is the median probe RTT minus its 60 s minimum (qos.rs:466-514, 613-623; RTT_WINDOW qos.rs:50).
  - Cuts start at 150 ms by RustDesk steps, down to min_fps or half of it (qos.rs:630-668).
  - Bits per frame step down 5-20% per 3 s window from 150 ms (qos.rs:735-743).
  - The ack queue is the cut's witness (session.rs:352-357).
- The shadow ReceiptRate also runs on host-timed receipts (qos/receipt_rate.rs:128).

Result: a queue on the viewer's upload is taken for video congestion.
candidates.change:
Rust only. No FFI, Dart or native-runner change.

1. protocol.rs
- Add `CAPABILITY_ARRIVAL_TIME = "arrival_time"`, listed both ways.
- `Received { seq, #[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")] at_us: Option<u64> }`.
- `ProbeEcho { nonce, at_us: Option<u64> }`, with the same serde attributes.
- at_us is microseconds on the viewer's session clock (an Instant epoch taken in Viewer::start, viewer/mod.rs:388-470), at the moment the reader finished reading that record's header.

2. Viewer
- config.rs:115-129 lists the capability.
- handshake/start keep `arrival_time = accepted.capabilities contains it`.
- Reader::run takes `let header_at = Instant::now()` right after read_header_with returns (session.rs:279-288) and passes it to handle. Reads are sequential, so this equals airhand's max(first byte, previous done).
- Video calls `outbound.receipt(seq, header_at)`; Probe calls `outbound.probe(nonce, header_at)`.
- outbound.rs slots become `receipt: Option<(u64, Instant)>`, which keeps the time of the max seq, and `probe: Option<(u64, Instant)>`.
- `next()` fills at_us only when the host listed the capability.

3. Host writes
- session.rs:201-208 gets `arrival_time: listed(CAPABILITY_ARRIVAL_TIME)`, and Accepted lists it (host/acceptor.rs:284, 362).
- For such a session only, B-send writes a video message as two writes: the header records (write_all), then the payload (write_all_buf), with one flush. The header becomes its own small TLS record, so the viewer stamps the unit's first bytes rather than the end of a 16 KiB record.
- No copy is added. The cost is one extra TLS record and send per unit.

4. New crates/pb-mapper-desktop/src/oneway.rs
- `WindowMin`: a monotone deque of (value, at) over RTT_WINDOW (60 s, the same window as the probe base, so semantics match today).
- Samples are bucketed to one per 250 ms. At most 256 entries are reserved once: a bounded table that allocates nothing per receipt.
- `OneWay { forward: WindowMin, reverse: WindowMin, recent_forward: [i64; 3], recent_reverse: [i64; 3] }`.
- `sample(at_us, sent_host_us, recv_host_us)` returns forward_queue = (at - sent) - min and reverse_queue = (recv - at) - min, both saturating at 0.
- Host times are microseconds since SessionShared.epoch (shared.rs:53).
- A sample more than 1 s below the window's minimum resets it (viewer clock jump).
- `reset()` is called wherever qos.reset_baseline is (session.rs:404-412).

5. credit.rs
- `on_receipt(seq, now, at_us)` computes the newest covered unit's one-way sample. `Receipt` gains `forward_queue` and `reverse_queue` options.
- `ack_samples` store the forward queue when present, so `ack_queue` returns its median with no base subtraction.
- `window()` uses t = base + min(median of the last 3 reverse queues, 1 s) + WINDOW_MARGIN, so receipts held up on the way back no longer block admission. The frame and byte maximums still apply.

6. qos.rs
- `on_probe_echo(nonce, now, at_us, ack_queue)`: with at_us, the probe's forward queue feeds a separate DELAY_HISTORY ring. `delay_ms` and `raw` use it.
- RTT still feeds `rtt`, `base_rtt` and `last_rtt` for the window and the diagnostics.
- The ReceiptRate shadow takes the forward queue and the viewer-clock spacing when present. Those are the inputs a later receipt-driven controller (the deferred stage 1 of the earlier D-fast-rate-control research) would read.

7. Optional diagnostics
- `Stats.forward_queue_ms` and `reverse_queue_ms`, written only to a viewer that listed the capability.
- They reach the quality panel's Network group through the existing viewer_status op: FFI status JSON, Dart DesktopViewerStatus, the panel row and the test fake.

8. Tests
- protocol round trips.
- An old host (no capability) never receives at_us (viewer/tests.rs).
- oneway: minimum tracking, the bound, reset, a negative clock offset.
- credit: reverse delay widens t; the forward queue drives the clamp.
- qos: a reverse-only delay never cuts; a forward delay cuts as today.
- pb-mapper-testkit shaped.rs: per-direction shapes. Today one Shape covers both copies (shaped.rs:55-56); add `shaped_link_each_way(relay, up, down)`.
- Two ignored slow_link cases: `reverse_path_queue_is_not_congestion` and `reverse_queue_with_forward_limit_still_cuts`.

9. Docs and changelog
- remote-desktop.md: Send credit, QoS, Viewer, the capability list.
- A CHANGELOG bullet.
candidates.protocol:
New capability `arrival_time`, listed by the viewer in Authenticate and by the host in Accepted. Only when both listed it:
- ViewerMessage::Received carries an optional `at_us: u64`.
- ViewerMessage::ProbeEcho carries an optional `at_us: u64`.
Both are omitted otherwise.

Optionally, StatsRecord gains `forward_queue_ms` and `reverse_queue_ms` (u32, omitted when unset), written only to a viewer that listed it.

What stays as it is:
- ALPN stays pb-mapper/desktop/2.
- deny_unknown_fields is kept. An old host never sees the field, and an old viewer never gets the Stats fields.
- HELPER_PROTOCOL and the pipe names are unchanged: the helper never sees viewer messages.
- No new FFI export; the optional panel fields ride the existing viewer status op.
- No relay or direct wire change.
candidates.expected_effect:
Scenario: the viewer's upload gains a standing queue, such as a cloud backup or a video call on a bufferbloated home link. Estimates from the code paths for +300 ms of queue, at pace 60 with a 20 ms base RTT:

Today:
- The probe delay reads about 300 ms, so the fps cut goes to 150 x min_fps / delay, about min_fps/2 (qos.rs:655-668).
- Bits per frame fall 15% per 3 s window toward the floor (qos.rs:735-743).
- The frame window of ceil(60 x 0.12) = 8 units is held by receipts in flight for about 320 ms, so admission is capped near 8 / 0.32 s, about 25 fps (credit.rs:164-166, 189-196).
- The ack-queue clamp (over 100 ms) spirals the byte window toward its 32 KiB floor, about 0.8 Mbit/s at a 320 ms round trip (credit.rs:171-176).
- In short: a perfectly good link toward the viewer collapses to roughly 10-25 fps at floor quality.

After:
- The forward queue stays about 0, so pace and bits per frame hold at the ceiling.
- The window grows by the reverse queue.
- Input latency still carries the uplink queue, which nothing on the video side can remove.

Precision on true forward congestion:
- The queue estimate no longer includes each unit's own transfer. At 8 Mbit/s a 60 KB P-frame takes about 60 ms to cross, and that is in every receipt delay today.
- It no longer includes the up-to-16 KiB first record either: about 13 ms at 10 Mbit/s, 131 ms at 1 Mbit/s.

None of these figures is measured yet.
candidates.measure:
Run on this Mac in release mode.

1. Measurement commit first: the testkit per-direction shape plus the two new ignored cases, without the change. That is the "before".
2. On both builds, 3 runs each:
`cargo test -p pb-mapper-desktop --release --lib -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 slow_link`
3. reverse_path_queue_is_not_congestion: 6 s clean, then +300 ms on the viewer-to-relay direction only for 15 s, then lifted.
- Record pace_fps, fps, bpf, clamped, encoder_bitrate and adaptation from desktop_feedback_interval, plus the viewer's received fps.
- Before: the pace collapses. After: the pace stays at the ceiling, bpf holds and clamped stays false.
4. reverse_queue_with_forward_limit_still_cuts: a 3 Mbit/s limit toward the viewer plus +300 ms up. The forward cut must still happen.
5. The ten existing cases must still pass, and the bandwidth-limit recovery must stay within the recorded spread.
6. Zero-cost check for the split header record, 3 runs before and after:
`RUST_LOG=off cargo run --release -p pb-mapper-desktop --example host_send_bench`
Compare frames/s and allocations per frame.
7. Record everything under docs/benchmarks/<date>-arrival-time/ with the environment.
candidates.risk:
Medium.

- Clock rates: viewer and host Instants differ by tens of ppm. Over the 60 s window that is a few ms (estimate). A clock jump is handled by the reset rule.
- Changed semantics: the live controllers, which were tuned on round trips, now read the queue toward the viewer only. Congestion in both directions reads smaller. The existing slow_link cases guard the forward-congestion behaviour.
- A starved viewer reader still reads as forward queue, as it does today.
- Coordination: the rate-control area (a later receipt-driven controller) should consume Receipt.forward_queue rather than add its own timing.
- Interop: capability-gated; an old peer behaves exactly as today.

candidates.title: Give the viewer's fps cap a remembered decoder capacity, so it stops raising past a slow decoder into backlog drops and freezes
candidates.airhand_evidence:
airhand's rate controller (crates/airhand-link/src/flow.rs):
- On a cut it remembers the busy rate as `capacity` (flow.rs:580-586).
- Raises are 15% a second far from capacity, but only 4% a second once the estimate is within 0.9 x capacity (flow.rs:601-604).
- It forgets capacity once the estimate exceeds 1.2 x capacity (flow.rs:606-607).
- The module doc summarises this (flow.rs:20-24).
candidates.pb_current:
FpsCap (viewer/fps_cap.rs):
- Lowering: two consecutive 250 ms ticks with more than 2 queued, or a backlog drop, set the cap to floor(presented x 0.9 direct, or 0.8 relayed) (fps_cap.rs:92-117).
- Raising: after 3 s with at most one queued, it adds 5 every second up to the ceiling (fps_cap.rs:13-24, 118-134).
- `presented_fps` counts pictures the compositor took (stats.rs:112-115; sink.rs:509-514), not decoder throughput.

The sink drops to the next IDR when the head has waited over 250 ms with 3 or more queued (sink.rs:46-52, 249-257, 399-402, 599-601). That means a freeze until an IDR arrives.

Nothing remembers what the consumer could do, so every raise past it rebuilds a queue. Recorded on this Mac: a decoder taking 67 ms (about 14.9 frames a second) saw the caps go 11, 16, 12 within 10 s, with backlog_drops=3, keyframes_requested=3 and a mean pace of 12.4 (docs/benchmarks/2026-11-24-desktop-pipeline/slow_link.txt:12). slow_link.rs:860-904 does not assert on drops.
candidates.change:
1. sink.rs
- In `take()` (sink.rs:598-625), count units handed out into a 4-slot ring of per-tick counts. No allocation.
- Note whether the queue was non-empty at both this tick and the last, with no drop in between. Under that backlog the pull rate is the consumer's decode throughput:
  - Darwin and Windows decode synchronously between pulls (DesktopVideo.swift:823-852; desktop_video.cpp:1070-1100).
  - Linux pulls only while its pipeline has room (desktop_video_gst.cc:865-915).
- Pass `pulled_fps`, `busy` and the head's wait (`queue.front().received_at` age) to `FpsCap::tick` (sink.rs:509-514).

2. fps_cap.rs: new fields `capacity: Option<f32>`, `capacity_at: Option<Instant>` and `raised_at: Option<Instant>`.

Lowering:
- On a lowering, capacity = the pulled rate measured under backlog, else max(presented, pulled).
- The cap becomes floor(capacity x 0.9 direct, or x 0.8 relayed). The factors are unchanged, so the queue still drains.
- CAP_MIN and the halving bound are kept.

Early lowering:
- Within PROBE_WATCH (5 s) after a raise, one tick is enough: at least 2 queued and a head wait over max(2 frame intervals at the cap, 40 ms).
- That catches an overshoot before the 250 ms age drop. Outside a raise, the 2-tick rule applies as today.

Raising:
- While capacity is known, raises stop at floor(0.95 x capacity).
- After CAPACITY_TTL (60 s) without backlog, or once the cap is above 1.2 x capacity (airhand's forget rule), capacity is dropped and today's +5 probing resumes.
- Far from capacity, raises run as today.

Forgetting: capacity is also dropped on a new generation or picture size (decode cost changes), on a preset change, and on resume.

3. Tests
Unit tests in fps_cap.rs, keeping today's sequence for raises far from capacity:
- a 15 fps consumer settles at 14 and probes at most once a minute;
- the one-tick watch fires only after a raise;
- capacity is forgotten above 1.2 x and after the TTL;
- the capacity comes from the pull rate under backlog, not the presented rate.

slow_link changes:
- Extend slow_presenter_is_capped_by_fps_cap_not_host_backpressure to 60 s and assert backlog_drops == 0 after the first 10 s.
- Add a case with a 10 ms decoder and fps_override 120 that reports the sink wait p95 (handed_us - received_us from the desktop_frame_view trace).

4. Docs: update "Viewer: newest decodable frame, fps cap and recovery" in docs/remote-desktop.md (around line 1660) and add a CHANGELOG bullet.

candidates.expected_effect:
Recorded baseline, 67 ms decoder (about 14.9 fps), over 20 s: 3 backlog drops, each a frozen picture for a round trip plus the IDR's transfer, 3 keyframe requests, and a mean pace of 12.4.

After, for the same consumer (estimates):
- No drops in steady state.
- The cap holds at 14, so mean pace is about 14: roughly 13% more presented frames.
- One re-probe a minute, caught at 2 queued frames (about 130 ms) before any drop.

For a consumer that can decode about 100 fps (for example 4K at 120 on an integrated GPU, or a Linux software decode plus RGBA conversion):
- Today: an overshoot about every 5 s that queues around 5 frames, about 50 ms of added lag.
- After: no more than about 2 frames, once a minute.

A consumer that keeps up never builds a queue, so it is unaffected. Apart from the recorded baseline, these figures are estimates.
candidates.measure:
Run on this Mac in release mode, 3 runs before and after:
`cargo test -p pb-mapper-desktop --release --lib -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 slow_presenter`

Compare:
- backlog_drops
- keyframes_requested
- mean_pace_fps
- the caps trace
- the new 10 ms-decoder case's sink wait p95

The baseline is already recorded (slow_link.txt:12: backlog_drops=3, keyframes_requested=3, mean 12.4). Also run `cargo test -p pb-mapper-desktop` for the fps_cap and sink unit tests. Record the results under docs/benchmarks/.
candidates.risk:
Low to medium.

- After the consumer speeds up (CPU or GPU freed), the cap stays at 0.95 of the old capacity until the 60 s TTL or the 1.2 x rule lets probing resume.
- A network burst right after a raise can trigger the one-tick rule. That costs 10% of fps for at least 3 s, at most once a second.
- Android's feeder shares the sink. Its pull rate under backlog follows MediaCodec input availability, which still reflects its throughput.
- Each platform's decoders differ only in how they pull, and all of them pull only when they can take a unit.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's 8 ms ack coalescing (client/src/lib/ack.ts:1-9, 46-58)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper writes at most one receipt per unit: at most 120 a second, about 25 bytes of JSON each. The Outbound slot already folds receipts into the newest cumulative seq while the writer is busy (outbound.rs:195-197). Upload traffic is dominated by QUIC's own ACKs for the video, so coalescing receipts changes nothing measurable.

not_worth_it.title: Binary acks instead of JSON (ack.ts:15-23; airhand-link console.rs:126)
not_worth_it.reason: One small serde_json record per receipt costs microseconds, at most 120 a second. No effect.

not_worth_it.title: Acks as unreliable QUIC datagrams with repeats (airhand-link controller/session.rs:41-43, 153-216)
not_worth_it.reason: Receipts ride the desktop's one TLS stream through a byte tunnel. Datagrams would need the per-session QUIC plumbing that B-frame-streams rejected. The upload direction carries only small control messages, so head-of-line blocking there costs at most one loss recovery. R5-arrival-time-receipts takes the way back out of the controllers anyway.

not_worth_it.title: Acknowledge after the UI hop so in-flight includes it (controller/mod.rs:169-171; console-worker.ts:258-262)
not_worth_it.reason: airhand's hop is WebView IPC, which is unbounded. pb-mapper's hop from sink to decoder is in-process and bounded (32 units, 8 MiB, 250 ms; sink.rs:46-52), and the fps cap owns presentation lag (rule 1, docs/remote-desktop.md:1214-1218). Counting decode in credit would let a slow decoder shrink the network window, and it could not bound latency below what the sink already does.

not_worth_it.title: Draw on decoder output to a desynchronized canvas, no vsync wait (client/src/lib/session.ts:8; console-worker.ts:139)
not_worth_it.reason: Not part of the shared path. Presentation goes through each platform's Flutter texture: the main-thread hop in DesktopVideo.swift:782-798, MarkTextureFrameAvailable in desktop_video.cpp:1060, frame_ready in desktop_video_gst.cc:759. Whether to present outside Flutter's compositor belongs to the Windows, macOS and Linux presenter areas.

not_worth_it.title: Video jitter and AV-sync scheduling (avsync.ts:65-91; jitter.ts)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper has no audio. Holding video back only adds latency. The sink already decodes every unit and each runner shows only the newest picture.

not_worth_it.title: Keep hidden sessions at 5 fps instead of pausing (session.ts:10)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper pauses a hidden viewer, so the host stops capturing, and resumes with one IDR. That costs fewer host and link resources, and the IDR on return is the only difference.

not_worth_it.title: Decoder queue resets at decodeQueueSize > 8 or 120 queued (video.ts:34-35, 108-112, 171)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper's sink already drops earlier (32 units, 8 MiB, 250 ms age), and an arriving IDR supersedes whatever is queued (sink.rs:377-394).

not_worth_it.title: Zero-copy hand-off: lend the Bytes to the native decoder instead of pull_into's memcpy, and drop Windows' second memcpy (desktop_video.rs:213-236; desktop_video.cpp:878-881)
not_worth_it.reason: About 10-40 µs per unit of 100-400 KB (estimate), against an 8.3 ms frame at 120 fps. It would change the ABI on four runners for no measurable effect.

not_worth_it.title: Remove the loopback TCP hop between the tunnel and the desktop's TLS (client.rs:351-391, 580-594)
not_worth_it.reason: It costs two syscalls and one task hop per forwarded chunk each way, tens of µs. Removing it needs new SDK surface in pb-mapper-client for no perceptible latency gain.

not_worth_it.title: Avoid rustls' 4 KiB reads and its Vec per record (rustls buffers.rs:220, common_state.rs:557)
not_worth_it.reason: That is about len/4 KiB recv calls and len/16 KiB allocations per unit: under 0.5% of a core at 100 Mbit/s (estimate). It is also third-party code.

not_worth_it.title: Split the viewer's reader and writer into separate tasks (viewer/session.rs:211-215)
not_worth_it.reason: The biased select polls the writer first on every wake, and tokio's coop budget limits a reader burst to about 128 socket reads (about 0.4 ms). Input waits at most that long, so there is nothing to gain.

not_worth_it.title: Cap the host at the presented rate when the display, not the decoder, is the limit (a viewer on a 60 Hz monitor while display_max_hz is the fastest screen's, DesktopVideo.swift:1057-1060, desktop_video.cpp:262)
not_worth_it.reason: The effect is mixed. Sending above the refresh keeps a fresh picture for every vsync despite network jitter and lowers the mean frame age by about 3-4 ms. A cap near the presented rate (for example 66 into 60 Hz) adds beat judder. It saves bandwidth only where QoS is not already cutting.

not_worth_it.title: Lost/decoded-frame reports for recovery from long-term references (merge.rs:67-95; refs.rs)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper's video is one ordered, reliable stream, so at the viewer frames are late, never lost. Recovery needs encoder long-term references first (C-ltr-recovery), which is outside the viewer pipeline.

critique.area: R5: the viewer pipeline every platform shares (network to native decoder input, and receipts back to the host)

reviews.factual_errors:
Most of the claims check out against the code.

pb-mapper (all confirmed):
- Receipts are queued after the whole payload is read (viewer/session.rs:317-321).
- The receipt and probe slots carry no time (outbound.rs:111-112, 191-197). They are written before input (outbound.rs:315-321).
- The host writes header and payload as one vectored write (wire.rs:103-108). rustls 0.23.46 cuts the chained slices into records as if they were one buffer (conn.rs:338, send_plaintext). So the first record holds the header plus up to about 16 KiB of payload.
- credit.rs: t = base + 100 ms (line 164); frames = ceil(pace x t) (line 165); the clamp is 1.25 x delivery x t with a 32 KiB floor (lines 171-176); ack_queue is the median minus base (lines 306-331).
- qos.rs: the delay is the median of 3 RTTs minus the 60 s minimum (lines 613-623). In the 300-600 ms band the cut is 150 x min_fps / delay, so Balanced falls to 5 fps once two probes agree (lines 655-668). Bits per frame step x0.85 per 3 s in the 300-500 ms band (lines 735-743).
- The ack-queue clamp does spiral down. The window is 1.25 x rate x 0.12 s, but each unit is in flight for 0.32 s, so the achievable rate falls to about 0.47 of the last one each round, down to the 32 KiB floor (about 0.8 Mbit/s).

airhand (all confirmed):
- Ack{seq, arrived} (airhand-proto session.rs:704-712).
- The arrival time is taken after the length prefix (airhand-link wire.rs:111-121), handed over as max(arrived, handed) (merge.rs:288-292), and attached to the cumulative ack (controller/mod.rs:727-746).
- The queue is the one-way delay minus a 10 s WindowMin (flow.rs:270-276, 101-126, 71).

Corrections:
1. The "clock jump" reset (a sample more than 1 s below the minimum) has no purpose. Both ends use monotonic Instants. A faster path just becomes the new minimum in the monotone deque, and route changes already reset through the Path message (session.rs:404-412). Drop the rule.
2. The design does not mention transport behaviour under a large reverse queue. Quinn uses its default Cubic (only the windows are configured: protocol quic.rs:63-65, client direct/identity.rs:138-139). Kernel TCP on the relay leg also needs cwnd at the inflated RTT. While cwnd grows, data waits in quinn's or the relay's buffer. That shows up correctly as forward one-way delay, because sent_at is stamped at book, before the write. So the gain is bounded by how fast the transport grows its window.
3. The proposed slow_link cases cannot show that cwnd interaction. The testkit shaped hop delays bytes in userspace on loopback TCP (testkit shaped.rs:58-96), so kernel TCP never sees the 300 ms. The cases measure the app controller only.
4. The "before" collapse lasts only while the 60 s RTT minimum still holds the clean RTT. A perfectly constant queue longer than 60 s gets absorbed into the base. Bufferbloat from a bulk upload saw-tooths (Cubic), so the minimum stays low and the collapse lasts as long as the upload. The proposed 15 s case is inside the window either way.
5. D-fast-rate-control deferred these timestamps (research/D-fast-rate-control.json, protocol section) only because no traces showed reverse-path noise. Its own risk list names false cuts from reverse-path jitter on Wi-Fi and cellular. Under this round's rule (judge on effect), that deferral reason no longer applies.
reviews.effect_assessment:
The effect is real and large in one common situation, and moderate in another.

Large: the viewer's upload has a standing queue, for example a cloud backup, photo sync or a large send on an asymmetric home link, or cellular uplink scheduling. Today a perfectly good link toward the viewer collapses to about 5 fps (Balanced min_fps 10 / 2):
- bits per frame fall 15% every 3 s;
- admission is capped near 25 fps by the frame window;
- the byte window spirals to its 32 KiB floor.
This lasts as long as the 60 s RTT minimum stays clean. After the change, pace and bits per frame stay at the ceiling. Only input latency carries the uplink queue, which the video side cannot remove.

Moderate: Wi-Fi uplink stalls of 200-600 ms. They delay probes and receipts alike, so the receipts witness the cut (qos.rs:506, 654) and fps halves. With one-way delay, no cut happens.

Small but real: a better estimate of true forward congestion, because each unit's own transfer and the first 16 KiB record (131 ms at 1 Mbit/s) leave the receipt delay.

Peers without the capability behave exactly as today. Every figure is still an estimate from the code paths.
reviews.corrected_design:
1. Protocol (protocol.rs)
- CAPABILITY_ARRIVAL_TIME = "arrival_time". The viewer lists it in Authenticate (config.rs) and the host in Accepted (host/acceptor.rs).
- ViewerMessage::Received{seq, at_us: Option<u64>} and ProbeEcho{nonce, at_us: Option<u64>}, both #[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")].
- The viewer fills at_us only when Accepted listed the capability. deny_unknown_fields stays.
- at_us is microseconds since the viewer session's Instant epoch.

2. Viewer
- Reader::run takes `let at = Instant::now()` right after read_header_with returns (session.rs:278-288) and passes it to handle.
- outbound.receipt(seq, at) keeps (max seq, its at) in the slot; outbound.probe(nonce, at) does the same for the probe.
- Outbound::next writes at_us from that.
- No FFI, Dart or runner change.

3. Host write, only for a session whose viewer listed the capability
- write_message_with gets a split mode: write_all(records), which holds the header length, header and payload length; then write_all(payload); one flush.
- The header becomes its own small TLS record, so the viewer stamps the unit's first bytes, not the end of a 16 KiB record.
- No copy is added. Other sessions keep the single vectored write.

4. New platform-neutral module oneway.rs
- WindowMin: a monotone deque over RTT_WINDOW (60 s), at most one sample per 250 ms bucket, capacity reserved once (at most 256 entries, no per-receipt allocation).
- OneWay holds one forward WindowMin shared by receipts and probes (same clock offset), one reverse WindowMin, and a 3-slot ring of recent reverse queues.
- sample(at_us, sent_host, recv_host) returns forward = (at - sent) - min_f and reverse = (recv - at) - min_r, both saturating at 0. It uses i64 microseconds since SessionShared.epoch.
- reset() goes everywhere qos.reset_baseline does (Path, session.rs:412) and in Qos::resume.
- There is no clock-jump rule.

5. credit.rs
- on_receipt(seq, now, at_us) samples OneWay for the newest covered unit.
- Receipt gains forward_queue and reverse_queue: Option<Duration>.
- When present, ack_samples store the forward queue, and ack_queue returns its median with no base subtraction.
- window() uses t = base + min(median of the last 3 reverse queues, 1 s) + WINDOW_MARGIN. The frame and byte maximums are kept, and so are fits() and the JPEG window.

6. qos.rs
- on_probe_echo(nonce, now, at_us, ack_queue): when at_us is present, the probe's forward queue feeds history/delay_ms and raw.
- RTT still feeds rtt, base_rtt, last_rtt, short_path and FAST_START.
- tainted handling is unchanged, and the witness is the forward ack_queue.
- ReceiptRate (the shadow estimator) takes the forward queue and viewer-clock spacing. This is the input the deferred D stage 1 should consume rather than adding its own timing.

7. Diagnostics
- StatsRecord forward_queue_ms and reverse_queue_ms, written only to a viewer that listed the capability.
- They reach the quality panel through the existing viewer_status op: FFI JSON, Dart DesktopViewerStatus, panel row, test fake.
- Host trace fields too.

8. Tests
- protocol round trips.
- viewer/tests.rs: an old host never receives at_us, and an old viewer never gets the Stats fields.
- oneway: minimum tracking, the bound, reset, a large constant offset either sign.
- credit: a reverse delay widens t; the forward queue drives the clamp.
- qos: a reverse-only delay never cuts; a forward delay cuts as today.

9. Docs and changelog
- remote-desktop.md: send credit, QoS, viewer, the capability list.
- A CHANGELOG bullet.

reviews.invariant_risks:
Wire and pipe compatibility:
- Capability-gated. at_us goes only to a host that listed arrival_time, and the Stats fields only to a viewer that listed it, so deny_unknown_fields holds both ways.
- ALPN stays pb-mapper/desktop/2.
- HELPER_PROTOCOL and the pipe names are untouched: the helper never sees viewer messages.
- No relay or direct wire change, so there is no relay-path cost.

Data path:
- The split write adds one small TLS record and one write per unit only in capable desktop sessions. No copy, queue or spawn is added. host_send_bench must show no allocation change.
- WindowMin reserves its bounded table once (the bounded-observation-table invariant).

FFI: the optional panel fields ride the existing viewer_status op.

Behaviour change: the live controllers now read the forward queue only. Congestion in both directions reads smaller, and the forward slow_link cases guard that.

Coordination: D stage 1, if another area proposes it, must consume Receipt.forward_queue rather than add its own timing.

reviews.factual_errors:
1. Recorded baseline.
- backlog_drops=3 and keyframes_requested=3 are the session totals at 20 s, including the climb down from 60 at the start (slow_link.rs:867-886 reads status at the end).
- In the 10 s steady window the caps trace shows one overshoot (11, 11, 11, 11, 16, 16, 12, ...; slow_link.txt:12). The period is about 5-6 s: a 3 s hold, +5, about 2 s to detect, then a cut to floor(14.9 x 0.8) = 11 or 12, because the Rig is relay-only (slow_link.rs:506-513, so direct=false).

2. Linux. The claim that Linux pulls only while its pipeline has room is true, but room means fewer than kMaxInFlight = 4 units (desktop_video_gst.cc:82, 443-448). pending_ is erased only when the RGBA sample reaches appsink (desktop_video_gst.cc:949-954).
- So a saturated Linux decoder hides up to 4 units of lag that the sink's queue, head age and the proposed pull-rate signal never see.
- The proposed early-lowering rule (2 queued in the sink) would fire only after about 6 frames of lag on Linux.
- docs/remote-desktop.md (around line 2249) says a backlog "stays in Rust's sink"; that is only true beyond those 4 units.

3. The early lowering cannot work as specified. CAP_CHANGE_MIN (1 s, fps_cap.rs:20, 102-104) blocks any change within 1 s of the raise, and the design does not exempt the revert. A +5 raise past a 15 fps decoder adds about 4 queued per second, and the age drop (at least 3 queued, head older than 250 ms) can fire within about 1 s.

4. Remembering capacity for 60 s and stopping raises at 0.95 x capacity regresses recovery after a transient slowdown. Suppose the viewer machine is busy for a few seconds, so the measured capacity is 8. Today the cap climbs back +5 a second after a 3 s hold. In the proposal it stays at 7 for a minute.

5. The forget-above-1.2x rule is unreachable while raises stop at 0.95 x capacity. airhand only slows its raises near capacity (4%/s against 15%/s) and never stops them (flow.rs:601-607).

Verified as stated:
- Darwin decodes synchronously (DesktopVideo.swift:371-372, 490-491).
- Windows Feed/Take is synchronous on the decoder thread (desktop_video.cpp:1047-1060, 1078-1092).
- presented_fps counts accepted presentations (stats.rs:112-115, sink.rs:509-514, 727-734).
reviews.corrected_design:
Everything is in Rust (viewer/sink.rs, viewer/fps_cap.rs). No protocol, FFI or runner change, and no allocation per unit (fixed rings).

1. Signals the sink gathers each 250 ms tick
- Pulls: units handed out by take() during the tick.
- Backlogged tick: the queue was non-empty at both ends of the tick, with no restart or drop between.
- Measured capacity: pulls in backlogged ticks divided by their time, over the last 8 ticks. Valid once at least 4 backlogged ticks (1 s) are in the window. Synchronous consumers pull at their service rate under backlog; Linux pulls at its decode throughput once its 4 slots are full.
- Head wait: the age of the queue head at the tick.
- Consumer lag (new; the reason is Linux's hidden in-flight units):
  - presented_at() already has handed_at and presented_at (sink.rs:704-741).
  - Record presented_at - handed_at in a 128-slot ring.
  - excess = (median over the last 1 s) - (minimum over the last 10 s).
  - On Darwin and Windows the excess stays near 0 (decode plus at most one raster interval). On a saturated Linux pipeline it grows by a decode time per unit hidden.

2. Lowering
- Triggers:
  - today's rules: a drop, or more than 2 queued on two ticks;
  - new: excess consumer lag over max(2/cap s, 40 ms) on two ticks.
- capacity = the measured capacity when valid, else presented_fps as today.
- cap = floor(capacity x 0.9 direct, or x 0.8 relayed), at least CAP_MIN.
- The halving bound applies only when capacity came from presented_fps: a 1 s pull measurement is direct evidence.
- Remember capacity and when it was measured.

3. Raising
- With no known capacity, or up to hold = floor(0.95 x capacity): as today (3 s hold, then one change a second), but the step is max(5, ceil(0.25 x cap)). That gives faster recovery far from capacity, in the spirit of airhand's 15%/s far from capacity.
- A raise above hold is a probe, in the spirit of airhand's 4%/s near capacity:
  - step max(1, ceil(0.1 x capacity));
  - allowed only after probe_backoff since the last failed probe (3 s, doubling to 60 s);
  - the backoff resets when a probe succeeds.

4. Probe watch (PROBE_WATCH = 3 s after a probe)
- One tick is enough: either (at least 2 queued and head wait over max(2/cap s, 40 ms)), or excess consumer lag over the same.
- On that tick, revert immediately to the pre-probe cap, exempt from CAP_CHANGE_MIN, and double probe_backoff.
- A probe that survives the watch forgets capacity and resets the backoff.
- So a transiently low capacity costs at most one 3 s backoff before probing resumes, and a persistently slow decoder is probed at most once a minute, each probe caught before the age drop.

5. Forget capacity on a new generation, a picture-size change or a preset change: the decode cost changes.

Unchanged: CAP_MIN, the factors, the ceiling and its removal (sending max_fps), freeze() and the 500 ms IDR_GRACE judging.

reviews.invariant_risks:
None for the protocol: the existing FpsCap message (1..=120) carries every value.

- The bounded tables (rings of 8 and 128) are allocated once.
- No OS API and no FFI change; the platform runners are untouched.
- The sink lock is held as briefly as today.

Risks:
- A network burst within 3 s of a probe can revert that probe early. The cost is one backoff step, not a cut below capacity.
- Android shares the sink. Its feeder's pull rate under backlog follows MediaCodec input availability, so the capacity signal still holds there.

missed.title: On an age backlog, ask for the IDR but keep draining the queue, and let the arriving IDR supersede it, instead of dropping it and freezing until the IDR lands
missed.design:
The idea comes from airhand. Its viewer drains moderate backlogs and resets only at decodeQueueSize > 8 or 120 queued (client/src/lib/video.ts:34-35, 108-112, 171). Its comment, "Do not burst 120 stale frames into the decoder after a stalled UI", shows it drops only large backlogs.

pb-mapper today (sink.rs):
- The queue is dropped on age at push (sink.rs:399-402) and again at take (sink.rs:599-601) as soon as the head is older than 250 ms with at least 3 queued.
- The drop sets wait_key, discards every later P-frame and requests an IDR (drop_to_idr, sink.rs:428-441).
- So a fast consumer whose thread stalled 300 ms and then returned finds nothing to decode. It waits for the requested IDR: 250 ms plus RTT, host encode and IDR transfer from the stall's start.

Change, in sink.rs only (Rust, platform-neutral, no protocol or FFI change):

1. Split the age backlog from overflow. On age, at push or at take, when no age episode is open:
- open one;
- request the IDR through Recovery as today (KeyframeReason::Backlog; the limiter and backoff are unchanged, so the IDR request time is unchanged);
- count it in backlog_drops, whose meaning becomes "backlog episodes", so the panel and tests keep working;
- tell the fps cap once per episode;
- do NOT clear the queue or set wait_key, and keep enqueueing the arriving units.

2. The episode closes when an IDR is pushed, which already clears and supersedes the queue with discontinuity (sink.rs:377-394), or when the head's age falls below BACKLOG_AGE / 2.

3. Overflow (32 units, 8 MiB) still drops to the next IDR exactly as today. It is the hard bound on memory and on the lag shown, together with the IDR's arrival.

4. Recovery is unchanged: the awaited-IDR episode ends only when the IDR, or a later frame, is presented. The stall watchdog is unchanged.

5. Update the doc section "Viewer: newest decodable frame, fps cap and recovery" and the sink module doc.

It is never worse than today in time to a current picture. The same IDR is requested at the same moment and supersedes everything when it lands; meanwhile a returning consumer shows progressively newer pictures instead of a frozen one.
missed.expected_effect:
Scenario: a decoder thread stalls for S of 250 ms or more, then resumes. Causes include GPU contention from a game or another app on the viewer, a VideoToolbox or Media Foundation hiccup, the Windows GPU conversion wait (up to kConversionWait = 100 ms per picture, desktop_video.cpp:53) repeated, or a Linux pipeline hiccup.

Today the picture resumes only once the requested IDR is decoded: 250 ms + RTT + encode + IDR transfer after the stall began, even if the consumer came back sooner. After the change it resumes at S plus the catch-up, a few ms per queued unit on a hardware decoder.

The saving per event is up to one RTT plus the IDR transfer (estimates):
- tens of ms on a LAN;
- about 100-300 ms on a typical relay path;
- over a second on a 1 Mbit/s link, where a 162 KiB IDR took more than 1 s (slow_link.txt:8).

For a slow consumer that overshoots, the user sees continuing, lagging motion instead of a freeze until the IDR, with the same bound.

How often such stalls happen on users' machines is not measured; the effect is per event.
missed.verifiable_here: measure-on-this-mac (sink logic and slow_link cases with a test decoder that stalls); real-decoder stalls are device-only

research.area: R6: macOS viewer decoding and presentation (ui/darwin/DesktopVideo.swift, its plugin registration, the Dart texture widget, and the Flutter macOS embedder it rides on)
research.summary:
The macOS viewer is already lean on the decode side. One userInteractive feed thread (DesktopVideo.swift:614-621) pulls each unit straight from Rust. It rewrites start codes to AVCC in place (182-335) and wraps the unit in a borrowed CMBlockBuffer and CMSampleBuffer, which measured 0.25-1.5 us per unit. It decodes synchronously with kVTDecompressionPropertyKey_RealTime and hardware enabled (402-498).

The cost is in two places: what it asks VideoToolbox for, and how the picture reaches the glass.
- **Output format.** It asks for 32BGRA (441-450). On this M6 that makes the synchronous decode call 2.7-3x slower than VideoToolbox's native 420v: H.264 1.5/2.3-4.0/4.6 ms against 0.55/0.82/1.7 ms at 1080p/1440p/4K, and HEVC 1.5/2.2/4.5 against 0.6/0.83/1.5 ms. Those are scratch harness figures; the notes are in the scratchpad's notes/R6-macos-viewer-measurements.txt.
- **Path to the glass.** The picture goes through a Flutter texture:
  1. publish() hops to the main thread (797). Under Flutter 3.50's default merged platform/UI thread (FlutterEngine.mm:752), that is Dart's thread.
  2. textureFrameAvailable schedules a texture-only frame at the next vsync interval (shell.cc:1344-1375, animator.cc:287-300, FlutterVSyncWaiter.mm:80-95).
  3. The raster thread calls copyPixelBuffer (702-731), which is zero-copy through CVMetalTextureCache (FlutterExternalTexture.mm:115-135), and redraws the whole window.
  4. FlutterSurfaceManager holds the commit to the middle of the frame interval (FlutterSurfaceManager.mm:253-280) and commits on the main thread.

The queue holds one picture: newest wins, and a superseded one counts as dropped (790). Flutter cannot take 420v correctly because its macOS YUV path is hard-wired to BT.601 (FlutterExternalTexture.mm:104-107). That is why the runner pays for the BGRA conversion today.

airhand does the opposite: it draws each decoded frame at once from a worker, on a desynchronized canvas, with no queue and no UI thread (video.ts:196-239, console-worker.ts:139).

macOS, unlike Windows, has platform views (AppKitView, platform_view.dart:353; registerViewFactory, FlutterPluginRegistrarMacOS.h:94). A scratch CARenderer test here showed that Core Animation composites a VideoToolbox 420v IOSurface with its BT.709 matrix. Tagged with an sRGB transfer, it reproduces today's look within 2 levels. So pb-mapper can present like airhand: commit the 420v IOSurface to a native layer from the decoder thread, with no conversion and no Flutter frame.

Smaller gaps:
- The session frame rate is fixed at connect to the window's display (desktop_store.dart:1340, 2393-2400). It never follows the window to a display with another refresh rate.
- The panel's refreshHz is the fastest screen, not the window's (1146-1149).
- The Mac stats lack a decode time. airhand reports one (video.ts:221-227); Windows reports convert and its decoder thread's CPU cycles (desktop_video.cpp:559-579).

(2) For layer mode, withBt709 (341-368) also forces kCMFormatDescriptionExtension_TransferFunction to sRGB, keeping the BT.709 matrix and primaries. Core Animation then reproduces today's Flutter colours within 2 levels, where an untouched 709 transfer would shift mid-greys by 12 levels.
(3) New `LayerPresenter`, owned by DesktopVideoViewer:

- publish (782-798) calls the presenter instead of hopping to main. There is no framePosted or main-queue work in layer mode.

(4) New `DesktopVideoView: NSView`, a layer-hosting view whose layer is the presenter's layer:

candidates.expected_effect:
Measured on this M6 with a scratch harness (synthetic desktop-like content, synchronous decode as the runner does it, median per P-frame), the decode call drops from BGRA to 420v as follows:
- H.264 1080p: 1.49-1.71 to 0.53-0.55 ms
- H.264 1440p: 2.27-3.96 to 0.82 ms
- H.264 4K: 4.64 to 1.67-1.73 ms
- HEVC 1080p: 1.43-1.50 to 0.58-0.60 ms
- HEVC 1440p: 2.21-2.24 to 0.83 ms
- HEVC 4K: 4.47-4.53 to 1.52-1.55 ms
That is about 1, 1.4 and 3 ms less per frame at 1080p, 1440p and 4K. A 4K IDR, measured at 21-23 ms, also loses its share.

Estimate, from the Flutter source: today a picture waits for the main thread, then for the start of the next vsync interval (about half a refresh period on average). The commit is then held to mid-interval and needs the main thread again, targeting glass about one period after the frame starts: about 1.5 periods from decode to glass. A commit at decode time waits only for the WindowServer's next composite. The expected saving is about half to one refresh period: 8-17 ms at 60 Hz, 4-8 ms at 120 Hz, 3.5-7 ms at 144 Hz. It also removes the jitter of the main thread being busy with Dart (merged threads).

Also estimated: no full-window Flutter raster per video frame (raster-thread CPU and GPU), less memory bandwidth (4K NV12 is 12.4 MB a frame against 33 MB for BGRA, written by VideoToolbox and read again by Flutter), and a smaller VideoToolbox pool.

- On this Mac, the acceptance viewer's report shows native.timings.decode and decoderCpuMs. Compare against the scratch harness numbers for the same clip size.
candidates.risk: Panel clutter: show the rows only when reported. Windows' convert and the Mac's decode measure different spans, so they get separate labels.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's optimizeForLatency decoder hint (video.ts:209-210, codec.ts:146-147)
not_worth_it.reason: Already in place. pb-mapper sets kVTDecompressionPropertyKey_RealTime (DesktopVideo.swift:420-421) and decodes synchronously (490-491), so each picture leaves the decode call. There is no lower-latency VideoToolbox mode to add.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's hardwareAcceleration prefer-hardware (codec.ts:146): require the hardware decoder
not_worth_it.reason: Hardware is already enabled (DesktopVideo.swift:430-439), and H.265 is offered only where VideoToolbox has it in hardware (1041-1050). Requiring hardware would only fail H.264 sessions on Macs that need software for a size, which today still decode.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's decoder-queue and backlog limits (video.ts:34-35, 108-112, 171)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper's decode is synchronous with nothing queued in the decoder. Backlog stays in Rust's VideoSink, which already drops to an IDR and lowers the host's frame rate (docs/remote-desktop.md:1643-1666).

not_worth_it.title: airhand's A/V sync deferral of video (avsync.ts, video.ts:102-106)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper has no remote audio. Deferring pictures would only add latency.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's worker plus OffscreenCanvas to keep video off the UI thread (console-worker.ts:1-7)
not_worth_it.reason: Already achieved for decoding: a userInteractive feed thread pulls from Rust and decodes (DesktopVideo.swift:614-621, 823-852), never through Dart. The remaining main-thread hop (797) is removed by R6-native-yuv-layer.

not_worth_it.title: A tearing, desynchronized present beyond committing on decode
not_worth_it.reason: A windowed macOS app's layers are always composited by the WindowServer at refresh; there is no immediate-flip mode for a composited window. Committing at decode time (R6-native-yuv-layer) is the most this can gain on macOS.

not_worth_it.title: Own Metal NV12-to-BGRA conversion feeding Flutter's texture, instead of VideoToolbox's BGRA
not_worth_it.reason: Flutter's macOS YUV path is BT.601 only (FlutterExternalTexture.mm:104-107), so the conversion must happen before Flutter. Measured here, 420v decode plus a Metal compute conversion and wait took 0.85/2.2-2.4/4.1-4.2 ms (H.264 1080p/1440p/4K). VideoToolbox BGRA took 1.5-1.7/2.3-4.0/4.6 ms. The gain is at most about 0.5 ms at 4K and is noisy at 1440p; R6-native-yuv-layer removes the conversion entirely.

not_worth_it.title: AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer, or a CAMetalLayer pass, as the base presenter
not_worth_it.reason: A plain CALayer holding the 420v IOSurface composites with the correct BT.709 matrix (CARenderer test here). It adds no GPU pass in the app and lets the runner keep its receipts and size checks. AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer brings its own render pipeline and timebase, and a Metal pass adds 0.25-2 ms of GPU latency at idle clocks. Both stay as the fallback (thread safety) and the enhancement path.

not_worth_it.title: Reuse the decoder session when a keyframe's parameter sets change (VTDecompressionSessionCanAcceptFormatDescription)
not_worth_it.reason: Measured here: creating a session costs 3-25 ms, only on a keyframe whose sets changed without a size or codec change, which needs a new session anyway. That is rare, so the gain is negligible.

not_worth_it.title: Pooling or reusing CMBlockBuffer and CMSampleBuffer per unit
not_worth_it.reason: Measured wrap cost is 0.25-1.5 us per unit. The bytes are already borrowed, not copied (DesktopVideo.swift:471-485), and the start codes are rewritten in place (299-335).

not_worth_it.title: Asynchronous VideoToolbox decode (kVTDecodeFrame_EnableAsynchronousDecompression)
not_worth_it.reason: Units depend on each other and arrive one at a time. Asynchronous decode adds a callback hop with nothing to overlap; the synchronous call is already the shortest path.

not_worth_it.title: Real-time thread policy for the decoder thread
not_worth_it.reason: It is already userInteractive (DesktopVideo.swift:619) and mostly waits on the media engine. Round F measured no gain from raised priority on this Mac under an all-core load (docs/benchmarks/2026-11-24-desktop-pipeline/README.md, priority_ab); withdrawn items stay withdrawn.

not_worth_it.title: Call textureFrameAvailable on unit arrival, before decode, in the texture path
not_worth_it.reason: It helps only when the 0.5-4.6 ms decode straddles Flutter's vsync request. Otherwise it costs a wasted full-window raster whenever Flutter's frame starts before the decode ends. Subsumed by R6-native-yuv-layer.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's scale-only-once resolution request (fit.ts; docs/architecture.md:213)
not_worth_it.reason: This is J, rejected last round. In R6-native-yuv-layer the WindowServer does the one scaling inside the composite it performs anyway.

critique.area: R6: macOS viewer decoding and presentation (ui/darwin/DesktopVideo.swift, its plugin registration in ui/macos/Runner/MainFlutterWindow.swift, the Dart texture widget, and the Flutter macOS embedder it rides on)

reviews.factual_errors:
**Checked and correct:** DesktopVideo.swift:441-450 (BGRA), 490-491 (synchronous decode), 782-798 (newest wins, superseded counted at 790), 689-695 and 702-731 (frame-available hop; the receipt in copyPixelBuffer). Also the Flutter 3.50.1 sources:
- shell.cc:1344-1375: platform-thread DCHECK, then ScheduleFrame(false)
- animator.cc:287-300
- FlutterVSyncWaiter.mm:80-95: a frame starts at the start of the interval
- FlutterSurfaceManager.mm:253-280: commit held to the midpoint, then run on the main run loop (ResizeSynchronizer.swift:124-141)
- FlutterEngine.mm:752: merged platform/UI thread by default
- FlutterExternalTexture.mm:104-107: YUV path is BT.601 only
- FlutterMutatorView.mm:350-370

**1. Decode figures understate the gap.** They were measured back to back. Paced at 60 fps, clocks idle between frames and the gap is larger. Scratch harness r6rev_vtidle.swift, this M6; notes in R6-review-measurements.txt. Median per P-frame, BGRA then 420v:
- H.264 1080p: 2.15-2.22 vs 0.91-1.53 ms
- H.264 4K: 6.06-6.30 vs 2.10-2.62 ms
- HEVC 1080p: 1.92-2.88 vs 1.45-1.51 ms
- HEVC 4K: 5.22-5.81 vs 2.32-2.42 ms
- First decode after a 2 s still desktop, 4K: 6.5-12.2 vs 2.7-6.0 ms

r6rev_vtpool.swift showed no new IOSurface after any gap. The after-idle cost is clock ramp-up, not pool allocation.

**2. Colour: the reasoning is wrong; the sRGB tag is still right.** cayuv.swift fed an sRGB-tagged BGRA source to a VT encoder set to a 709 transfer. VideoToolbox therefore converted the transfer at encode, which is why '709 tf' reproduced the source and VT-BGRA came out 12 levels darker. pb-mapper hosts do not do this:
- The Mac host captures sRGB values straight into NV12 with the 709 matrix (platform/macos/capture.rs:291-301), and only tags the VUI as 709 (encoder.rs:338-351).
- The Windows host's NV12 conversion does no transfer conversion either.

So the YUV carries sRGB-encoded values, and an sRGB transfer tag is the correct tag, not just today's look. A 709 tag would make Core Animation lift mid-greys (sRGB 128 to about 140).

**3. The override cannot live in withBt709.** withBt709 returns early whenever the stream names a matrix (DesktopVideo.swift:342-344), and every Mac-host stream does. Placed there as proposed, Mac-host streams would keep the 709 transfer and show too light.

**4. Hit testing is not as described.** FlutterPlatformViewContainer passes nil through, but FlutterMutatorView.hitTest (FlutterMutatorView.mm:540-549) returns itself through NSView's default. With DesktopVideoView returning nil, the mutator view becomes the hit target. Clicks still reach FlutterViewController through the responder chain, but:
- FlutterMutatorView does not accept the first mouse, while FlutterView does (FlutterView.mm:105). The first click into an inactive viewer window would stop reaching the remote.
- FlutterView.cursorUpdate refuses to restore Flutter's cursor wherever its hitTest is not FlutterView itself (FlutterView.mm:125-130). The cursor coordinator only invalidates the platform view's cursor rects (FlutterMutatorView.mm:83-88). So the hidden or host-shaped local cursor over the picture (remote_cursor_layer.dart:158-178, SystemMouseCursors.none at :68) is at risk.

**5. Use opaque, not transparent.** PlatformViewHitTestBehavior.transparent makes the render box return false from hitTest (rendering/platform_view.dart:358-363). The Texture it replaces hits itself (rendering/texture.dart:93).

**6. The saving is about one period, not a half to one.** By the cited code:
- Today: decode, main-thread hop, the next interval start (0.5 period on average), raster, the commit held to mid-interval, glass at the interval end. About 1.5 periods.
- Commit on decode: about 0.5 period plus the WindowServer's deadline.

The saving is therefore about one refresh period minus that margin. It is still an estimate.

**7. Receipt and dropped counts change meaning.** In layer mode every committed picture earns a receipt, even one the WindowServer never shows. The dropped counter would read 0 on a 60 Hz window fed 120 fps. The panel's 'presented below received' reading would lose its meaning on a Mac.

**8. Choose the widget from the texture, not from the platform.** Picking it with a Platform.isMacOS check in the widget tree would make widget tests, which run on a macOS host here, build an AppKitView.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real for every macOS viewer user, every frame.

**Measured here, paced at 60 fps:**
- Decode: about 0.7-1.3 ms less per frame at 1080p and 3-4 ms less at 4K.
- The first picture after a still desktop (typing after a pause) arrives 3-6 ms sooner at 4K.

**Estimated from the Flutter source, not yet measured:**
- About one refresh period less from decode to glass: roughly 12-16 ms at 60 Hz, 6-8 ms at 120 Hz, 5-7 ms at 144 Hz.
- No more jitter from a busy merged platform/Dart thread.
- Lower power:
  - VideoToolbox's 4K BGRA pass (33 MB written per frame) is gone.
  - So is Flutter's full-window raster per video frame.
- The video keeps moving during a live window resize.

Together this is the largest latency gain open to the Mac viewer, and the airhand idea (present on decode, off the UI thread) maps onto it directly.
reviews.corrected_design:
**Scope.** macOS only (`#if os(macOS)`). iOS, and a macOS escape hatch, keep the texture path. The presenter is chosen per viewer at create.

**Swift (ui/darwin/DesktopVideo.swift)**

1. **Create.** It takes `presenter: 'layer'|'texture'` and still replies with an Int id. In layer mode the id comes from the plugin's own counter, with no FlutterTexture registration. The texture limit and instance check are unchanged.

2. **Output format.** In layer mode, VideoDecoder.attributes asks for kCVPixelFormatType_420YpCbCr8BiPlanarVideoRange, with IOSurface properties and Metal compatibility (kept for R6-upscale-enhance).

3. **Colour.** In layer mode, after describe(), always rebuild the format description: TransferFunction = kCMFormatDescriptionTransferFunction_sRGB (available since 10.13; the app targets 10.15), primaries 709, and the stream's matrix (709 when absent). This holds regardless of withBt709's early return and of the VUI. At configure, check that the first decoded buffer carries the sRGB transfer attachment. If VideoToolbox did not carry it over, set it per picture with CVBufferSetAttachment(.shouldPropagate) before the commit.

4. **LayerPresenter, created at create** (so commits can happen before the view exists).
- A container CALayer and a content CALayer: isOpaque = true, contentsGravity .resize, linear min/mag filters, autoresizingMask width and height.
- `present(picture)` on the feed thread: CATransaction.begin(); setDisableActions(true); content.contents = CVPixelBufferGetIOSurface(buffer); CATransaction.commit().
- Keep the last three CVPixelBuffers referenced, and set `shown`.
- Then the receipt logic of copyPixelBuffer:
  - Under the lock: the revision check, presented += 1, `timings.present` from decode end to commit end.
  - After the commit, outside the lock: library.presented.
- publish() calls the presenter instead of hopping to main.
- No layer property is touched on that thread outside an explicit transaction, and no NSView is touched there.

5. **DesktopVideoView: NSView**, layer-hosting. Set `layer = container` before `wantsLayer = true`.
- Keep the default hitTest (the view is the hit target).
- `acceptsFirstMouse` returns true, for parity with FlutterView.
- `acceptsFirstResponder` returns false, so keys stay with FlutterView.
- No mouse, scroll or magnify overrides: NSResponder forwards them up to FlutterView and FlutterViewController.
- `layerContentsRedrawPolicy = .never`; `layerUsesCoreImageFilters = true`.
- Cursor: `resetCursorRects` adds none. A tracking area [.cursorUpdate, .inVisibleRect, .activeAlways] gets a `cursorUpdate(with:)` that leaves the current cursor (no super call, so AppKit does not reset it to the arrow). If the check below still shows the arrow, that method re-sets `NSCursor.current`.

6. **View factory.** DesktopVideoPlugin also conforms to FlutterPlatformViewFactory, with `createArgsCodec` = FlutterStandardMessageCodec, registered with `registrar.register(self, withId: "pb_mapper/desktop_video_view")` in register(). `create(withViewIdentifier:arguments:)` hosts that viewer's container layer. If Flutter recreates the view, the container moves on the main thread (the old view's layer becomes nil).

7. **Grey still.** New channel method `grey {textureId, on}`, on the main thread: content.filters = [CIColorMatrix with GreyStill's coefficients (viewer_overlays.dart:395-400)], or nil.

8. **Display link.** While attached and not paused, on macOS 14 and later, an NSView.displayLink on the view asks for preferredFrameRateRange up to the screen's maximum. Its callback does no per-frame work beyond one thing: while stats timings are on, it counts commits beyond the first in each refresh as `dropped` (superseded at the WindowServer). Before macOS 14, use a CVDisplayLink for that counting only. Keep the frame-rate request only if the ProMotion device check shows it is needed.

9. **Snapshot** keeps using `shown`; VTCreateCGImageFromCVPixelBuffer takes 420v.

**Dart**
- **desktop_video.dart:** send `presenter: 'layer'` on macOS, unless `--dart-define=presenter=texture`. DesktopVideoTexture gains `String? platformViewType` (null in texture mode) and `Future<void> grey(bool on)`. FakeDesktopApi's texture returns null and a no-op, so tests keep the Texture.
- **viewer_stage.dart:186-196:** when platformViewType is not null, build `AppKitView(key: ValueKey(id), viewType: type, creationParams: {'textureId': id}, creationParamsCodec: const StandardMessageCodec(), hitTestBehavior: PlatformViewHitTestBehavior.opaque)`; otherwise the Texture.
- **GreyStill:** calls `texture.grey(on)` when the texture has a view type; BackdropFilter cannot reach native content.

**Docs**
- 'The app's video path' (docs/remote-desktop.md:1990-1996) and 'macOS, iOS and Linux decoders' (2215-2227): the receipt now means committed to the WindowServer.
- The quality panel's Mac row.
- A CHANGELOG bullet.
reviews.measurement_plan:
**(a) Decode cost, done on this Mac:** r6rev_vtidle.swift and r6rev_vtpool.swift (paced at 60 fps, plus idle gaps) and vtbench.swift (back to back).

**(b) Colour, on this Mac.**
- Build a pb-mapper-like stream: NV12 made from sRGB values with the 709 matrix and no transfer conversion, encoded with VUI 709 as encoder.rs:338-351 does.
- Decode it to 420v with the forced sRGB tag and render it with CARenderer. Compare with VT-BGRA, which is today's on-screen value; expect within 2 levels on the 8 patches.
- Then on screen: a known-pattern clip through desktop_ui_host, screenshotted with Screenshot.app (the owner's screenshot needs no permission) for both presenters.

**(c) End to end, on this Mac.**
- Write AUD-delimited Annex B clips (1080p, 1440p, 4K) from a VT harness.
- Host them: `cargo run --release -p pb-mapper --features desktop --example desktop_ui_host -- --clip ... --size WxH --fps 60|120 --dir target/desktop-ui --relay-only --view-only`.
- Build the acceptance viewer twice (scripts/test/desktop-ui-acceptance.md:114-131) with `--dart-define=presenter=texture` and `=layer`. For the 120 fps runs, use the Smooth preset and `maxFps=120`.
- Record:
  - native.timings.decode, and timings.present against surface_consume
  - presented, received and dropped per second
  - In a measurement build, os_signpost events at decode end and at commit or receipt
- Run `xcrun xctrace record --template 'Animation Hitches'` (each transaction's commit and display time) or 'Metal System Trace'. Correlate with the signposts to get a decode-end-to-glass distribution per presenter on the 144 Hz G24H2, and again with it switched to 60 Hz.
- Run 'Time Profiler' for the main, raster and feed threads and for WindowServer's CPU. Use Metal System Trace for the app's and WindowServer's GPU time, so the YUV composite does not just move the cost.
- Do not compare picture_latency_ms across presenters: the receipt point moves.
- Acceptance: the decode-to-glass median lower by at least half a refresh period at both 60 and 144 Hz, p95 no worse, WindowServer GPU not higher than today's VT pass plus Flutter raster.

**(d) Functional checks, on this Mac:**
- The first click into an inactive viewer window reaches the remote.
- The local cursor over the picture stays hidden or host-shaped.
- Pinch, pan and zoom, the compact frame, overlays above the picture.
- The grey still, the snapshot thumbnail's colour, the picture kept across a reconnect.
- The video keeps moving during a live window resize.

**(e) Device only:**
- ProMotion MacBook: 120 Hz cadence with and without the display link.
- CI's Flutter 3.44.9 macOS build: AppKitView and registerViewFactory behave the same.
reviews.invariant_risks:
**Protocol:** none. No wire, capability, helper-protocol or FFI change; receipts still go through pb_mapper_desktop_video_presented_v1. Only the app-internal method channel changes (a create argument, `grey`, a view type, `timings.present`).

**Receipt rules to keep:**
- A receipt goes only to a current-revision picture, once.
- Detach and attach still start a revision.
- Older-revision pictures stay visible and earn nothing.

**Threading:** the feed thread may touch only CALayer properties, inside explicit transactions. Views, filters and the container move stay on the main thread.

**iOS** must stay on the texture path (`#if os(macOS)`).

**Platform-view behaviour on Flutter 3.44.9 (CI)** must be confirmed against the 3.50.1 sources read here.

**Measurement before and after:** CLAUDE.md asks for it on any data-path change. This one is in the app runner, so the acceptance runs above are the before and after; Rust's video path is untouched.

reviews.factual_errors:
**Checked and correct:**
- refresh_hz is sent once, at connect (desktop_store.dart:1340, 2393-2400).
- VideoLimits::choose fixes max_fps from it (video.rs:74-91).
- FpsCap lowers the rate only under backlog (fps_cap.rs:78-131).
- The host accepts FpsCap values 1-120 (session.rs:372-375).
- Flutter updates the display on a screen change (FlutterEngine.mm:1542-1550) and on a mode change (1124-1162), and both fire onMetricsChanged (platform_dispatcher.dart:327-342).
- The Mac panel's refreshHz is the fastest screen's (DesktopVideo.swift:1146-1149).

**1. The effect is narrower than stated.** The preset ceilings are Quality 30, Balanced 60 (the default) and Smooth 120 (fps_cap.rs:86-90; docs/remote-desktop.md:1940-1944). Moving between 60 Hz and 120 or 144 Hz screens changes nothing under Balanced or Quality. It matters for Smooth sessions, and under Balanced only for displays below 60 Hz. The proposed acceptance run (`--fps 120` with the default preset) would show no change.

**2. A design bug.** FpsCap::tick removes the cap by sending max_fps whenever a raise reaches the ceiling (fps_cap.rs:121-129), and the host clears its cap for any value at or above max_fps (fps_cap.rs:34-37). With a display ceiling below max_fps, the first recovery from backlog would send max_fps and clear the display limit on the host.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real, for a smaller group than claimed: Smooth-preset (or sub-60 Hz display) users whose viewer window changes display mid-session, or whose display mode changes.
- **Moving from a 120 Hz to a 60 Hz screen:** host encode, send and decode work halves, and each shown frame gets about twice the bits at the same bitrate. Today on the Mac the extra frames are superseded and never seen. In layer mode they would not even show up as dropped.
- **Moving from 60 Hz to 120 Hz:** 120 fps resumes without a reconnect.
- **Otherwise:** nothing changes.

The Mac panel's refresh row becomes the window's display, which is correct.
reviews.corrected_design:
**Rust, crates/pb-mapper-desktop/src/viewer/fps_cap.rs**
- New fields: `display_fps: Option<u32>` and `display_changed: bool`, set through `set_display(fps)`.
- `ceiling = if fps_override { max_fps } else { min(ceiling_fps(preset), max_fps, display_fps) }`. A frame rate the user chose ignores the display: the frames are fresher.
- New `release = display_fps.filter(|d| !fps_override && *d < max_fps).unwrap_or(max_fps)`, the value that means 'no backlog cap'. Every place that sends max_fps today sends `release` instead. That covers the raise-to-ceiling branch, so a backlog recovery can never clear the display limit.
- On display_changed, the next tick sends the new effective value at once:
  - It bypasses CAP_CHANGE_MIN, the high-tick gate and the 3 s raise hold.
  - It sends min(backlog cap, display) when lowering, and `release` when the backlog cap is none.
  - While frozen (paused), it applies at the first tick after resume.
- Backlog lowering keeps working beneath the display ceiling.

**Rust, the plumbing**
- sink.rs: `set_display_fps`.
- viewer/mod.rs: `Viewer::set_display_refresh(hz: f64)`, rounded and clamped to MIN_VIEWER_FPS..=MAX_FPS as in VideoLimits::choose. Android ignores it, as choose does.
- session.rs:583-585 already forwards what tick returns.

**FFI, ui/native/pb_mapper_ffi/src/desktop/viewer.rs:** `DisplayRefresh { hz: f64 }`, a new op of pb_mapper_desktop_viewer_call_json. Its Dart lookup, DesktopApi interface, implementation and FakeDesktopApi change together.

**Dart**
- On macOS, Windows and Linux, connect with displayMaxHz (desktop_store.dart:341) as refresh_hz. Android is unchanged.
- A PlatformDispatcher.onMetricsChanged listener sends display_refresh with the viewer window's display refreshRate whenever it differs from the last value sent, and once after connect.

**Mac runner:** stats refreshHz is the FlutterView window's screen maximumFramesPerSecond, falling back to the fastest screen.

**Tests:**
- FpsCap: lower at once, raise at once, override honoured, backlog lowers beneath the display, and a backlog recovery sends `release`, not max_fps.
- An FFI op test.
- A store test with the fake.

**Docs:** 'Viewer: newest decodable frame, fps cap and recovery' (docs/remote-desktop.md:1643-1683) and the panel's refresh row.

**Wire:** no change. It reuses ViewerMessage::FpsCap, which every peer accepts.

**FFI:** one op on an existing *_call_json export, so all five sides change at once.

**fps_override** stays authoritative.

reviews.factual_errors:
The airhand citations hold:
- enhance.ts:1-12, PEAK at 19-20, renderPlan at 35-40
- the render path at video.ts:241-263
- docs/architecture.md:213

The design has these errors:
1. **It needs two passes, not one.** airhand upscales into an intermediate texture, then sharpens (enhance.ts:183-213). CAS needs the neighbourhood of the upscaled image, so YUV-to-RGB plus Catmull-Rom into an intermediate texture at display size, then CAS into the drawable. At 1:1, only the sharpen pass runs; airhand sharpens at 1:1 too.
2. **The drawable size is wrong.** Zoom and pan are a Flutter Transform (remote_surface.dart:260-273), which Flutter applies as a mutator transform on the platform-view container. convertToBacking(bounds) is therefore not the on-screen pixel size. It must come from the layer's accumulated transform: convert the bounds to the window's root layer, times backingScaleFactor.
3. **A presented handler cannot avoid blocking.** CAMetalLayer.nextDrawable blocks, and no non-blocking query exists. The pass must run on its own presenter thread with a newest-wins slot, so the decoder thread never waits.
4. **The last picture must be redrawn.** On a geometry or level change, redraw it even when no frame arrives; a still desktop sends nothing (airhand keeps the last frame for this, docs/architecture.md:213).
reviews.effect_assessment: A real quality gain, for users who turn it on, when the picture is enlarged. That is common on Retina Macs: a 1920×1080 or 2560×1440 host full-screen on a 3024×1964 to 3456×2234 panel, or on a 4K or 5K external display, is enlarged 1.2-1.8× bilinearly today, so text is soft. Off by default, it costs nothing. When on, it costs one or two GPU passes at display size; airhand quotes about 0.5 ms on an RTX 4080 laptop, and this M6 is unmeasured.
reviews.corrected_design:
Builds on R6-native-yuv-layer, macOS only.

**Mode switching**
- A second presenter mode, active only while enhancement is on and the on-screen pixel size is at least the picture's on both axes. Below that, the plain YUV layer is used, as in airhand's renderPlan.
- The on-screen size is the layer bounds converted to the window's root layer times backingScaleFactor, recomputed in layout() and when the mutator transform changes.
- A CAMetalLayer sits beside the plain content layer. A switch toggles their `isHidden` in one main-thread transaction, so the picture never blanks.

**The CAMetalLayer:** .bgra8Unorm, colorspace sRGB, framebufferOnly, maximumDrawableCount 3, drawableSize = on-screen pixels.

**The presenter thread** holds a newest-wins slot. The feed thread puts the decoded 420v picture there and returns at once. The presenter thread:
- Wraps both planes through CVMetalTextureCache (R8, RG8; zero copy).
- Pass 1 converts with the BT.709 limited-range matrix and no transfer conversion, giving the same sRGB look as the plain layer. It upscales with 9-tap Catmull-Rom clamped to the 4 nearest texels into a private intermediate texture. At exactly 1:1 it skips the upscale.
- Pass 2 applies CAS-style luma-only sharpening with airhand's peaks (low -0.06, medium -0.1, high -0.14) into the drawable.
- Commits with present.
- The receipt and `timings.present` are taken at the scheduled present.
- It keeps the last picture and redraws it when the geometry or level changes.

**Unchanged:** snapshot keeps using the decoded buffer.

**Dart**
