not_worth_it.title: Per-frame QUIC streams and a separate control/video stream (airhand protocol v10, docs/architecture.md:63-69, host/write.rs)
Long-term reference recovery (C; airhand refs.rs, mf.rs, docs/architecture.md:68-81)
not_worth_it.reason:
pb-mapper's network never loses frames. It drops them only on the host side, and that is rare: stale heads over 1 s, overflow in rooms, late encoder output. R8-receipt-rate-control makes it rarer still by keeping the queue near 40 ms.

airhand's own table trusts LTR only for MF H.264 on NVIDIA and Intel. HEVC, pb-mapper's preferred codec, is not usable, and VideoToolbox is not wired.

It also costs:
- a silent-corruption failure mode;
- per-decoder gap tolerance to verify;
- a helper-protocol bump.

R8-disposable-frames covers the remaining drop cases without trusting each vendor.

not_worth_it.title: Keyframe supersedes the hand-off, restricted to IDRs another room member caused
not_worth_it.reason:
The measured gain applies only to that case (room wait median 487 → 275 ms). A room-only rule would remove the single-viewer recovery regression by construction, but what remains is small and rare: joins, control grants and other members' recoveries.

With R8-receipt-rate-control holding the queue near 40 ms, few units wait for credit in the hand-off, so even that gain shrinks.

not_worth_it.title: Mirroring the control lane on relay and direct with a counter-based merge (airhand paths.rs, merge.rs; docs/architecture.md:56-58)
not_worth_it.reason:
A TLS 1.3 stream has implicit record sequence numbers. It cannot be duplicated over two transports and merged without a new record layer and a new ALPN, and the ALPN must stay pb-mapper/desktop/2.

Mirroring would also copy every control message on the data path.

R8-session-standby-pair gives the failover effect with two ordinary sessions.

not_worth_it.title: Loss-rate cuts from stalled-frame reports (airhand flow.rs:362-380, 533-548, LOSS_HIGH/LOSS_LOW)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper's single ordered stream already turns loss into receipt delay. R8-receipt-rate-control's recurring-stall rule answers policers and lossy paths, and pb-mapper has no frame-stall report to compute a loss rate from.

not_worth_it.title: 8 ms ack coalescing (airhand client/src/lib/ack.ts)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper's outbound receipt slot already merges receipts under writer backpressure (viewer/outbound.rs:195-196, 319-320), and a receipt is a small record on the reverse path. Coalescing on a timer would only delay the controller's samples.

not_worth_it.title: BBR on every QUIC connection, including the relay carrier (airhand net.rs:214-230)
not_worth_it.reason:
The relay QUIC carrier is opt-in and pooled per process, shared with generic tunnels.

This fork's BBRv1 ignores loss, and its bandwidth maximum only rises (bbr/bw_estimation.rs:64), which is unfair to bulk cross traffic.

Only the desktop host's direct registration should get it (R8-host-direct-bbr).

not_worth_it.title: 8 MiB UDP send buffers (airhand udp.rs:20-52)
not_worth_it.reason: In quinn a full UDP send buffer means EAGAIN backpressure, not loss. Round A shipped receive buffers only, and no measurement shows a send-side drop.

not_worth_it.title: 2 s QUIC keep-alive and 10 s idle timeout (airhand net.rs:221-222)
not_worth_it.reason:
Desktop liveness is at the application level: host 3 s, viewer 4 s (session.rs:53, viewer/session.rs:25). R8-session-standby-pair adds faster dead-path detection where a standby makes a false positive cheap.

Shortening the tunnel's QUIC timers would change every generic tunnel.

not_worth_it.title: A larger Cubic initial window on its own
not_worth_it.reason:
It helps only a connection's first burst. After the first loss Cubic stays in congestion avoidance and does not grow while app-limited (cubic.rs:113-121), so later IDRs still take size/cwnd round trips.

R8-host-direct-bbr covers both, with BBR's 240 KB initial window.

not_worth_it.title: Path selection by minimum RTT, moving back to the relay when it is faster by max(5 ms, 10%) (airhand direct/select.rs:1-50)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper's default order (LAN, then direct, then relay) is an invariant with no RTT gate. A relay that beats a direct path by 10% or more is rare, and every switch costs an IDR.

not_worth_it.title: Shared encoder at the highest estimate among viewers still receiving (airhand docs/architecture.md:120)
not_worth_it.reason: With one encoder and no temporal layers, a viewer below the room's rate can only skip to keyframes, and each of its resyncs forces an IDR on everyone's stream. That is not a clear gain over today's minimum rule (capture.rs:224-227). R8-disposable-frames is the mechanism that makes per-viewer rates safe.

not_worth_it.title: Fixing the fork's BBR bandwidth filter (bbr/bw_estimation.rs:64 updates the max only for a higher sample)
not_worth_it.reason:
A fix would turn BBR into a second, noisy controller underneath pb-mapper's end-to-end one. airhand's arrangement relies on the transport not limiting app-limited video, with the credit window as the bound.

Revisit only if R8-host-direct-bbr's bench shows queues the credit window does not bound.

not_worth_it.title: QUIC connection migration for a viewer's network switch
not_worth_it.reason:
It survives only where the host's NAT admits the viewer's new address, through a port mapping or endpoint-independent filtering. The direct path is punched per address pair, so most switches still die.

R8-session-standby-pair covers every case.

critique.area: R8: rate control, transport and loss recovery (re-judged): D stage 1+, BBR from A, K path migration, C LTR, B frame streams

reviews.factual_errors:
1. The 1 Mbit/s record does not show the encoder overshooting.
- encoder_bitrate 3.48 Mbit/s is the Nominal model's bpf × limits.max_fps (qos.rs:536-539).
- The synthetic encoder budgets bitrate/nominal per frame (slow_link.rs:238-243). At pace 10 it sent about 58 kbit a frame, about 0.58 Mbit/s.
- So the record shows the fps-first policy (pace 10, bpf barely moved), not 3.48 Mbit/s on the wire.
- Overspend is real only for encoders that budget per second. That is VideoToolbox with wall-clock pts: scratchpad notes/rate.txt, 3.97 Mbit/s at pace 30 and 15 against a 4 Mbit/s target, and L's ratios of 1.6-15.7.

2. "Mac hosts get a working congestion response because the encoder bitrate is cut" is half right.
- A bpf cut does move encoder_bps = bpf × max_fps at once on a Mac.
- The rate_fps cap the design uses below the floor does not: it sheds nothing on a Mac at Nominal until the latch.
- The direct fix is to start Mac sessions at Timestamp (missed item R8-mac-timestamp-start), with the faster latch as a backstop.

3. `owned` has a hole. It is true when an episode is active, when a cut came within the last 2 s, or when standing < 40 ms.
- standing is measured against own_min. That is a 10 s windowed minimum: it absorbs any queue that stands for 10 s, and Rebased resets it.
- After either, owned stays true and the probe backstop is held off up to 600 ms.
- Meanwhile the queue against the 60 s probe base (qos.rs:50, 552-554) can be hundreds of ms.
- airhand has no backstop to lose and accepts this creep (flow.rs:105-126, 555-616). pb-mapper should not.

4. The recovery estimate is optimistic.
- airhand's near-capacity rule raises 4%/s while estimate ≥ 0.9 × capacity, and clears capacity only above 1.2× (flow.rs:600-606).
- After a 1 Mbit/s episode, crossing 0.9 to 1.2 Mbit/s alone takes about 7 s.
- Back to 3.2 Mbit/s is about 12-15 s, not 7-10 s, unless the accelerator the proposal calls optional is kept. Today's 1.0-2.0 s comes only from bpf barely moving.

5. Two effects are missing from the proposal.
- raise_step (15%/s plus 100 kbit/s per s, gated on moving content) takes bpf from the preset start to the preset max in about 5 s on a clean link. Today that takes about 80 s of moving content, because each 3 s window rises by at most +150 kbit/s (qos.rs:76, 735-751).
- Cursor and typing-echo messages ride the same TLS stream as video. A standing queue near 40 ms, instead of one bounded only by the window, also shortens their wait on congested links.
reviews.effect_assessment:
The effect is real on Windows and macOS hosts, for every viewer platform.

Where it matters: links between the preset floor × pace and the current rate. For Balanced at 1080p60 that is about 1-4 Mbit/s: relays over cellular or home uplinks, and congested Wi-Fi.

Gains (estimates):
- The measured 1 Mbit/s case ends at pace 10 (docs/benchmarks/2026-11-24-desktop-pipeline/slow_link.txt).
- Holding bpf at the floor (16.7 kbit) with the pace set from the delivery rate should give about 45-55 fps, with the standing queue near 40 ms instead of the 100 ms ack-queue clamp.
- On clean LAN and direct links, the faster raise reaches the preset's bpf_max within seconds instead of a minute of motion.
- On the Mac host, the fps-cap part sheds bandwidth only together with R8-mac-timestamp-start.

Costs:
- Blurrier motion at the floor. Quality keeps a higher floor.
- More frequent encoder rate changes; how vendors respond is unmeasured.
- Slower bitrate recovery, unless the accelerator below is kept.

On an uncongested LAN, the only effect is the faster ramp.
reviews.corrected_design:
Keep the researcher's steps 1-7, with these changes.

(a) Ownership and baseline.
- control_fps yields to receipts only while an episode is active, or within 2 s of a receipt cut or rebase. Drop the "standing < 40 ms" term.
- On Rebased, record rebase_offset = own_min − probe_base, capped at CUT_DELAY (150 ms). control_fps computes delay against probe_base + rebase_offset.
- Clear the offset when the 60 s probe base itself rises past it, and on Path, resume, set_preset and reset_baseline. Both controllers then share one baseline, and queue creep is bounded by 150 ms plus the probe steps.

(b) The recovery accelerator is required.
- When an episode has ended and standing has stayed under 10 ms for at least 500 ms, raise at 50%/s toward 0.9 × the expected rate held when the episode began. Do this once per episode and skip the 4%/s near-capacity band while it runs.
- If that climb is cut below 0.9 × that rate, fall back to 15%/s and 4%/s.

(c) Prerequisites.
- The per-tick latch (R8-tick-rate-model-latch), so cuts in the middle of a window never latch Timestamp.
- R8-mac-timestamp-start, so rate_fps sheds bandwidth on a Mac.

(d) When R8-receipt-arrival-time is negotiated, standing and busy come from one-way arrival times. Otherwise they come from RTT receipts with stage 0's allowance, min(frame interval, bytes × 8 / busy).

(e) For H.264 and H.265, Balanced starts at its ceiling whatever the first probe's RTT. Remove the FAST_START_RTT gate at qos.rs:503-505, since receipts now cut within a round trip.

(f) macOS backend: if the VideoToolbox step test shows FrameDropped or starved units after a cut, set_bitrate (macos/encoder.rs:411-430) keeps DataRateLimits at the pre-cut rate for 1 s and only then tightens it. The 1.5× / 1 s window at encoder.rs:187-188 otherwise still holds the previous second's bytes.

(g) Hold until both have passed: max(rtt + standing, 100 ms), and used ≤ 1.1 × target, for at most 1 s.
- Cut to min(0.85 × busy, 0.9 × used), or to 0.85 × used when stalls recur.
- Stage 0's stall and burst rule stays as it is.
- `blocked` counts only while the window is clamped.

(h) One owner for `adaptation`. Quality's order stays: bpf falls to bpf_start/2, then fps from the delivery rate, then bpf to the floor. Resets stay as proposed.

Everything is host-neutral (qos.rs, qos/receipt_rate.rs, credit.rs, session.rs, sender.rs). Nothing changes on the wire, the helper pipe or the FFI.

reviews.factual_errors:
1. The analysis misses two round-trip couplings that keep throughput collapsed under reverse-path delay even after the fps decision is made one-way.

(a) The credit window's time term is the probe base RTT + 100 ms (credit.rs:164-167).
- Frames in flight are at most pace × (base + 100 ms): 9 at 60 fps over an 18 ms path.
- With +300 ms queued on the receipts' path, each receipt takes about 336 ms. Then at most about 27 fps reach the viewer, whatever QoS decides.

(b) The delivery clamp (credit.rs:171-176) fires on the RTT ack_queue above 100 ms.
- It sets the window to 1.25 × delivery rate × (base + 100 ms). When the RTT is far above base + 100 ms, that cuts throughput every round, spiralling toward the 32 KiB floor (credit.rs:23).

The proposal's "after: pace ≥ 55 and bitrate ≥ 0.9×" cannot be met without changing both.

2. A busy rate from arrival spacing needs each unit's cumulative byte offset, airhand's `before` (flow.rs:131-139, 319-331). Each receipt's own byte count is not enough, so Sent must carry the offset.

3. airhand uses a 10 s minimum for both the one-way delay and the base RTT (flow.rs:84, 403-405). pb-mapper's 60 s probe base for window sizing stays.

The rest checks out:
- Received and ProbeEcho carry no time (protocol.rs:172-178).
- The receipt goes out after the payload read (viewer/session.rs:316-321).
- At +300 ms two persisted probes take Balanced to 150 × 10 / 300 = 5 fps (qos.rs:654-668), and bpf steps ×0.85 every 3 s.
reviews.effect_assessment:
The effect is real and common.

Who gains: any viewer whose uplink is loaded on a home router with a deep upstream buffer. Typical loads are cloud backup or sync, uploads and video calls.

Today, during the load:
- fps falls to 5;
- bpf steps down every 3 s;
- the credit window and clamp cap delivery.

After the change, the session is unaffected.

It applies to every PC viewer, because the Rust viewer core is shared through the FFI (Windows, macOS, Linux and the SDK), against Windows and macOS hosts. Nothing changes when the uplink is idle, or against old peers.

reviews.factual_errors:
1. The effect statement, and the plan's "network switches: device-only", imply that a standby survives a viewer's network switch. It does not.
- The standby's relay connection is bound to the old interface and address too. A switch from Wi-Fi to tethering, or a VPN going up, kills both, and a full reconnect is still needed.
- The standby helps only where the direct path fails while the relay connection lives:
  - UDP blocked or throttled mid-session;
  - a host-side NAT rebinding (QUIC has no server migration);
  - a lost port mapping;
  - and, for the upgrade, a transient setup fallback.

2. The outage arithmetic is right. A failure after commit does not back off direct, since only fallbacks before commit do (consumer.rs:306-372), so a reconnect spends the 3 s + 2 s budget again.

The strongest argument is unstated: the host ends the primary at HOST_READ_TIMEOUT, 3 s (session.rs:53). That empties a single-viewer room, pauses capture and runs display-mode restore before the app reconnects.

Other citations check out:
- Paused sessions still get Stats every STATS_INTERVAL, plus probes (session/sender.rs:120, 186-196), so the rule "the standby received a message in the interval" works.
- NotOffered costs one status query (consumer.rs:244-253).
reviews.effect_assessment:
Per event the effect is large.
- A direct-specific failure goes from an estimated 8-9 s outage to about 2 s, with no room emptying and no display-mode restore in between.
- A relayed session that fell back transiently moves to direct for the rest of its life. The deployed TCP relay measured a 194 ms median ping (docs/remote-desktop.md:2533).

How often either happens is unknown: no telemetry counts direct deaths while the relay was alive, nor relayed sessions that could later have gone direct.

No effect on:
- LAN sessions;
- a viewer's network switch;
- structurally unpunchable paths.

It covers Windows and macOS hosts, and every PC viewer through the Rust core.
reviews.corrected_design:
Keep the two-ordinary-sessions design. No splice, no new ALPN.

1. When standbys open:
- A relay standby opens only for an internet-direct primary (punched or port-mapped QUIC), never for LAN QUIC or LAN TCP.
- A direct-only standby opens only after a NegotiationTimeout, NegotiationFailed or Unreachable fallback.
  - It obeys the shared cooldown (R8-shared-direct-cooldown) and the NetworkHints generation, and is never tried after NotOffered.
  - It reuses one Consumer and Network per Viewer across attempts.
  - A failed direct-only attempt records its own outcome. It must not log session_path_selected path=relay or count as a fallback.

2. Protocol:
- capability `standby` both ways;
- `Accepted.ticket`: 32 bytes from ring's SystemRandom, base64url;
- `Authenticate.standby_for`;
- each sent only to a peer that listed the capability.

3. Host acceptor:
- Check the token first in constant time, then the ticket in constant time over SHA-256 digests.
- A standby takes a standby permit (one per active slot), starts paused, causes no room keyframe, and does not appear in HostStatus or in peer cursors.

4. Promotion is a Resume on the standby. Under the room lock, the room moves display-mode ownership, the admission lease and the ticket to the promoted slot, then ends the primary with End::Closed.
- Held input is released at the primary's end, failing closed.
- The resume IDR is forced, and reset_baseline runs only if the route differs.
- Restore runs when the pair ends.

5. Viewer: viewer/standby.rs.
- Promote at once on a transport error on the primary.
- Or when the primary has had no bytes for max(1.5 s, 4 × base RTT) while the standby received at least one message in that interval.
- Promote a committed direct standby at once, with no RTT gate (default order).
- Attach to the VideoSink with a discontinuity so it waits for the IDR (sink.rs:377-386), then swap the metrics connection slot. Document that an earlier subscribe_metrics stream ends at a switch.

6. Telemetry, trace only:
- desktop_viewer_promoted{cause, outage_ms}
- desktop_viewer_standby{route, outcome}
These show the real frequency.

7. SDK: `Client::connect_tcp_direct` stays #[doc(hidden)]. No PathPolicy variant and no ConnectOptions field.

8. Docs:
- the user-guide.md / user-guide.zh-CN.md pair;
- the remote-desktop.md lifecycle and constants;
- a relay operator note: one extra relay stream per internet-direct viewer.

reviews.effect_assessment:
Real, in two ways:
- It is the false-latch fix that receipt-driven control needs.
- It cuts the time a per-second encoder overspends after a pace drop from 6 s or more to about 2 s. That covers AMD and Intel MFTs if they budget per second, and SDK backends.

On Mac hosts the effect is superseded by starting at Timestamp. On NVIDIA it changes nothing, beyond the false-latch guard below.
reviews.corrected_design:
qos.rs:
- tick() diffs ProducedSnapshot every 250 ms into 8 fixed buckets: a sliding 2 s span. Each bucket holds frames, unique, non-IDR bits, integrated expected bits (bpf at that tick × Δ non-IDR frames) and a paced-low flag.
- Latch Timestamp when:
  - the 2 s span has at least 6 unique frames;
  - every bucket was paced at or below 0.75 × nominal;
  - and non-IDR bits > max(1.3, 0.6 × nominal / mean pace) × the integrated expected bits.
- The second term stops a per-frame encoder at its content floor from latching falsely. NVIDIA measured up to 1.79 at pace 5 with a nominal of 120 (remote-desktop.md:1586-1592). A per-second encoder overshoots by about nominal / pace and still latches.
- close_window keeps only the bpf step. The latch stays one-way and keeps its trace.

slow_link.rs:
- Sizes::PerSecond: bytes = bitrate × (now − the previous capture) / 8, with the gap capped at 1 s. This models a per-second encoder, including its burst after idle.

Unit tests:
- mid-window bpf cuts never latch a per-frame encoder;
- a per-second encoder latches within 2.5 s;
- a fixed-size (content-floor) encoder at pace 5 never latches.

reviews.factual_errors:
1. "invalidate() and a NetworkHints generation change clear it" has no carrier for connect_tcp.
- Only listener workers watch Wake::Network and call Consumer::invalidate (client/mod.rs:330-336). An owned stream's Consumer never sees a change.
- The shared entry must therefore store the network generation (endpoint.network_generation(), endpoint.rs:177) when it backs off, and treat a different current generation as cleared.

2. The saving applies to NegotiationTimeout, NegotiationFailed and Unreachable. NotOffered already costs only one status query (consumer.rs:244-253).

The central claim is right: run_owned_stream builds a new Consumer per call (client/mod.rs:422-432), so the cooldown never carries over. That breaks the CLAUDE.md invariant that an unpunchable path costs one attempt, not one per connection.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real, on every PC viewer through the Rust core, where direct cannot be punched (symmetric NAT, blocked UDP).
- Every reconnect and every new session inside the cooldown saves about 2-3 s of setup, measured to the first byte.
- The app's reconnect backoff of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 15 s (desktop_store.dart:22) falls inside a cooldown of 10 s that doubles while fallbacks repeat.

No change where direct works. It also restores a documented invariant.
reviews.corrected_design:

1. ClientInner gets `direct_memory: Arc<parking_lot::Mutex<DirectMemory>>`.
- At most 64 entries, evicting expired ones first.
- The key is (relay endpoint identity, namespace, service key).
- Each entry holds Cooldown, the TCP Cooldown, and the network generation of its last back-off.

2. run_owned_stream passes the entry into Consumer::new.
- cooldown() and tcp_cooldown() read through it and report it cleared when the generation differs.
- A direct success clears it, as today. diagnostics.direct_cooldown is reported as today.

3. Listener workers are unchanged; they already share one Consumer.

4. Step 2, sharing the consumer Network (UDP sockets, STUN result, port-mapping lease) per entry with a 60 s idle expiry, comes only if the existing SetupTimings diagnostics show discovery plus mapping of at least 100 ms per connect on devices.

reviews.factual_errors:
1. "After the first loss, the window stays near what the average rate needs" is imprecise.
- Before any loss, Cubic's slow start grows on every IDR burst that is cwnd-limited (cubic.rs:123-125), so the window often ends above an IDR.
- A loss cuts it to 0.7× (cubic.rs:217-221).
- In congestion avoidance it grows only on cwnd-limited ACKs, by at most one MTU per ACK (cubic.rs:166-182).

The material effect is repeated random loss. Per-event cuts settle near a Mathis-like ceiling, about 1.2 × MSS / (RTT × √p):
- about 3.7 Mbit/s at 0.1% loss on a 100 ms path;
- about 1.2 Mbit/s at 1% loss on a 100 ms path.
Both are at or below Balanced and Quality video rates. IDRs are slowed as well.

Persistent congestion (2 MTU) needs real loss across 3 PTOs. A Wi-Fi stall that buffers rather than drops does not trigger it.

2. In this fork, BBR's pacing_rate does not drive sending.
- quinn paces at 1.25 × cwnd / sRTT (connection/pacing.rs:107; connection/mod.rs:651-664).
- The bandwidth filter takes only samples that are not app-limited and exceed the current max (bw_estimation.rs:64-66), so max_bw never decays.
- BBR here is in effect cwnd = 2 × the highest delivery rate ever seen × min RTT, blind to loss. The credit window is the real bound.

3. RegisterOptions is not #[non_exhaustive] (sdk/types.rs:347-372), so a public field breaks struct literals.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real on WAN direct paths with random loss of about 0.1% or more and RTTs of 50 ms or more: cross-border links, cellular hotspots, long-haul paths. It lifts the throughput ceiling and lets IDRs and scroll bursts leave at path speed.

It does nothing on LAN or on clean paths.

On policed uplinks, only receipt control protects the path, so this ships after it.

It affects Windows and macOS hosts as video senders, for every viewer.

Host:

research.area: R9: deferred encoder-side work (G AV1, H static refinement, E phase 2 present anchoring, L encoder tuning)
research.summary:
At 1515eda, pb-mapper picks its codec in this order: H.265 if the viewer listed the `h265` capability and the backend probed H.265 successfully, otherwise H.264, otherwise JPEG (host/acceptor.rs:60-71, 332-354; host.rs:174-216). No AV1 exists anywhere in the code: not in VideoCodec (video.rs:6-17), not in any of the four native viewers, and not in the FFI flags.

Windows hosts encode H.264 at the Baseline profile, so CAVLC entropy coding and no 8x8 transform (platform/windows/video/codec.rs:234-237). Windows viewers decode H.265 only with the Store HEVC extension (ui/windows/runner/desktop_video.cpp:168-170), so most Windows-to-Windows sessions run Baseline H.264.

A still picture is re-encoded only by the 250 ms liveness repeat (codec/pipeline.rs:22-24):
- On NVIDIA's MFT, which is measured to give each frame its own fixed budget (nominal model), a blurred change sharpens at one frame's budget per 250 ms.
- On VideoToolbox, which budgets by timestamp, the first repeat already gets several frames' worth of bits.

Phase 1 of capture pacing shipped (armed ticks, 2 ms hot polls, helper protocol 10). The pacer's grid still only moves later (pacer.rs:36-39). So when continuous content runs at the display's refresh rate on a display slightly faster than the host clock, the wait from present to capture becomes a sawtooth averaging half a frame period, with a periodically dropped frame. airhand's pace.rs:1-11 describes this exact symptom.

Mac hosts start at the nominal rate model, although VideoToolbox budgets by timestamp. The last round's sweep measured the nominal model overspending 1.6x to 15.7x at reduced paces. The Mac encoder's dwell (7.5 to 10.5 ms median on an M3 Pro) has never been tuned. Under RealTime, Apple's header says VideoToolbox may pace its energy use to ExpectedFrameRate.

airhand has, in this area:
- AV1 > HEVC > H.264 negotiation, with AV1 encoded through MF on Windows.
- A refinement burst 200 ms after the picture stops changing, measured 42 to 58 dB on VideoToolbox text (pipeline.rs:11-14). This is new evidence since the last round.
- A present-anchored pacer.
- H.264 High with CABAC.

A correction to the earlier G study: the QoS presets cap bits per frame on every link (Balanced 1080p: 66,667 to 133,333 bits, remote-desktop.md:1532). A more efficient codec therefore shows as a sharper picture on a LAN too, not only on relayed or WAN links.

The last round's sweep (fixed 4 Mbit/s at every pace, platform/macos/tests.rs:307-310) measured nominal ratios of 1.6-15.7 at reduced paces in every case. The timestamp model fit within ±25% for H.264 low-latency at all sizes and H.265 low-latency at 1080p.

The misfits come from the method. A fixed bitrate gives per-frame budgets up to 800 kbit at pace 5, above the ~340 kbit per-unit cap VideoToolbox showed without low latency. QoS under Timestamp would instead ask for bits per frame × pace, which keeps each frame's budget at bits per frame.
candidates.change:
1. platform/macos/tests.rs: add a follow-pace mode to rate_model_sweep. At each step, `set_bitrate(bpf_scaled × pace)` with Balanced 66,667 at 1080p scaled by the 0.75-power rule. Classify bits per unit against bits per frame ±25%, for both codecs, low latency on and off, at 1080p, 1440p and 4K.

2. If every case fits: in platform/macos/video.rs set `const RATE_MODEL: RateModel = RateModel::Timestamp` under `cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")`. Intel Macs keep Nominal and the latch. The plumbing through BackendCaps.rate_model, fallback_caps, Qos::new, Room and acceptor already shipped.

3. No live ExpectedFrameRate change.

4. Docs: an Apple M6 subsection in "Encoder rate model per GPU" with the numbers, and a CHANGELOG bullet with measured figures.
candidates.protocol: None. Stats.rate_model already carries `timestamp`.
candidates.measure:
On this Mac first:
`cargo test --release -p pb-mapper-desktop --lib -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 video_toolbox_rate_model` with follow-pace, on a quiet machine. The decision rule is that every case fits.

After the change: the qos and host tests that already pin the Timestamp start.

On a device: a Mac host over a shaped link (the slow_link cases or a real relay) shows `rate_model=timestamp` from its first Stats, no `desktop_rate_model_latched`, and produced bitrate following the pace after an fps cut.
candidates.risk:
If VideoToolbox budgeted per frame on some chip or mode, a Timestamp start would underspend for the whole session; the latch is one-way and only leaves Nominal. Mitigations: the gate covers low latency on and off, and the change is scoped to aarch64.

Only one chip (M6) is measured here.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's LowDelayVBR with MaxBitRate = 1.5x the mean (host/encoder/mf.rs:522-535)
not_worth_it.reason: It replaces the CBR per-frame budget that the measured `nominal` model and the latch rely on (docs/remote-desktop.md:1554-1566). Microsoft documents LowDelayVBR as an H.264 extension. VBR banks bits on a still screen and spends them in bursts, which risks false latches and longer transmit time near link capacity. airhand itself falls back to CBR when the mode is refused.

not_worth_it.title: Copying airhand's fixed QualityVsSpeed = 60 (mf.rs:540)
not_worth_it.reason: 60 only requests the encoder's default bucket, and airhand chose it without measurement. R9-win-quality-vs-speed replaces it with a measured per-vendor choice.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's plain H.264 High under VideoToolbox low-latency rate control (host/encoder/vt.rs:237)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper already uses Constrained High, the profile low-latency rate control is meant for (platform/macos/encoder.rs:301-308). Plain High would signal possible B-slices to decoders for no gain.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's 'nothing more is sent' after refinement, with no liveness repeat (pipeline.rs:430-432; docs/architecture.md:206)

The 250 ms liveness repeat keeps that fresh on a still screen. Once converged it costs a near-empty P-frame, so dropping it saves nothing measurable and would block keystrokes after an idle pause.

not_worth_it.reason: On dual-GPU laptops the enumerated encoder may sit on another adapter than the capture GPU. pb-mapper's per-LUID activation probe (video/probe.rs:44-110) avoids a failed first session; R9-av1-negotiated keeps it.

not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper's NVIDIA HEVC already encodes 1080p in 1.65 ms mean (remote-desktop.md:1605), so at most about 1 ms is left. AV1 is justified by quality per bit, not latency.

not_worth_it.reason: VideoToolbox has no AV1 encoder. The previous critique checked VTCopyVideoEncoderList on this M6 and found only avc1/hvc1. Mac hosts stay at H.265/H.264; Macs gain AV1 only as viewers (M3+).

not_worth_it.title: airhand's dedicated capture thread blocking in AcquireNextFrame(timeout) (capture/dxgi.rs:588-596; capture/mod.rs:558-644)

It would also need generation-tagged pictures for input authorisation, the encoder's same-thread check (video/mod.rs check_thread) and a shared immediate context. The gain over anchored 2 ms polls is about 0.5 ms (E research).

not_worth_it.reason: An always-ready source (pace below the refresh rate) would then run about 1.6% above the QoS pace. R9-present-anchored-pacing creeps only for a dated present inside the early window and keeps the grid step otherwise.

not_worth_it.reason: Every supported pb-mapper host requires a hardware encoder. A software path adds about 50 ms encode (airhand's own figure, architecture.md:217) and would be a capability change, not a performance gain.

not_worth_it.reason: Belongs to area C (LTR recovery), not to codec negotiation. AV1 adds no LTR requirement here.

not_worth_it.title: Stamping a refined frame's capture time as now, for A/V sync (pipeline.rs:440-443)
not_worth_it.reason: pb-mapper streams no audio. Its duplicate units already carry their own pts and are excluded from unique-frame metrics.

critique.area: R9: encoder features and refinement re-judged: G (AV1), H (still refinement), E phase 2 (present anchoring), what is left of L (encoder tuning), plus the Windows viewer's codec reach

reviews.factual_errors:
1) 'Most Windows-to-Windows sessions run Baseline H.264' is unmeasured. Many OEM Windows images ship the manufacturer's HEVC extension. The population that gains is 'Windows viewers without an HEVC decoder MFT'.

2) 'AV1 decode needs only the free AV1 Video Extension and AV1 DXVA' leaves out two requirements of pb-mapper's Windows decoder:
- the MFT must be synchronous (SyncDecoders enumerates with MFT_ENUM_FLAG_SYNCMFT, ui/windows/runner/desktop_video.cpp:171-180);
- it must be D3D11-aware (MF_SA_D3D11_AWARE check at :750).
Whether the AV1 extension's MFT qualifies, and whether it is preinstalled, is unknown until a device run.

3) The order AV1 > H.265 comes from natural-video figures. For MF hardware encoders on desktop text it is unmeasured, so the bench must decide it.

4) On text, codec gaps can be much larger than the literature figures used. On this M6, VideoToolbox H.265 reached 43.2 dB at 1.84 Mbit/s where H.264 reached 35.2 dB at 3.71 Mbit/s on the same scrolling text (scratch R2 probe, scratchpad/notes/dwell.txt). That supports a large H.264-Baseline-to-AV1 step on Windows. It says nothing about NVENC AV1 against NVENC HEVC.

Everything else cited checks out:
- pb-mapper: video.rs:6-17; protocol.rs:26 and 45 (9 capabilities defined); acceptor.rs:60-71 and 332-354; worker.rs:63-69 and 276-306; pipeline.rs:42-52; desktop_video.cpp:168-170, 237-258, 307-317; DesktopVideo.swift:40, 147-156, 281-293, 1042; desktop_video_gst.cc:62, 90-93, 246-251, 283; desktop_video_module.h:57-60, 109.
- airhand: codec.ts:119-158; encoder/mod.rs:175-189; mf.rs:28-35 and 570-577; airhand-proto session.rs:580; architecture.md:76 and 217.
reviews.effect_assessment:
The effect is real: picture quality at the bits QoS already grants. Those bits are capped per frame on every link (Balanced 1080p: 66,667 to 133,333 bits per frame), so the gain shows on a LAN too.

Who gains:
- Windows hosts with an AV1 encoder (RTX 40/50, Arc and Core Ultra, RDNA3+) paired with Windows viewers that have no HEVC MFT but do have AV1 DXVA and a usable AV1 MFT. This pair goes from H.264 Baseline (CAVLC) to AV1, the largest quality step in this area.
- The same hosts paired with Mac M3+ viewers (H.265 to AV1) or Linux viewers with VA-API/NVDEC AV1. This gain is modest and unmeasured, and could be nil on text with hardware encoders.
- Mac hosts gain nothing. This M6's VideoToolbox lists no AV1 encoder.

Latency gain is negligible: NVIDIA HEVC already encodes 1080p in 1.65 ms mean. Smaller IDRs shorten keyframe recovery through send credit.

As designed, every helper session pays a second cold MFT activation on the Accepted path (worker per connection, remote-desktop.md:753-756; about 320-950 ms cold, remote-desktop.md:1415-1420) unless the probe is made concurrent or cached.
reviews.corrected_design:
Build the researcher's design (G plus its critique's corrections), changed as follows.

1. Ranking decided by measurement.
- The host ranks AV1 > H.265 > H.264 only if the RTX bench shows AV1 at least 0.3 dB PSNR above H.265, at equal bitrate, on the text pattern at both 1080p and 4K.
- Otherwise the host ranks H.265 > AV1 > H.264, so AV1 only replaces H.264 for viewers without HEVC.
- The rank is a host constant in choose_codec and Room::negotiate_codec. Viewers offer every codec they decode either way.

2. No serial cold probe per helper session.
- The worker probes H.265 and AV1 on two threads at once, each answering its own oneshot or Response field.
- The background host caches the answers by adapter identity. LUIDs change across reboots, so the key is VendorId/DeviceId/SubSysId/Revision plus the UMD driver version.
- The host hands the cache to each new worker, which then skips the activation (see missed item R9-M3-helper-probe-cache).
- The in-process backend keeps its per-process PROBED cache, generalised to (luid, codec).

3. Bitstream.
- codec/obu.rs parses in place into a reused Vec. It requires has_size_field, rejects the forbidden bit, truncation and more than 4096 OBUs, and defines a keyframe as a shown KEY_FRAME.
- shown_frames()==1 per temporal unit (TU) is enforced in Windows collect(); a violation is a codec_error, which latches AV1.
- SequenceHeader works like ParameterSets and is prepended after a leading TD.
- Only platform/windows calls it. macOS keeps avcc.rs and answers false for AV1.

4. Per-codec failure latches [H265, Av1].
- codec_error maps Av1 to EncoderFailed.
- Add the `desktop_av1_failed` and `desktop_av1_probe` events.
- Supervisor Retry.drop: Option<VideoCodec>, giving the chain AV1 → H.265 → H.264.

5. Windows host.
- subtype MFVideoFormat_AV1 with no MF_MT_MPEG2_PROFILE.
- Same low-latency, CBR and infinite-GOP read-back as H.264/H.265.
- encoder_available(luid, codec).
- video_bench --codec av1 and --dump-source.

6. Viewers.
- Windows: Av1Limit over D3D11_DECODER_PROFILE_AV1_VLD_PROFILE0/NV12. Offer av1 only when SyncDecoders(MFVideoFormat_AV1) is non-empty and the MFT is D3D11-aware. Aperture alignment up to 128. Set MaxCodedWidth/Height for AV1 too.
- Darwin: 'av01' FourCC behind #available(macOS 14, iOS 17), an OBU splitter that drops TDs, and an av1C built from the sequence header.
  Confirm on this M6, with a fixture, whether VTDecompressionSession needs VTRegisterSupplementalVideoDecoderIfAvailable. The probe answers VTIsHardwareDecodeSupported('av01').
- Linux: caps video/x-av1,stream-format=obu-stream,alignment=tu with av1parse, hardware only, PbVideoProbe.av1, PB_VIDEO_MODULE_ABI 2.
- Android and iOS stay without av1 for now.

7. Wire and SDK.
- Capability `av1`. `av1` in codecs is InvalidRequest. FLAG_AV1 = 1<<5. DecoderOffer.av1 with serde(default). Dart keeps a declined-codec set.
- HELPER_PROTOCOL 11 adds Request::Av1, Response.av1, Av1 in Video and EncoderFailed{Av1}. Both pipes move to .v11, in one bump shared with R9-present-anchored-pacing and R9-M3.
- SDK minor bump with CHANGELOG SDK notes.

8. Fixture: commit a small AV1 OBU clip made by a software encoder elsewhere (no AV1 encoder exists on this Mac). test_source gets its own sequence-header size parse.

reviews.invariant_risks:
- Capability gating holds: `av1` travels only as a viewer capability, and the value appears only in Accepted to a viewer that listed it. ALPN stays pb-mapper/desktop/2.
- HELPER_PROTOCOL 11 must change together with both .v11 pipe names (helper/mod.rs:129,137; background.rs:8), the history comment and docs. Both pipe ends validate the new fields.
- FFI layout is unchanged (bit 5 only). Linux module ABI moves to 2.
- Media Foundation stays under platform/windows.
- No per-packet copy: OBUs are parsed in place, and only a keyframe that lacks its sequence header is copied once.
- SDK semver break (VideoCodec variant, Decoders field, Retry) needs the minor bump and the matching version pins in the workspace, js/package.json and ui/pubspec.yaml.
- The new Darwin symbols must stay behind availability guards, since the app deploys to macOS 10.15 and iOS 13.

reviews.factual_errors:
1) macOS: measured here, the burst gains nothing on VideoToolbox (scratchpad/notes/r9_refine.txt). The probe used H.264 1080p, 4 Mbit/s, low latency and wall-clock pts, as pb-mapper does, after 1 s of scrolling text.
- Repeats at 17 ms spacing produced 99 B, 231 B, 1.3 KB, 3.9 KB, then 81 KB (to 36.2 dB), then about 100 B units stuck at 36.2 dB.
- Repeats at 250 ms spacing spent about 100 KB each, reaching 36.5, 40.3, 43.1, 46.1 and 47.4 dB.
- With synthetic 1/60 pts, both spacings gave identical small units.
VideoToolbox therefore refines by elapsed time, and today's 250 ms liveness repeat already refines at about the session's full bitrate. The proposed 'two small repeats in a row' stop would end the burst after the first two starved repeats.

2) 'The helper path already spends every tick' is outdated. Since helper protocol 10 (Response.submitted, oop/proto.rs:178), an unchanged capture leaves the tick armed through the helper too. The mid-burst wait for a fresh picture therefore applies to helper-hosted sessions as well.

3) REFINE_REPEATS=8 at about 8.3 KB each is far too little for dense text. The VideoToolbox run needed about 480 KB to go from 34 to 47 dB. At one nominal frame budget per repeat that is about 58 repeats, about 1 s at pace 60. airhand's 40 KB figure (pipeline.rs:11-14) is for its own, easier content on VideoToolbox.

Citations otherwise check out: pipeline.rs:22-24; windows/video/mod.rs:509-519 and 559; macos/video.rs:85-120; encoder.rs:692; airhand pipeline.rs:35-39, 306, 399-402, 430-431.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Windows, real and large, though unmeasured on a device.
- NVIDIA's MFTs budget per frame (measured nominal; output byte-identical under three timestamp schemes, remote-desktop.md:1568-1590). A liveness repeat therefore refines by one frame budget per 250 ms: about 33 KB/s at Balanced 1080p, against the session's 500 KB/s, i.e. 1/15 of it.
- Easy text that needs about 40 KB sharpens about 1.25 s after a scroll or window switch stops today, about 0.28 s with a burst.
- Dense text that needs about 480 KB takes about 14 s today, about 1.2 s with a burst. Both figures are estimates.
- Whether MF CBR on NVIDIA, AMD and Intel refines rather than pads is device-only.

macOS: no burst gain (measured).

macOS, separate effect that is real: VideoToolbox low latency drops 3-8% of pictures while scrolling (scratchpad/notes/drops.txt) and more under heavy content. When the last picture of a motion is dropped, the viewer shows the previous one until the 250 ms liveness repeat.

Cost on Windows: a fresh picture landing during a burst waits up to one tick, in-process and through the helper. For typing at 250-400 ms intervals with a short burst that is roughly 1 ms on average. Measure it.
reviews.corrected_design:
1. codec/pipeline.rs: a neutral `Repeats` with an injected clock.
- Methods: fresh(at, pts), repeated(at), output(pts, duplicate, keyframe, len), repeat_now(now, last_submit), next_due(last_submit).
- Constants:
  - REFINE_AFTER = 200 ms (const-asserted below LIVENESS_INTERVAL).
  - REFINE_DONE_BYTES = 512.
  - REFINE_MIN = 3 repeats before any stop.
  - REFINE_MAX_TIME, start 1 s of repeats at the pace, final value from the device bench.
- Stop after two consecutive repeats under 512 B once REFINE_MIN have gone, or at REFINE_MAX_TIME.
- Only duplicates newer than the last fresh pts count. A fresh picture or keyframe re-arms the burst. After the burst, today's 250 ms liveness rule applies unchanged.

2. The burst is a per-platform const: on for Windows, off for macOS, per the measurement. If a Windows vendor MFT is later measured to budget by timestamp, gate it by adapter VendorId. Thread C's latch does not reach the encoder.

3. Windows (video/mod.rs).
- Lines 513-518 become one `repeat_now` call.
- Record fresh or repeated after ProcessInput; call `output` where collect builds Encoded.
- Statistics.refined.
- video_bench gets --still <ms>, a GDI text pattern with a freeze flag, per-unit lines after the freeze, and --dump-source.

4. macOS: no burst. Re-send a picture that VideoToolbox dropped.
- In receive(), a FrameDropped output of a non-duplicate, non-keyframe unit sets State.redo and wakes thread C. Keyframe drops already re-request at :692-695.
- MacVideo::idle_until returns None while redo is set.
- submit treats redo as a repeat and encodes the last picture with duplicate=false, since the viewer never got it. redo clears on that submit or when a newer fresh picture is taken.

5. No change to thread C, the wire, the helper, the FFI or the viewers. Document the protocol.rs duplicate meaning, Diagnostics (presented_fps and present_interval change after a stop) and the constants table.

6. If the device shows a typing-echo cost above 1 ms mean, add the soft-tick option:
- a provided Backend method says the last submit was a duplicate, carried by a helper field in the shared protocol-11 bump;
- Pacer then lets a fresh picture follow a refinement repeat after P/4 instead of 3/4 P.

  - stale outputs ignored;

  - the cap;
  - liveness after the burst.
- A receive() unit test with VTEncodeInfoFlags::FrameDropped sets redo and wakes thread C.
- An ignored release test drives VideoToolbox with ±64 noise at 1080p 4 Mbit/s (75% drops per scratchpad/notes/drops.txt) and asserts that the last dropped picture is re-sent at the next submit with duplicate=false.

On the Windows RTX host, release mode, 1515eda against the branch:

reviews.corrected_design:
A. Seam.
- A provided `Backend::submitted_picture(&self) -> Option<Presented { at: Instant, presents: u32 }>`, defaulting to None. It is forwarded by Box, PlatformBackend/NativeBackend, RemoteBackend and the guarded example.
- VideoSource::presented() gives the same for a fresh submit.
- Duplicates and keyframe repeats return None.

B. Pacer.
- consume(now, done, presented: Option<Presented>). Clamp `at` to at most done; ignore it if older than one period.
- Keep the last four dated consumes. The pacer is locked while each of them took exactly one new present (`presents == 1`).
- While locked: next = max(at, next − P/64) + P (airhand's done() rule), and earliest() = max(next − P/4, last + 3/4 P).
- Not locked, or undated: today's rule, byte-identical, and earliest() = next.
From any phase this converges in at most 48 frames. The rate stays at most 1/64 above the pace, and only while one present per tick is coming.

C. Thread C. capture_at() uses earliest(); hot polls run inside the window; the drain long-poll is bounded by capture_at(). No dynamic dispatch.

D. Windows.
- Convert LastPresentTime to Instant by age: QueryPerformanceCounter, with the frequency in a OnceLock. Add Win32_System_Performance at crates/pb-mapper-desktop/Cargo.toml:45.
- Sum AccumulatedFrames over the acquires since the last submit, and store the latest stamp next to latest_pending.
- Accept the duplication's first frame when LastPresentTime == 0 and latest is None (airhand dxgi.rs:633).

E. macOS. Under the existing Latest lock, record the arrival Instant and count Complete frames since the last take.

F. Helper protocol 11 (shared bump). Response.presented_ago_us: Option<u32> and presented_count: Option<u8>, omitted when None. RemoteBackend converts them at absorb and ignores ages over 1 s.

G. Measurement and docs.
- Debug event `desktop_capture_pacing`, once a second: p50/p95 present-to-submit wait, locked, presents per capture.
- video_bench mirrors the pacer and prints the wait from LastPresentTime.
- Reword performance-model rule 2 (remote-desktop.md:1219-1222) and the host capture paragraph.

missed.title: Extend present anchoring to paces at an integer fraction of the refresh: capture every k-th present as it lands, not a stale picture at a grid tick
missed.design:
This builds on R9-present-anchored-pacing's seam (stamp plus presents since the last submit) and its protocol-11 bump.

When to lock:
- The source presents continuously: the last 4 dated captures each took k new presents.
- The source period is known: DXGI_OUTDUPL_DESC.ModeDesc refresh on Windows, the cadence of SCK arrivals on the Mac.
- k = round(refresh / pace) ≥ 2 and |refresh / k − pace| < pace / 64.

While locked, the next capture targets the predicted k-th present after the last one taken, at last_stamp + k × Pd:
- The window opens Pd/4 before it.
- A waiting picture stamped earlier than predicted − Pd/4 is not taken while the prediction is still due.
- It is taken anyway at predicted + 1 ms if nothing newer came.
- The floor stays last + 3/4 P, so the rate is bounded by the display.

Thread C passes the target as a 'not before' stamp:
- a provided Backend method;
- an internal VideoSource argument, so DXGI and SCK return Unchanged for an older picture;
- through the helper, Request::Video.not_before_in_us, relative to now.

Non-integer ratios (45 on 60 Hz, 60 on 144 Hz) and non-continuous content keep the grid byte for byte.

areas.name: high frame rate end to end (120 fps)

research.area: R10: 120 fps end to end (Windows and macOS hosts; Windows, macOS and Linux viewers)
research.summary:
Today pb-mapper reaches 120 fps only when the viewer picks Smooth (ceiling 120, qos.rs:117-124) or Max fps 120, which sends fps_override (viewer/config.rs:82-84). Balanced, the default (desktop_store.dart:299), stops at 60 (qos.rs:109-116). airhand is similar: its presets top out at 60 (presets.ts:12-20) and 120 is a custom rate (docs/usage.md:229).

Once 120 is chosen, most of the path does not limit it:
- QoS on a short path climbs from 50 to 120 inside the 1 s startup hold (qos.rs:597-601, 630-690).
- Send credit scales with pace.
- The viewer's fps cap moves only on backlog (viewer/fps_cap.rs).
- Capture runs at the display rate on both hosts. SCK's minimumFrameInterval is 0.9/fps (platform/macos/capture.rs:367); DXGI follows the display's presents.
- Encoders are configured at nominal 120 (VT ExpectedFrameRate at encoder.rs:320-323; MF_MT_FRAME_RATE at codec.rs:460).
- The Windows and macOS viewers present at the display rate: Flutter ticks at DWM's rate on Windows and at a per-display CVDisplayLink on macOS.

These are the real caps and costs, from code, Flutter's engine source, a VideoToolbox harness run on this M6, and the pacing model:
1. **Mac host encoder.** VideoToolbox with pb-mapper's low-latency rate control cannot encode 120 fps above about 2560x1664. It delivered 64-97 units/s at the native sizes of MacBook Pro and 4K displays.
   - At 16-aligned sizes it encodes inside VTCompressionSessionEncodeFrame on thread C: 8-16 ms per call, 48-100% of the thread's time. Input injection waits behind it.
   - Where it is slower than the pace, four pictures queue (38-50 ms dwell).

candidates.measure: Here: worker tests (samples per second) and host_send_bench's peer-cursor latency at pace 120. On a device: two viewers, one moving the pointer, the other watching at 120 Hz.
candidates.risk: Slightly more work on thread C at 120. The echo rules (CursorEcho) do not depend on the cadence.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's dedicated capture thread per screen, blocking in AcquireNextFrame(timeout) (capture/mod.rs:558-644; capture/dxgi.rs:588-596)
not_worth_it.reason: E rejected it, and that still holds. DXGI duplication is desktop-affine, and pb-mapper authorises input only against a presentation of the same desktop generation. A second desktop-bound thread would need its own binding, kept in lockstep with thread C's (binding.rs), and every picture would have to carry its generation. It would also share the D3D11 immediate context and break the encoder's same-thread check (video/mod.rs check_thread). With R10-anchored-pacer, 2 ms hot polls already put capture within about 1 ms of the present (model).

not_worth_it.title: Rebuild the encoder at each frame-rate change so the nominal rate always matches (airhand encoder/mod.rs:308-315)
not_worth_it.reason: airhand's rate is a fixed user choice. pb-mapper's is adaptive (QoS, viewer cap, startup hold), and every rebuild costs an IDR. The nominal/pace mismatch is better fixed by the rate model (R10-mac-timestamp-rate-model). Per-frame-budget Media Foundation encoders already spend bpf per frame at any pace.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's presets: tie high frame rates to 1080p and default to 30 fps (presets.ts:12-20); or let Balanced follow the display up to 120
not_worth_it.reason:
pb-mapper fixes the resolution per session by design (J was rejected), and the Display menu already offers 1080p and 1440p. On the measured Mac, R10-mac-hevc-standard-rc reaches 120 at native size.

Making Balanced 120 by default is a policy trade, not an optimization: it doubles bandwidth and host and viewer power in every Balanced session. Smooth or Max fps 120 already give 120 on demand, and airhand's own default is 30.

not_worth_it.title: Frame rates above 120 (144/165/240 Hz)
not_worth_it.reason: Beyond airhand, whose range stops at 120 (docs/usage.md:229). It would need a new capability, because older hosts reject max_fps > 120 in VideoLimits::validate (video.rs:52-62). On the measured Mac, VideoToolbox cannot sustain even 120 above about 2560x1664 at low latency.

not_worth_it.title: 1 ms hot capture polls instead of 2 ms
not_worth_it.reason: Model at 120 with anchoring: mean capture wait 1.0 → 0.5 ms, for about 50% more capture calls (245 → 369 a second). Negligible next to the other items.

not_worth_it.title: VideoToolbox's PrioritizeEncodingSpeedOverQuality
not_worth_it.reason: Measured here: refused under low-latency rate control. With standard rate control, H.264 at 4K still gave 96.7 units/s with 36.8 ms dwell, no gain. airhand does not set it either.

not_worth_it.title: H.264 on VideoToolbox's standard rate control
not_worth_it.reason: Measured here: at 4K it pipelines deeply (dwell 37-39 ms, 93-97 units/s) and at 3024x1964 it runs at 25 ms. That is worse latency than low latency behind R10-mac-vt-feeder. Only H.265 gains from standard rate control.

not_worth_it.title: Raise capture/encode thread priority as airhand does (capture/mod.rs:729-739; macos.rs:336-340)
not_worth_it.reason: Item F was withdrawn after measurement: no gain under an all-core load on this Mac (docs/benchmarks/2026-11-24-desktop-pipeline). Nothing here removes that result. Windows stays unmeasured.

not_worth_it.title: macOS viewer: call textureFrameAvailable straight from the decoder thread instead of hopping to the main queue (ui/darwin/DesktopVideo.swift:797)
not_worth_it.reason: Flutter's contract runs MarkTextureFrameAvailable on the platform thread (shell/common/shell.cc:1346 DCHECK). With merged UI and platform threads the hop shares the queue with Dart, but how often it costs a frame at 120 Hz is unmeasured. Not proposed without a measurement.

not_worth_it.title: Linux: present the video natively beneath a transparent Flutter view, at the monitor's rate
not_worth_it.reason: Stock Flutter on Linux has no platform views. Its renderer differs by backend: a GL area on X11, a subsurface on Wayland in recent versions. Overlays and pointers would still draw at the 60 Hz fallback. It cannot be made to work reliably with the stock embedder, so R10-linux-viewer-present-60 takes the certain part.

not_worth_it.title: Clamp the pace to the host display's refresh (a 60 Hz host for a 120 Hz viewer)
not_worth_it.reason: Per-frame-budget encoders spend bpf per frame whatever the nominal rate, and the timestamp model spends bpf x pace per second, so bandwidth matches expectation. The only cost is cold polls at 120 a second instead of 60 on a still Windows desktop.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's jitter buffer and audio/video sync (client/src/lib/jitter.ts, avsync.ts)
not_worth_it.reason: It delays video to line up with audio, adding latency. pb-mapper streams no audio.

not_worth_it.title: airhand's refine pass, re-encoding the last frame after motion stops (pipeline.rs:9-14, 33-38)
not_worth_it.reason: That is H (static refinement), a quality item for still pictures. It neither limits nor raises 120 fps motion.

critique.area: R10: 120 fps end to end (Windows and macOS hosts; Windows, macOS and Linux viewers)

reviews.corrected_design:
1. Prerequisite: R10-mac-vt-feeder. Standard RC needs two pictures in flight to reach 120; depth 1 gave 64-74 units/s.

2. The switch is dynamic and for H.265 only. Every Encoder starts with low latency, as today. The feeder counts encoded units and mailbox replacements per second. The rule, a pure function with a unit test: over a 1 s window with pace >= 0.9 x nominal, units < 0.95 x pace and replacements >= nominal/10. When it holds, MacVideo rebuilds the Encoder once at the next submit with low_latency = false, carrying an IDR. It logs `macos_encoder_low_latency_dropped` {units, pace, dwell_p50, width, height}. The mode never switches back during that Encoder's life (a new context builds LL again).
   Optional fast path: start in standard mode when width x height x nominal > 600 Mpx/s, above the LL capacity measured here. That saves the first second.

3. In standard mode:
   - never set kVTCompressionPropertyKey_DataRateLimits, in build() or in set_bitrate();
   - set AverageBitRate = encoder_bps x STD_RATE_FACTOR. The constant is fixed from the ported test; start at 0.75. Here, 0.7 gave 0.86-1.0x of the intended rate.
   - Encoder keeps its mode, so set_bitrate applies the factor and skips the cap.
   - Keep the H.264 profile and every other property unchanged.

4. Rate model unchanged: nominal plus the existing latch.

5. Port the harness as the ignored test `video_toolbox_120` in platform/macos/tests.rs, using production settings: wall pts, Encoder::with_low_latency, the feeder.
   - Sizes 2560x1440, 2560x1664, 3024x1964, 3840x2160; paces 60 and 120 at nominal 120.
   - Both codecs; LL, and standard with DataRateLimits on and off; STD_RATE_FACTOR 1.0, 0.85 and 0.75.
   - Scroll and grain content, with kVTCompressionPropertyKey_CalculateMeanSquaredError for PSNR.
   - Print units/s, dwell p50/p95, encode() call p50, produced/target and PSNR.

6. Docs: the macOS hosting paragraph (remote-desktop.md:1303-1322) and the Mac note under 'Encoder rate model per GPU' (LL below the knee, standard RC without the cap above it, the switch event). Add a docs/benchmarks record of the quiet run.
reviews.invariant_risks:
- No wire, capability, helper or FFI change.
- Without the cap, a unit after a pause can be large: L measured 3.4 Mbit for H.265 at 4K even with the cap. Send credit, the hand-off bounds and the 4 MiB access-unit limit still bound it.
- The switch costs one IDR.
- Other Apple chips are unmeasured; the dynamic rule adapts to a lower knee, and the fast-path constant must stay above any chip's LL capacity.

reviews.factual_errors:
- 3456x2234 is not an encoded size: a 16-inch MacBook Pro encodes 3340x2160.
- The design is internally inconsistent. "set_bitrate takes the same lock, so the session is touched by one caller thread at a time" does not serialize anything when encode_frame runs outside that lock. If the lock were held across encode_frame, thread C would block up to about 15 ms inside set_rate, which runs before every capture (native.rs:213-216). That would reintroduce the stall.
- Otherwise confirmed here with vt120b and r10rev_vtq2 (notes/r10rev_out1.txt, out2, out4): the LL encode call takes
  - 14.2-14.6 ms at 3840x2160, 100% of wall time at pace 120 and 87-88% at 60;
  - 8.06 ms at 2560x1664 (97%);
  - 7.2 ms at 2560x1440.
- At 3024x1964 the call returns at once, but depth 4 gives 94 units/s at 38.7 ms, against 94.8 at 17.2 ms with depth 2.
reviews.effect_assessment:
Real for most Mac hosts.

Input latency: wherever the encoded height is 16-aligned (1440p and 1664-line panels, 4K/5K externals at 2160, MacBook Air 13), thread C sits inside VTCompressionSessionEncodeFrame for 7-15 ms per frame. Input queued meanwhile waits for it (worker.rs:828-857), against the documented p99 <= 5 ms gate.

Dwell: wherever VideoToolbox is slower than the pace (3024x1964 at 120), dwell halves at the same throughput.

It does not raise LL throughput at 4K (about 70 fps); R10-mac-hevc-standard-rc does that.
reviews.corrected_design:
As proposed, with these changes.

1. Every VideoToolbox session call happens on the feeder thread: EncodeFrame, AverageBitRate/DataRateLimits and ForceKeyFrame. No lock is held across a VT call.
   - Thread C's set_bitrate only stores `pending_bitrate` in Shared.state and signals the condvar. The feeder applies it before its next EncodeFrame, or at once when idle.
   - Drop sets stop, joins the feeder, then invalidates.

2. Mailbox replacement:
   - keyframe = old || new;
   - duplicate = old && new, so a liveness repeat never hides a fresh picture from the unique counts;
   - at = the new picture's mailbox time.
   Pending.at is the mailbox time, so encode_us and late() include the mailbox wait. pts comes from `at` with the existing +1 rule.

3. VT_DEPTH is 2, because standard-RC H.265 needs 2. For LL, measure depth 1 against depth 2 through the feeder: with a mailbox, depth 1 may keep throughput at about 11 ms dwell instead of 17. Allow a per-mode depth if it does.
   const _: () = assert!(VT_DEPTH + 1 < ENCODER_DEPTH).

4. pending() = in-session + ready + a filled mailbox + failure.

5. Counters (units and replaced pictures per second, peak in_session) go into a once-a-second debug event `macos_encoder_load`. R10-mac-hevc-standard-rc's switch rule reads the same counters.

6. An EncodeFrame error, or a feeder panic caught by a guard, sets state.failure and wakes thread C. drain() returns it as today.

7. The feeder runs at user-interactive QoS.

8. Tests on synthetic IOSurfaces:
   - the researcher's list;
   - set_bitrate returns in under 1 ms while the feeder is inside a 14 ms 4K call;
   - a duplicate never replaces a fresh picture's uniqueness.
reviews.invariant_risks:
- Thread C still calls its Backend statically.
- No per-frame allocation or spawn: one thread per encoder, and the mailbox holds a retained CVPixelBuffer.
- SCK QUEUE_DEPTH 6 still covers 2 in the session + 1 mailbox + 1 latest + 1 being delivered.
- skipped_ticks no longer show a slow Mac encoder; the replacement counter does. Update the docs that describe ENCODER_DEPTH for macOS.

reviews.factual_errors:
1. The effect is broader than "a display a hair faster than the grid, about half of devices". Thread C's grid period is 1 s/120 truncated to whole nanoseconds, so a display at exactly the nominal rate keeps the phase it started with. Every host pays a random phase at session start, mean about P/2 while content moves. It lasts until ppm-level clock drift moves it, which takes minutes, and hosts whose display runs faster than the grid pay it for good.
   The E-round model (notes/r9/anchor2.out) shows this:
   - 60.000 Hz at pace 60: 5.84 ms on the grid, 1.01 ms anchored;
   - 120.02 Hz at pace 120: 2.85 ms, 1.00 ms;
   - only slower displays (59.94 or 119.9 Hz) are already near 1 ms.

2. The ScreenCaptureKit stamp needs neither the CMSync feature nor host-clock conversion. The Instant at which stream_did_output stores the picture is exactly when thread C could take it.

3. An anchored pace of 59 follows a faster source only up to 59 x 64/63 = 59.94. It does not replace R10-win-viewer-exact-refresh.
reviews.corrected_design:
As proposed (E phase 2), with these changes.

1. pacer.rs, as designed:
   - earliest() = next until anchored, then max(next - P/4, last + 3/4 P);
   - consume(now, presented: Option<Instant>): None keeps today's rule byte for byte; a stamp after the capture's completion is clamped to it, and one older than a period counts as None;
   - Some(at): base = if at >= next - P/4 { max(at, next - P/64) } else { next }; next = base + P.

2. macOS: take Instant::now() under the existing lock in stream_did_output and store it in Latest. take() returns it only for a fresh picture, and MacVideo::presented_at exposes it. No CMSync.

3. Windows: convert LastPresentTime by its QueryPerformanceCounter age, as airhand's clock.rs:42-76 does. Add Win32_System_Performance to the windows features. Store it beside latest_pending, and have the Encoder expose the stamp of the last Submitted. A stamp in the future or older than 1 s is dropped.

4. Plumbing:
   - Backend gets the provided method submitted_picture_at() -> None, forwarded by Box, PlatformBackend/NativeBackend, RemoteBackend and examples/input_acceptance/guarded.rs;
   - VideoSource gets presented_at();
   - worker/capture.rs: capture_at() uses earliest(); the submit path calls consume(now, backend.submitted_picture_at()); the skip path passes None; the drain long-poll bound uses capture_at(). Liveness and keyframe repeats pass None.

5. Helper: HELPER_PROTOCOL 11 with both pipe names moved to .v11.
   - Response gains presented_ago_us: Option<u32>, serde default, omitted when None. The helper computes it just before it writes the response.
   - client.rs checks it is at most 1 s and converts it at absorb time.
   - Bump once, together with R10-encoder-throughput-cap's `full` field.

6. Trace a once-a-second debug event `desktop_capture_pacing` with p50/p95 of submit time minus stamp (worker/window.rs). video_bench mirrors the pacer.

7. Docs: reword rule 2 (remote-desktop.md:1219-1221) and the capture paragraph.
reviews.invariant_risks:
- HELPER_PROTOCOL changes together with both .v<n> pipe names, and background-service users get the helper update prompt.
- The provided Backend method is a semver-minor SDK change.
- Zero cost: one Option<Instant> per picture, no allocation.
- A dated source may run up to 1/64 above the pace.
- Documented rule 2 changes.

No effect on other modes or platforms.

reviews.effect_assessment:
Asking for 60 halves host encoding, bandwidth, and viewer decoding and CPU conversion. On a Linux viewer whose decoder keeps up with 120, it also has two costs:
- the picture Flutter's unsynchronised 60 Hz tick takes gets older: its age goes from uniform over [0, 8.3] ms to [0, 16.7] ms, about 4.2 ms more on average;
- it brings back the 60/60 beat between the host's capture grid and Flutter's free-running fallback timer. When the arrival phase sits near the tick, LAN and decode jitter turn into repeats and skips, for minutes at ppm drift. A 120 fps source hides this.

A viewer that cannot keep up is already held down by the backlog-gated fps cap (viewer/fps_cap.rs), so the cap only trades smoothness and latency for CPU on viewers that have the CPU. That is not a net gain. The CPU part is better removed by converting on the GPU (missed item R10-linux-gpu-convert).

missed.design:
Today the GStreamer streaming thread runs videoconvert to RGBA (up to 4 threads) for every decoded picture (ui/linux/runner/desktop_video_gst.cc:550-577). FlPixelBufferTexture then uploads 4 bytes per pixel of the picture Flutter takes (desktop_video.cc:245-280). Flutter's Linux embedder presents at most 60 frames a second, so at 120 fps half of the conversions are discarded, and at 4K each upload is 33 MB.

Change:
1. appsink caps NV12 in system memory; drop videoconvert from the pipeline, keeping it only as a fallback when the decoder cannot negotiate NV12.
2. The texture becomes an FlTextureGL. Its populate (raster thread, Flutter's GL context current):
   - acquires the newest picture;
   - uploads Y as GL_R8 and UV as GL_RG8 (1.5 bytes per pixel);
   - renders BT.709 limited range to RGBA into the texture it returns, through a small FBO pass with the Windows runner's matrix.
   Only the picture shown is converted.
3. FLUTTER_LINUX_RENDERER=software keeps today's path; it draws no external texture anyway.
4. The decoder state, revision and receipt rules are unchanged: the acquisition stays the presentation receipt.
5. CI's linux-app job builds it. The clip decode test checks the colour of known patches against today's output (±2 levels).

- A 120 fps stream then costs the Linux viewer decoding only, so it keeps the lower present age a 120 fps source gives (about 4 ms on average) without the CPU that R10-linux-viewer-present-60 tried to save.

prs.name: capture-anchored-pacing
prs.title: Anchor thread C's capture pacing to when the display presented (E phase 2, in process on Windows and Mac) and add the capture seams later PRs use
prs.protocol_changes: None on the desktop wire (ALPN stays pb-mapper/desktop/2) and none on the helper pipe: HELPER_PROTOCOL and the .v10 pipe names stay, RemoteBackend reports no present stamp until helper-push adds one. Public SDK, semver-minor: provided Backend methods submitted_picture, capture_poll and video_paused, and the Presented type.
prs.design:
Why. Thread C's pacer (pacer.rs) lays ticks on an even grid unrelated to when the display presents. When the pace equals the present rate (Balanced 60 on a 60 Hz panel, Smooth 120 on 120 Hz, a ProMotion Mac) a picture waits up to a period for the next tick (model: mean 5.8-7.2 ms at 60 Hz and 2.9 ms at 120 Hz, falling to about 1 ms) and the grid drops one present per drift cycle, a visible hitch. airhand anchors its timeline on the present: client/src-tauri/src/host/pace.rs:34-50 (an early window of P/4, creep of at most P/64), stamps from host/capture/dxgi.rs:677-679 converted by host/clock.rs:42-76. This PR does it in process on both hosts (the helper path follows in helper-push) and adds every thread C seam the later PRs need, so none of them re-touches the five #[deny(clippy::missing_trait_methods)] impls.

1. Pacer (pacer.rs). Add `anchored: bool`. `earliest()` = if anchored { max(next - P/4, last + 3P/4) } else { next }. `consume(now, presented: Option<Instant>)`: None keeps today's rule byte for byte and clears `anchored`; a stamp later than now is clamped to now; a stamp older than one period counts as None; Some(at): base = if at >= next - P/4 { max(at, next - P/64) } else { next }; next = base + P; anchored = true. Keep the 3/4-period floor after a stall, ticks skipped only for backpressure, and the long-run bound of pace x 64/63. set_pace is unchanged.

2. Seams. All are provided methods whose defaults keep today's behaviour, each forwarded in Box (backend.rs:228), PlatformBackend and NativeBackend (native.rs:114 and 422), RemoteBackend (oop/client.rs:237) and examples/input_acceptance/guarded.rs:35.
- `pub struct Presented { pub at: Instant, pub presents: u32 }` (Copy, #[non_exhaustive], exported with the other backend types) and `Backend::submitted_picture(&self) -> Option<Presented>`: the present time of the picture the last capture_video submitted and how many presents it covered (1 = none skipped). None for liveness and keyframe repeats and for undated pictures. RemoteBackend returns None.
- `Backend::capture_poll(&self) -> Option<Duration> { self.drain_poll() }`: how often thread C re-polls an armed pull capture. capture_poll_after and the input hot-poll path (worker/capture.rs ~143-176) use it instead of drain_poll, so a source can push encoder output while its capture is still polled (win-mf-output-events relies on this).
- `Backend::video_paused(&mut self, paused: bool) {}`: thread C calls it with true on the transition into the all-paused branch (worker/capture.rs ~236) and with false on the way out, before the resume capture. RemoteBackend implements an explicit no-op (DXGI is pull and runs nothing while paused; no helper message). mac-capture-cadence implements it.
- VideoSource (platform/mod.rs): `fn presented(&self) -> Option<Presented> { None }`; `fn drain_poll(&self) -> Option<Duration> { Self::DRAIN }`; `const CAPTURE_POLL: Option<Duration> = Self::DRAIN;` with `fn capture_poll(&self) -> Option<Duration> { Self::CAPTURE_POLL }` (instance methods so one encoder instance can fall back to polling); `fn paused(&mut self, paused: bool) {}`; `fn retune(&mut self, display: &Display, limits: VideoLimits) -> Result<bool> { Ok(false) }`. PlatformBackend forwards each to the open source and uses the consts when none is open.
- configure_video (native.rs:151-156): validate the limits; if a source is open and `retune(&context.display, limits)` returns Ok(true), keep it, otherwise drop it as today; store the limits either way. A context change still rebuilds through capture_video's context compare (native.rs:191-206). Thread C still sets keyframe on a limits change.
- platform/synthetic.rs: SynVideo implements retune (true for an fps-only change, false for a size change) and gains a dated push mode (pictures stamped at a configurable rate and drift, waking its Waker) for the tests.

3. Thread C (worker/capture.rs, worker.rs; static dispatch only, Engine<B: Backend>). capture_at() uses pacer.earliest(). The submit path calls consume(now, backend.submitted_picture().map(|p| p.at)); the backpressure and skip paths pass None. The helper drain long-poll bound (HELPER_DRAIN_WAIT_MAX at worker/capture.rs:366) uses capture_at() instead of pacer.next().

4. macOS (platform/macos/capture.rs, video.rs). In the ScreenCaptureKit output callback, under the existing Latest lock (capture.rs:138-144), store `arrived = Instant::now()` and count Complete pictures, Idle samples and pictures replaced before a take in capture::Shared (no allocation). take() returns, for a fresh picture, its arrival and the number of Complete pictures since the last take; MacVideo::presented returns them for a fresh submit and None for repeats. SCStreamFrameInfoDisplayTime feeds diagnostics only, converted by its age against mach_absolute_time with the cached timebase (airhand host/clock.rs:29-40); no CMSync feature.

5. Windows in process (platform/windows/video/mod.rs and mod.rs; add Win32_System_Performance to the windows crate features). Convert LastPresentTime by its age: QueryPerformanceCounter now minus the stamp, with QueryPerformanceFrequency cached in a OnceLock; a negative age (read-order race) counts as 0, an age over 1 s gives None; result Instant::now() - age (std's Instant is QPC-based on Windows, so this is exact up to read skew). Keep `latest_at` and the summed AccumulatedFrames beside latest_pending; a picture left pending by Full or an empty allocator keeps its old stamp and consume ignores it once it is older than a period. Fresh pictures use the present Instant, kept strictly increasing, for pts_us and the sample duration; repeats use now. Statistics and video_bench gain `coalesced_presents` (sum of AccumulatedFrames - 1 over fresh acquires). First frame (R3-first-frame; airhand host/capture/dxgi.rs:632-633): in acquire (video/mod.rs ~571-618), when `latest` is None and the resource is present, copy it as a new image whatever LastPresentTime says, leave it undated, and log once per encoder at debug the first acquire's LastPresentTime and AccumulatedFrames. video_bench mirrors the new pacer and prints present-to-submit p50/p95.

6. Diagnostics. A once-a-second debug event `desktop_capture_pacing` from worker/window.rs roll(): present-to-submit wait p50/p95 (submit Instant - Presented.at), dated share of submits, captures/s, presents/s, coalesced presents/s (sum of presents - 1), empty polls/s. Fixed buffers, no allocation per frame.

7. Docs. Reword rule 2 of 'Video pipeline and performance model' (docs/remote-desktop.md ~1218-1222) and the host capture paragraphs, keeping its sub-rules (skips only for backpressure, the long-run rate, the 3/4-period floor, creep of at most P/64); the constants table; the new Backend methods. No model figures in docs; the CHANGELOG bullet says what changes and gains figures only from the device runs.

prs.name: mac-wake-display
prs.title: Mac host: wake a sleeping, unlocked display when a viewer's capture starts, resumes or finds no picture
prs.protocol_changes: None.
prs.design:
Why. The Mac host keeps the display awake only while it captures (platform/macos/timer.rs:28-40, NSActivity IdleDisplaySleepDisabled); it never wakes a display that is already asleep, and nothing calls IOPMAssertionDeclareUserActivity or checks CGDisplayIsAsleep. ScreenCaptureKit delivers no picture from a sleeping display, and input is admitted only for a presented frame produced within 2 s (auth.rs:11, 74-80), so the viewer cannot even wake the Mac by moving the mouse: the session shows nothing and rebuilds capture in a loop until someone touches the Mac. airhand wakes the display (client/src-tauri/src/host/power.rs:232-250, like `caffeinate -u`) and skips a closed lid (power.rs:255-260).

1. New platform/macos/power.rs.
- extern IOPMAssertionDeclareUserActivity and IOPMAssertionRelease with #[link(name = "IOKit", kind = "framework")], following desktop.rs:23-28 (objc2-io-kit's pwr_mgt would be a new direct crate).
- A pure `WakeLimiter` with an injected Instant: at most one declaration every 2 s. Build and test it on every platform, like geometry.rs (mod.rs:18-30).
- `wake(ids) -> bool`: for each id where CGDisplayIsAsleep (CGDisplayConfiguration feature, already on), declare kIOPMUserActiveLocal activity, reusing the returned assertion id as the header asks (a static Mutex<(Option<Instant>, IOPMAssertionID)>). Returns whether any display was asleep.
- Skip a built-in display (CGDisplayIsBuiltin) while the lid is closed: read AppleClamshellState from IOPMrootDomain as airhand power.rs:255-260 does; otherwise the panel lights behind the lid for about 10 s and goes dark again in a cycle.
2. Call sites, each only after desktop::available() has passed (unlocked, on the console); a locked Mac stays dark by design.
- (a) Macos::open (mod.rs ~153), before MacDesktop::open: if any online display (CGGetOnlineDisplayList) is asleep, wake it, then poll every 100 ms for up to 3 s for the selected display to become active (airhand waits up to 3 s before Hello).
- (b) MacVideo::open (video.rs:50-74), before Stream::start: wake(display.id). This also covers a resume, whose capture reopens here.
- (c) On MacVideo's no-picture failure (video.rs:96-103), or a DisplayLost from capture::display, while CGDisplayIsAsleep(id): wake it and fail with CaptureFailed 'the display is asleep; waking it'; the 200 ms retry then reopens.
3. Release the reused assertion id when the last timer guard is released (timer.rs:43-53).
4. Docs: 'Sharing a Mac' and the macOS host paragraph in docs/remote-desktop.md; the user-guide pair (English and Chinese together) where it describes a sleeping Mac; a CHANGELOG bullet.
(Merged duplicate R4-mac-host-wake-display: its resume case is (b), its no-frame case is (c) with the 2 s limiter.)

CI rust-macos-desktop and nat-traversal.yml (Linux: `cargo build -p pb-mapper-cli --features port-mapping`, `sudo python3 scripts/test_nat_traversal.py --binary target/debug/pb-mapper`).

Before: no presented frame and repeated desktop_capture failures; after: time to the first presented frame from the feedback log, and `pmset -g assertions` shows the user-activity assertion. prs.name: mac-session-check-cache
prs.title: Mac host: reuse a passing session and geometry check for 16 ms across capture and cursor verifies
prs.protocol_changes: None.
prs.design:
Why. Every Mac capture and cursor verify reads the session dictionary and display geometry from WindowServer (about 48 us). View-only at 60 fps that is about 120 capture plus 125 cursor verifies a second, 13-14 ms of thread C CPU a second plus WindowServer's side.

1. platform/mod.rs Desktop gains provided methods defaulting to today's behaviour: `fn prepare_recent(&mut self, on_switch: impl FnOnce()) -> Result<()> { self.prepare(on_switch) }` and `fn display_matches_recent(&mut self, expected: &Display) -> Result<bool> { self.display_matches(expected) }`.
2. native.rs: `verify(expected, recent: bool)`. capture_video (~188, ~218) and cursor (~257, ~261) pass recent = true; input_in_context (~278) passes false. display() and context() stay fresh, so the 100 ms context check and every input read WindowServer: the injection boundary is unchanged.
3. MacDesktop (platform/macos/desktop.rs) overrides both with a small pure `Reuse` policy struct (injected Instant), placed so it builds and tests on every platform like geometry.rs: a passing session check and the Geometry it read are reused while now < checked + 16 ms; a failure is never cached and clears the reuse; every fresh prepare, display or display_matches call refreshes it.
4. Unit tests of the policy on every platform: call counts, failures never cached, input always fresh.
5. Docs: 'inside each capture' becomes 'within 16 ms of each capture'; the injection-boundary wording stays.

CI rust-macos-desktop, rust-windows-desktop (the trait change compiles on Windows), nat-traversal.yml.
